scope: fleet adversarial re-audit (1 dedicated agent per service, target 20, evidence-disciplined)

findings.title: Group-by / export query runs a FULL rollup-table scan for EVERY bucket in range
findings.detail: RollupStore.scan_prefix() is implemented as `scan_all(_ROLLUPS, 100_000)` then a Python-side startswith() filter (stores.py:104-110). QueryService._grouped() calls scan_prefix() once PER BUCKET in the range: `for b in bucket_keys: ... scan_prefix(prefix)` (query_service.py:95-97). range_keys() for granularity='hour' over MAX_QUERY_RANGE_DAYS=400 yields ~9600 buckets (buckets.py:41-59, config MAX_QUERY_RANGE_DAYS=400). So a single authenticated /api/v1/analytics/query (or /export) with dimensions triggers up to ~9600 full scans of the entire cross-tenant rollups collection, each pulling/deserialising up to 100k JSONB rows.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller with analytics.read POSTs /api/v1/analytics/query {metric, granularity:'hour', dimensions:['url'], start_ts:T, end_ts:T+400d}. The service performs ~9600 sequential `SELECT value FROM kv_store WHERE collection='rollups' ORDER BY key LIMIT 100000`, each materialising the whole rollups table into Python and re-filtering. One request saturates the DB pool and event loop; a handful of concurrent requests wedge the service (readyz flips). check_groups() only fires AFTER the entire groups dict is built, so it provides no early cost cap.
findings.fix: Give the DataStore a real prefix/range read (e.g. `WHERE collection=$1 AND key >= $prefix AND key < $prefix||'\xff' ORDER BY key`) served by the PK btree, and call it ONCE per query with the tenant|metric|granularity prefix and the full bucket range, not once per bucket. Enforce the group/scan cap inside the store read, not after building the dict.

findings.title: scan_prefix truncates at 100k rows ordered by key, silently dropping whole tenants' rollups (memory/postgres divergence)
findings.detail: scan_prefix relies on scan_all(_ROLLUPS, _ROLLUP_MAX=100_000). Postgres scan_all is `... ORDER BY key LIMIT 100000` (postgres.py:236-249); rollup keys are `tenant|metric|granularity|bucket|dims` (models.py:83-85), so ordering by key groups rows alphabetically by tenant. Memory scan_all returns insertion order (memory.py:87-90) — a different, non-deterministic subset. Neither reads a tenant's rows in isolation.
findings.failure_scenario: Tenant 'acme' (alphabetically early) accumulates >100k rollup rows. Under Postgres, scan_all returns only 'acme' rows up to the cap; every OTHER tenant's group-by query calls scan_prefix, whose 100k window never reaches their prefix, so their grouped queries silently return {} / group_count:0 — a wrong answer, not an error, and one noisy tenant degrades all others. The same query on the memory adapter returns a different partial set, so tests that pass in memory hide the prod bug.
findings.fix: Replace whole-collection scan_all+filter with an indexed key-range read scoped to the requested tenant|metric prefix (see r2-01); a per-tenant range read is bounded by that tenant's cells and cannot be evicted by another tenant's volume.

findings.title: Idempotency key (event_seen) is GLOBAL, not tenant-scoped — one tenant's event_id suppresses another's
findings.detail: EventStore.reserve() claims `_SEEN` keyed by the raw event_id only (stores.py:35-38: `cas(_SEEN, event_id, 0, ...)`). event_id is caller-supplied per EventIn.id (internal.py:41) and tenant is a separate caller-supplied field (internal.py:43). Nothing namespaces the dedupe record by tenant. This is exactly the tenant-scoped-idempotency invariant the platform learned elsewhere (see MEMORY: tenant-scoped-idempotency).
findings.failure_scenario: Tenant A ingests event id='evt-123'. Tenant B (or a different upstream producer that reuses sequential/short ids like 'evt-123', or the flag.exposed/job.* bus which numbers per-source) ingests its own distinct event with id='evt-123'. reserve() finds the key taken and returns {duplicate:true}; tenant B's event is dropped with zero writes — permanent undercount for B, caused entirely by A. A malicious/compromised internal caller can pre-reserve a victim tenant's predictable event_ids to blackhole their analytics.
findings.fix: Key the dedupe record by (tenant, event_id) — e.g. reserve(f"{len(tenant)}:{tenant}|{event_id}") — and update erasure._SEEN deletion to match. Length-prefix the tenant so keys cannot be forged to collide.

findings.title: reserve()-first ordering turns at-least-once delivery into at-most-once: a crash mid-ingest loses the event forever
findings.detail: ingest() reserves the event_id FIRST (ingest_service.py:77), THEN writes the raw event (line 88) and updates rollups (line 95/93). The reservation is committed before the counted work. If the process dies (or the rollup CAS path throws) after reserve() succeeds but before/while _update_rollups completes, the event is marked seen but never (fully) counted.
findings.failure_scenario: Bus delivers evt-9 (at-least-once). reserve() commits; pod is OOM-killed after events.add() but before _update_rollups finishes all granularities. The bus redelivers evt-9; reserve() now returns False -> {duplicate:true, zero writes}. The event is permanently absent from rollups (and possibly present in raw but missing hour/day/month cells), defeating the very at-least-once guarantee the module docstring claims to protect. Revenue events (payment.*) undercount MRR.
findings.fix: Make the unit atomic (write event+rollups+seen in one transaction) OR reserve LAST / use an idempotent upsert on rollups keyed by event_id contribution so redelivery re-applies safely. Reserve-then-work is only safe if the work is transactional with the reservation.

findings.title: Rollup CAS retry exhaustion silently drops the increment (undercount / sum drift on hot cells)
findings.detail: The read-modify-write CAS loop runs at most _cas_retries (default 8) attempts; if all 8 lose the race the `for _attempt in range(...)` loop simply ends with no write, no raise, no log (ingest_service.py:118-132). The comment at stores.py:89-93 even names the outcome ('the increment is lost — the undercount bug') but the caller never detects it.
findings.failure_scenario: A popular metric's no-dims total cell is the single hottest row (every event of that metric hits it at all 3 granularities). Under a burst, >8 concurrent ingests contend the same (key,version); losers past attempt 8 exit silently. count and sum are under-reported, and because sum is used for revenue aggregations the money figure drifts DOWN with no error surfaced. The batch endpoint (1000 events) makes bursts routine.
findings.fix: On retry exhaustion, raise (so the caller/bus retries the whole idempotent ingest) or fall back to an atomic server-side increment. Never let the loop fall through silently; at minimum emit a telemetry counter and fail the request so at-least-once redelivery recovers it.

findings.title: Subject identity persists in rollup HLL sketches (unsalted sha1) after DSAR erasure; ack falsely claims 'no subject in rollups'
findings.detail: Erasure deletes raw events but declares rollups contain no personal data and retains them (erasure.py:47-52, comment 'rollups are aggregates with no subject in them'). That is false: the HLL unique-count sketch stores, in sparse mode, the actual per-subject hashes — `_hash64 = int.from_bytes(sha1(subject).digest()[:8])` (hll.py:59-60, add() appends h to sketch['s'] at hll.py:94-97). These are UNSALTED 64-bit sha1 truncations of the subject id, embedded in every rollup cell the subject touched and never removed on erasure. Contrast core/pii.subject_ref which correctly uses HMAC-SHA256(PII_SALT,...) — the sketch path ignores PII_SALT entirely.
findings.failure_scenario: A subject is an email/phone/user-id. Even after /internal/privacy/erase runs, sketch['s'] in surviving rollups still holds sha1(email)[:8]. An attacker (or auditor) with rollup/backup access brute-forces the small email/phone space against the unsalted 8-byte hashes and re-identifies exactly which subjects were active in each (tenant,metric,hour) cell — reconstructing behaviour the DSAR promised was erased. The erasure ack reports already fully handled, so the violation is invisible.
findings.fix: Salt subject hashing in the sketch with PII_SALT (HMAC), and/or force sketches to dense mode (which stores only register maxima, not per-subject hashes) so no per-subject value is retained. Correct the erasure declaration: either scrub sparse sketches of the subject or document that dense sketches carry no recoverable identity.

findings.title: No finite-number validation on `value` — inf/nan permanently poisons a rollup's sum/histogram
findings.detail: value is summed into the rollup (r.sum += float(value), ingest_service.py:126) and fed to hist.add (line 130). The batch endpoint accepts events as untyped dict[str,Any] (internal.py:52) and coerces `float(e.get('value',0) or 0)` (ingest_service.py:139), so 'inf'/'-inf'/'nan' pass straight through. histogram._index(inf) computes math.ceil(math.log(inf/1e-3, 1.25)) which raises OverflowError (histogram.py:28-33). nan makes r.sum and hist min/max nan forever; the poisoned rollup row persists and every future query over that range returns nan/inf or 500s.
findings.failure_scenario: An internal producer (or a bug upstream) sends a batch event {id, name:'checkout', value:'inf'}. Either the ingest 500s on OverflowError inside histogram, or (nan) r.sum becomes nan. The rollup cell is written with nan; sum/avg/percentile queries for that metric/bucket now return nan indefinitely, and there is no path to repair it short of manual DB surgery, because raw events prune away.
findings.fix: Reject non-finite value at ingest (math.isfinite check -> 400) for both the typed and untyped (batch) paths before any accumulation; also validate the batch events through the same pydantic EventIn model instead of raw dicts.

findings.title: Cardinality cap is per-dimension, not per-combination — multi-prop events multiply stored cells past the cap
findings.detail: _dims_for admits each property key/value INDEPENDENTLY against MAX_DIMENSION_CARDINALITY (ingest_service.py:64-70, CardinalityStore.admit at stores.py:123-136). _update_rollups then writes ONE cell for the full combined dims dict (ingest_service.py:109, dim_sets=[{}]+[dims]). So with k properties each under the 1000-value cap, the distinct combined cells per bucket can reach up to 1000^k, none of which the cap prevents. The module docstring claims 'a group by url cannot fill the disk' but a group by (url,referrer,device) can.
findings.failure_scenario: A producer emits events with props {a:<1000 vals>, b:<1000 vals>, c:<1000 vals>} within the cap on each key. Each distinct (a,b,c) tuple creates a new rollup row at 3 granularities. Disk grows with distinct tuples (millions), exactly the explosion the cap advertises protection against, and then feeds r2-01/r2-02's full-table scans.
findings.fix: Cap on the COMBINED dimension tuple (admit the composite), or cap the number of distinct dim-combinations per (tenant,metric,bucket), spilling excess tuples to __other__. Limit the number of prop keys promoted to dimensions.

findings.title: No upper bound on event_time — future-dated events create unbounded, never-pruned future rollups
findings.detail: is_late() only checks lateness (now-et > max); a FUTURE event_time yields a negative delta, so late=False and it is bucketed as a normal event in a future bucket (ingest_service.py:80-95, buckets.is_late at buckets.py:75-76). prune_raw deletes only events with event_time < cutoff (ingest_service.py:149, stores.py:65-74), so future-dated raw events and their rollups are never pruned. `et = float(event_time) if event_time else now` also accepts negative timestamps (event_time=-1 -> 1969 bucket).
findings.failure_scenario: A producer (buggy clock, or malicious internal caller) sends value-bearing events with event_time = year 3000. They land in far-future rollup cells that no query range reaches (so they look 'lost') yet consume storage forever and evade retention pruning; enough of them contribute to the r2-02 100k eviction. A future-dated revenue event also silently disappears from current-period MRR.
findings.fix: Reject event_time beyond a small future skew (e.g. now + late_max_seconds) and reject non-positive timestamps; treat clearly-future events as an ingestion error, not a silent future bucket.

findings.title: Changing HLL_PRECISION or HISTOGRAM_BUCKETS poisons queries that merge across the change (ValueError -> 500)
findings.detail: Sketch precision/bucket-count is captured at ingest time from config and stored in each rollup (ingest_service.py:123,128,130). merge() raises ValueError if two sketches disagree on p (hll.py:112-113) or n (histogram.py:61-62). QueryService._aggregate merges all sketches in range unconditionally (query_service.py:139-148). There is no migration or precision-normalisation on read.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator raises HLL_PRECISION 12->14 (or HISTOGRAM_BUCKETS) to improve accuracy. Older rollups carry p=12, new ones p=14. Any 'unique' or 'percentile' query whose range spans the change date calls merge_all across mixed precisions -> ValueError -> 500. The failure is data-dependent (only ranges crossing the boundary), so it passes tests and surfaces later as intermittent 500s on real dashboards.
findings.fix: Down-convert to the lowest common precision on merge (HLL supports folding to a smaller p; histograms to a coarser n) instead of raising, or pin these values as frozen product identifiers guarded like PII_SALT.

findings.title: rollup_key/scan_prefix use unescaped delimiters (| , =) over caller-controlled tenant/metric/dim values
findings.detail: rollup_key joins with '|' and dim parts with ','/'=' (models.py:83-85) and scan_prefix matches the raw string prefix (stores.py:104-110); _grouped rebuilds gkey with ','/'=' (query_service.py:104). tenant, metric (EventIn.name), and dimension values are caller-supplied strings up to 200 chars with no charset restriction (internal.py:41-47). None of these delimiters are escaped.
findings.failure_scenario: An internal caller ingests metric='m|day|2024-01-01|-' or tenant containing '|', crafting a rollup key that structurally collides with another cell (or, if tenant is attacker-influenced, another tenant's cell), corrupting counts. A dim value containing ',' or '=' also corrupts the _grouped gkey and the _matches filter parsing, mislabelling groups. Confidence is SPECULATIVE because the trailing-delimiter prefixes blunt some collisions and tenant is normally set by a trusted caller — but the fields are unvalidated.
findings.fix: Percent-encode or length-prefix each key segment in rollup_key (and the CardinalityStore key), and validate metric/dimension names against a safe charset at ingest. Never build a security boundary from unescaped user strings joined by delimiters.

findings.title: get_many issues one sequential DB round-trip per bucket (up to ~9600) for a single non-grouped query
findings.detail: RollupStore.get_many loops keys and awaits store.get() one at a time (stores.py:95-102). For granularity='hour' over MAX_QUERY_RANGE_DAYS=400 that is ~9600 serial `SELECT ... WHERE key=$1` acquisitions from a pool sized max ~5 (postgres.py:74). range_keys builds the full key list first (buckets.py:41-59).
findings.failure_scenario: A caller runs a 400-day hourly count query. The service serially executes ~9600 point reads on a tiny pool; the request occupies a pool slot for its whole duration and blocks other requests. A few such queries exhaust the pool (health flips to 'pool exhausted'). No per-request key-count cap exists beyond the time-range check.
findings.fix: Batch the keyed reads (single `WHERE key = ANY($1)` / IN query, or a key-range read) and/or cap the number of buckets per query (reject hour granularity beyond N days).

findings.title: `subject` is never PII-filtered — a raw email/phone is stored in events and unsalted-hashed into rollups
findings.detail: _filter_props scrubs PII_SUSPECT keys from props (ingest_service.py:54-62) but subject bypasses it entirely: it is written verbatim into Event.subject (ingest_service.py:86-87, models.py:28) and fed to hll.add unsalted (r2-06). Producers routinely pass a user id that may itself be an email or phone as the unique-count identity.
findings.failure_scenario: A producer sets subject='ahom59816@gmail.com' (or a phone). The raw email is persisted in the events collection (pruned only after RAW_RETENTION_DAYS=90) and its unsalted sha1 is embedded in surviving rollups indefinitely (see r2-06). Analytics thus becomes an unintended PII store, contradicting the module's 'analytics is where PII leaks' stance which it only enforces on props.
findings.fix: Pseudonymise subject at ingest via core.pii.subject_ref(PII_SALT, tenant, subject) before storing it in events and before hashing into the sketch, so no raw identifier is retained and the sketch hash is salted and tenant-scoped.

findings.title: CardinalityStore.admit read-modify-writes the value list with no CAS (lost update)
findings.detail: admit() does get -> append -> put with no version check (stores.py:123-136). Two concurrent admits for different new values of the same (tenant,metric,dim) both read the list, each append their own value, and the second put overwrites the first, losing one admitted value.
findings.failure_scenario: Two ingests concurrently introduce new dim values 'x' and 'y' under the cap. Both read values=[...], A writes [...,'x'], B writes [...,'y'] (dropping 'x'). Later events with 'x' see it absent, re-admit it (slipping the cap by one) or, once at cap, spill 'x' to __other__ even though it was legitimately admitted — a mis-bucketed dimension. The code comments acknowledge this as acceptable; flagged for completeness as it can also let the cap be exceeded under sustained contention.
findings.fix: Use the datastore CAS (as rollups do) on the cardinality row, or model the set as append-only members so concurrent adds do not clobber each other.

findings.title: ingest_batch is not atomic: a bad event mid-batch 500s the request after earlier events are already committed
findings.detail: ingest_batch iterates and ingests events one by one (ingest_service.py:134-142); a raised exception (e.g. KeyError on missing id/name -> internal.py:102, or the OverflowError from r2-07) aborts the loop after prior events are durably written and reserved. The endpoint returns 500 with no indication of how many of the 1000 were applied.
findings.failure_scenario: A 1000-event batch has a malformed event at index 500. Events 0-499 are ingested and their ids reserved; the request 500s. The producer retries the whole batch; 0-499 are now duplicates (correctly skipped) but the caller cannot tell partial success from total failure, and any non-idempotent side effect (gen bump) already ran. If the producer instead drops the batch on 500, 0-499 are double-counted only if ids differ on retry.
findings.fix: Validate every event up front (reuse EventIn) and either apply the batch transactionally or return a per-event result (accepted/duplicate/failed indexes) with 207-style semantics instead of a bare 500.

findings.title: Retention purge is not mutually exclusive with concurrent append — re-seal + set_head orphans and breaks the chain
findings.detail: purge() runs a multi-await read-modify-write with NO lock: (1) events=iterate(partition); (2) delete expired; (3) re-seal EVERY retained event in place (replace(), lines 321-326 change prev_hash/hash of survivors including the current head event); (4) set_head(last_seq, prev). Nothing serialises this against record(). The cas version on _META only protects the head cell; it does NOT protect purge's blind re-hashing of already-stored survivor rows against an event appended after purge's iterate() read.
findings.failure_scenario: Partition head at seq N (hash H_N_old). A concurrent record() lands fully: advance_head cas(V) succeeds -> head (N+1, H_{N+1}=seal(H_N_old,...)), append_event writes event N+1 with prev_hash=H_N_old. Meanwhile purge() re-seals event N to H_N_new (!= H_N_old) and set_head(last_seq, H_kept_last) with last_seq<=N. Now: event N+1 exists with prev_hash=H_N_old but the stored event N hash is H_N_new, and head_seq=last_seq<N+1. verify() reports 'broken chain (prev_hash mismatch)' at N+1 AND 'chain does not reach the recorded head'. The chain is permanently corrupted and a real (untampered) event is reported as tampering. A nightly retention cron overlapping normal ingest triggers this.
findings.fix: Serialise purge against append per partition (an asyncio.Lock is insufficient across pods — use a datastore-level guard: e.g. bump _META version at purge START so any append in-flight fails its cas, take events strictly below a frozen cutoff seq, and re-verify head version is unchanged before set_head; or run purge in a real DB transaction that also re-reads the head). At minimum, re-fetch the head after re-anchoring and abort/retry if seq advanced.

findings.title: Append is two un-transacted datastore writes (advance_head then append_event); a failure between them permanently bricks the chain
findings.detail: record() advances the head cas FIRST (line 66) and writes the event row SECOND (line 67, append_event -> store.put), in two independent datastore operations with no transaction and no compensating rollback of the head. The docstring claims a crash here 'shows as a (detectable) missing tail, never as two events sharing a seq' — but it is worse than a missing tail.
findings.failure_scenario: advance_head commits (head=(N,H_N)) then append_event raises (connection drop, row too large, pod killed) so event N is never written. The next successful record() reads head (N,H_N), builds event N+1 with prev_hash=H_N and seq N+1, and appends. verify() now walks ...,N-1,N+1: at N+1 prev_hash=H_N but running prev=H_{N-1} -> 'broken chain' forever. A single transient put error, not even a crash, cements an unrecoverable break that reads as tampering.
findings.fix: Make the head advance and event insert atomic: write the event row FIRST then advance the head (a crash then leaves an orphan row with no head reference, which the next append/verify can tolerate or reconcile), or wrap both in one postgres transaction. If keeping head-first, roll back the head on append_event failure and never let a subsequent append build on a head whose event row is absent.

findings.title: Crash after append but before idempo_commit yields a DUPLICATE chain event on stale take-over
findings.detail: record_idempotent() reserves the key, calls record() (appends the event), THEN idempo_commit() (lines 119-121). The stale take-over path (lines 111-117) assumes a pending entry means 'reserver crashed mid-append' and re-runs record(). But there is a window where record() already appended the event and the process died before idempo_commit — the entry is still 'pending', never 'done'. There is no content-level dedup.
findings.failure_scenario: Caller sends idempotency_key=K. reserve wins, record() appends event seq=100, then the pod is killed before idempo_commit. Entry K stays state=pending. After AUDIT_INGEST_STALE_SECONDS a retry with K judges it stale, take_over cas succeeds, record() runs AGAIN and appends event seq=101 for the same action. Two events in the tamper-evident chain for one idempotent operation — defeating the guarantee the whole reserve/commit machinery exists to provide (contradicts the 'exactly one event is ever appended' claim at lines 19-20/83-85).
findings.fix: Commit the idempotency receipt atomically with the append (same transaction), or write the receipt as part of append_event, so 'event appended' and 'key done' can never diverge. Alternatively, before re-running record() on a stale take-over, look for an already-appended event carrying this key and return its receipt instead of appending.

findings.title: INTEGRITY_DRIVER=none is not refused in production; disables tamper-evidence while verify() still returns ok:true
findings.detail: assert_audit_config_ok() (lines 387-409) guards AUDIT_SINK_DRIVER=null in production but never checks INTEGRITY_DRIVER. main.py (lines 45-47) calls only assert_audit/pii/cors_config_ok. So INTEGRITY_DRIVER=none boots fine in production: NoneIntegrity.seal() returns '' for every event, and AuditService.verify() then passes trivially (each e.hash=''==seal(prev,e)='' , head_hash='' so the final-hash check is skipped) -> {ok:true}. hash-chain (unkeyed sha256) is likewise unguarded, which the config's own comment (lines 285-290) argues is defeatable by any backend attacker (they can re-anchor with public sha256, exactly what purge does).
findings.failure_scenario: An operator sets INTEGRITY_DRIVER=none (perf, or a copied dev env). The service serves as a production audit log with zero tamper-evidence, and the scheduled /internal/audit/verify returns ok:true forever — a control that reports healthy while proving nothing. Nobody learns until a regulator asks.
findings.fix: Add a production boot guard mirroring the sink guard: refuse INTEGRITY_DRIVER in ('none') in production, and warn/refuse 'hash-chain' unless an explicit opt-out flag is set. Fail closed at boot, not silently at verify time.

findings.title: The `resource` field is never pseudonymized or scrubbed — raw PII in resource is permanent in the chain
findings.detail: PiiPolicy.apply() folds actor, scrubs ip, and redacts metadata keys, but takes no `resource` argument (line 73), and record() (audit_service.py lines 46-48) passes resource straight through unmodified into AuditEvent, which is hashed into the chain. `resource` accepts up to 512 chars (api/internal.py line 29) and is a pushdown query field.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller records resource='user:alice@example.com' or 'iqama:1098765432'. The raw identifier is canonicalised and HMAC/hash-chained permanently; it cannot be redacted later without breaking verify() from that seq onward. The erasure endpoint proudly reports 'the events carry a pseudonym, not an identity' while resource holds the real one. This is the exact leak AUDIT_PII_MODE claims to prevent, on a field the policy simply does not cover.
findings.fix: Route `resource` through the same fold/enforce policy (detect and pseudonymize identity-shaped values, or at least redact configured PII fields when resource is 'k:v' shaped), or document and enforce at the schema that resource must already be a subject_ref / non-PII opaque handle in fold/enforce mode.

findings.title: Metadata PII scrub matches only top-level KEY NAMES; PII in values, nested dicts, or free text lands permanently
findings.detail: apply() computes `leaked = [k for k in meta if k.lower() in self.fields]` (line 108) and only redacts those top-level keys. It does not inspect values, nested dicts/lists, or arbitrary free-text keys. metadata is hashed into the chain, so anything missed is permanent.
findings.failure_scenario: metadata={'note':'called alice@example.com from +9665...'} or {'payload':{'email':'alice@x.com'}} passes untouched ('note'/'payload' are not in AUDIT_PII_FIELDS). Raw email/phone/national-id embedded in values or one level down is hash-chained forever and cannot be erased. fold mode advertises 'raw PII cannot land, no matter what a caller forgets' — but only for exact top-level key-name matches.
findings.fix: Recurse into nested structures and apply the redaction to nested keys; optionally value-scan for identity patterns (email/phone/national-id regexes over string values) in fold/enforce mode. State the residual limit explicitly if value-scanning is out of scope.

findings.title: verify() reads events then head non-atomically — a concurrent append raises a spurious 'chain broken' 409
findings.detail: verify() calls iterate(partition) (line 191, reads all event rows) and THEN head(partition) (line 192) as two separate un-synchronised reads. record() advances the head BEFORE writing the event row, so there is a window where head_seq is ahead of what iterate() saw.
findings.failure_scenario: During verify's iterate/head gap a record() advances head to N+1 (and may not yet have written row N+1, or wrote it after iterate paged past). head()=N+1 but events[-1].seq=N -> line 214 returns ok:false 'chain does not reach the recorded head (truncated or reordered)'. /internal/audit/verify then raises 409 AUDIT_CHAIN_BROKEN (api/internal.py line 128), firing the tamper alarm on a perfectly intact, merely-busy chain. Repeated false positives train operators to ignore the one real break.
findings.fix: Take a consistent snapshot: read head first, then iterate and accept events with seq<=head_seq (ignore a newer tail), or read head after iterate and treat head_seq>last_event_seq as 'in-flight tail', not tamper. A DB-consistent read (single transaction / snapshot) removes the window entirely.

findings.title: purge re-seals hashes of RETAINED events, invalidating every receipt/anchor previously issued for them
findings.detail: purge() re-anchors survivors from prev='' and rewrites each retained event's prev_hash and hash (lines 320-326), even events that were NOT expired. The {id,seq,hash} receipt returned by ingest (record_idempotent, and stored in the idempotency row) and any hash an external party recorded as an anchor no longer match the stored event after any purge.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller stored the receipt {seq:500, hash:H} at write time as proof of an event. After a routine retention purge that removes an older prefix, event 500 is re-sealed to H'!=H. The caller's independently held anchor now 'fails to match' the log, and a stale idempotency 'done' row still returns the old H while the chain holds H' — undermining the exact non-repudiation the HMAC chain sells.
findings.fix: Prefer a purge model that does not rewrite survivors' content hashes (e.g. a segmented chain with checkpoint anchors, or keep a tombstone/genesis anchor so surviving events keep their original hashes). If re-anchoring is unavoidable, publish/record the new anchor and version the receipts so old ones are recognisably superseded rather than silently wrong.

findings.title: iterate() (backing verify and purge) loads an entire partition into memory with no cap
findings.detail: iterate() pages by _PAGE=500 but extends `out` to exhaustion with 'There is no cap here' (lines 72-91). verify(), verify_all() (per partition), and purge() all call it. Unlike query/export which are bounded by AUDIT_QUERY_LIMIT/AUDIT_EXPORT_LIMIT, there is no ceiling here.
findings.failure_scenario: In the default single 'global' partition an audit log naturally grows to millions of rows. A scheduled /internal/audit/verify (verify_all) materialises the whole chain in one list; on a multi-million-row log this is a multi-GB allocation that can OOM-kill the pod, and it happens on a timer, repeatedly. RETENTION_DAYS=0 (the default, keep-forever) guarantees unbounded growth.
findings.fix: Stream the verification: walk page by page maintaining only prev_hash and a running count/last-seq, never accumulating the full list. purge similarly should operate page-by-page. Add a configurable safety ceiling that fails loudly rather than OOMs.

findings.title: Cross-partition query sorts merged results by per-partition `seq`, so 'newest' is wrong across tenants
findings.detail: The tenant-partition cross-partition fan-out (lines 171-178) merges each partition's newest `limit` then does out.sort(key=lambda r: r['seq'], reverse=True)[:limit]. seq is monotonic PER PARTITION and resets per tenant, so sorting the merge by seq does not order by time across partitions.
findings.failure_scenario: Tenant A has 1,000,000 events (seq up to 1e6), tenant B has 50 (seq up to 50). A platform-wide 'newest 100 events' query returns only tenant A's high-seq rows and never B's genuinely-recent events, because B's max seq (50) sorts below A's. A platform officer investigating a recent incident silently misses the newest events of low-volume tenants. Should sort by `ts`.
findings.fix: Merge-sort the cross-partition results by `ts` (the actual timestamp), not `seq`. seq is only meaningful within one partition.

findings.title: Per-tenant purge is witnessed only in the GLOBAL partition, and `remaining` miscounts
findings.detail: purge() ends by calling self.record(service='audit-service', action='audit.purged', ...) with no tenant (lines 329-331). record() computes partition from tenant='' -> always 'global'. So when purging a TENANT partition, the audit.purged witness lands in the global chain, not the tenant's own chain, and `remaining: len(kept)+1` (line 332) counts a +1 event that is not in this partition.
findings.failure_scenario: In AUDIT_PARTITION=tenant mode, tenant T's chain is purged (evidence deleted) but T's chain contains no record that a purge occurred — the witness is in a different partition an investigator of T may not consult. verify(T) also sees head=last_seq with no purge marker, so the deletion of old evidence is not self-documenting within the affected chain.
findings.fix: Record the audit.purged witness INTO the partition being purged (pass tenant/partition through to record()), and fix the `remaining` count to reflect the actual partition.

findings.title: Backup import can reintroduce a purged prefix or a stale head, producing a chain verify() flags broken
findings.detail: import_archive() restores rows keyed by identity and, with overwrite=False (the default, lines 216-222), LEAVES existing rows alone — including the audit_meta head singleton. audit_events and audit_meta are restored independently with no post-restore chain reconciliation or verify.
findings.failure_scenario: A backup is taken; retention purge then removes an old prefix and re-anchors survivors (new hashes) and moves the head. The backup is later restored (overwrite=False) into the same partition: purged old-prefix events are re-INSERTED with their ORIGINAL pre-purge hashes, while surviving events keep their re-anchored hashes and the head is skipped (already exists). The chain now has a hash discontinuity at the old purge boundary and/or events beyond the head -> verify() 'broken chain'. Conversely overwrite=True can roll the head backwards below existing event seqs. No import path runs verify() to catch this.
findings.fix: After an audit import, recompute/reconcile the partition head from the restored events and run verify(partition), failing the import if the resulting chain does not verify; treat audit_meta specially so a restore cannot leave head and events inconsistent.

findings.title: Any flags.manage holder can enable GLOBAL maintenance mode (platform-wide DoS)
findings.detail: PUT /api/v1/maintenance is guarded only by _ADMIN = require_any_capability('platform.flags','flags.manage'). MaintenanceIn.module defaults to 'global' and there is NO tenant/module scoping in set_maintenance. Maintenance is a global catalogue keyed only by module (app/core/stores.py:167 MaintenanceStore, one row per module, not per tenant), and MaintenanceService.status() reports the global window as active for every module and every caller. The override endpoints in this same file (lines 177-183, 202-205) go out of their way to confine a 'flags.manage'-only (non-platform) caller to their OWN tenant, which is direct evidence that flags.manage is a tenant-delegatable capability. Yet maintenance has no such guard.
findings.failure_scenario: A tenant administrator holding flags.manage (but not platform.flags) sends PUT /api/v1/maintenance {"module":"global","enabled":true}. Every service and the gateway that poll GET /internal/maintenance now receive active=true and serve a maintenance/503 response to ALL tenants. One tenant took the whole platform down.
findings.fix: Require platform.flags (not merely flags.manage) for set_maintenance, or restrict a flags.manage-only caller to a tenant-namespaced module and forbid module='global'. Mirror the tenant-scope guard already applied to overrides.

findings.title: flags.manage holder can overwrite/kill ANY global flag definition (missing-half authorization)
findings.detail: POST /api/v1/flags (upsert_flag) and DELETE /api/v1/flags/{key} (archive_flag) are guarded only by _ADMIN (platform.flags OR flags.manage) with NO tenant scoping. Flags are a single global catalogue keyed by flag key (app/core/stores.py:9-17, FlagStore over collection 'flags'); there is no per-tenant flag ownership. upsert merges the request into the EXISTING document for that key (app/core/flag_service.py:98-104), so any flags.manage caller can flip enabled (the kill-switch), default, rollout_pct, rules, requires_entitlement, start/end on a flag owned/used by other tenants. The override handlers in the same router deliberately scope a non-platform (flags.manage) caller to their own tenant (lines 177-183), proving flags.manage is tenant-delegatable — but that restriction was never applied to full flag CRUD.
findings.failure_scenario: A tenant admin with flags.manage POSTs /api/v1/flags {"key":"billing.enforce_entitlement","enabled":false}. The evaluation engine now returns kill_switch/OFF for that flag for EVERY tenant (evaluate.py:48-49), turning a platform-wide security/billing control off. Or they set rollout_pct=100/default=true to force a gated feature on for all users.
findings.fix: Gate flag create/edit/archive on platform.flags, or introduce per-tenant flag ownership and enforce it in upsert/archive the same way overrides are scoped. Do not let a tenant-delegated cap mutate the global catalogue.

findings.title: flags.manage holder can create/delete GLOBAL segments other tenants' flags target
findings.detail: POST /api/v1/segments and DELETE /api/v1/segments/{key} are guarded only by _ADMIN with no scoping. Segments are a global, reusable catalogue referenced by name from any flag (app/core/stores.py:88-108 SegmentStore; app/core/flag_service.py:184-192 _in_segment resolves flag['segments'] names against the shared SegmentStore). Deleting or redefining a segment silently changes the targeting outcome of every flag across every tenant that references it.
findings.failure_scenario: Flag 'premium_ui' targets segment 'paying_customers'. A tenant admin with flags.manage DELETEs segment 'paying_customers'. _in_segment now returns False for all callers, so segment_match (evaluate.py:72-73) never fires and the flag falls through to rollout/default for everyone platform-wide. Or they redefine the segment's rules to broaden the audience.
findings.fix: Require platform.flags for segment mutation, or namespace segments per tenant and enforce ownership on write/delete.

findings.title: flags.manage holder can write/rollback GLOBAL versioned config
findings.detail: PUT /api/v1/config/{key} and POST /api/v1/config/{key}/rollback are guarded only by _ADMIN. ConfigService/ConfigStore are env-scoped (CONFIG_ENV) but NOT tenant-scoped (app/core/config_service.py:22-39, app/core/stores.py:110-164). Any flags.manage caller can overwrite or roll back platform configuration keys used by other services/tenants. GET /internal/config/{key} then serves these values fleet-wide.
findings.failure_scenario: A tenant admin PUTs /api/v1/config/{some_platform_key} with a value that changes another service's behaviour (a URL, a limit, a feature toggle stored as config), or rolls a key back to an older value, affecting all tenants.
findings.fix: Require platform.flags for config writes/rollbacks, or scope config keys per tenant and enforce ownership.

findings.title: requires_entitlement is silently a no-op under the default 'null' entitlement driver (fail-open gate)
findings.detail: ENTITLEMENT_CHECKER_DRIVER defaults to 'null' (app/config.py:271). NullEntitlement.allowed() unconditionally returns True (app/adapters/entitlement/null.py:8-9). In evaluate.py:57 the entitlement gate only denies when entitled is False; with the null driver entitled is always True, so 'requires_entitlement' never blocks. The billing driver is correctly fail-CLOSED, but it is opt-in. A deployment that ships defaults (or forgets to set ENTITLEMENT_CHECKER_DRIVER=billing-http + creds) treats every tenant as entitled to every gated feature.
findings.failure_scenario: A flag gating a paid or security-sensitive capability sets requires_entitlement='pro_plan'. On a deployment still on the default null driver, every tenant — including free/unpaid ones — evaluates the flag as entitled and receives the gated feature. The control that was supposed to be enforced by billing is off, silently.
findings.fix: Make the entitlement gate fail-closed by default when a flag declares requires_entitlement but no real checker is configured (e.g. treat null-driver + requires_entitlement as denied, or refuse to start with a warning), or default the driver to billing-http in production profiles and log loudly when a requires_entitlement flag is evaluated under the null driver.

findings.category: DoS / read+HTTP amplification on hot path
findings.title: evaluate_all does per-flag entitlement HTTP + per-flag uncached segment reads (no per-request memoization)
findings.detail: evaluate_all iterates every flag and calls _resolve per flag (flag_service.py:242-252). _resolve calls _entitled (line 229) which, for every flag with requires_entitlement, runs a blocking billing HTTP call via asyncio.to_thread (lines 219-221), and _in_segment (line 230) which does an uncached SegmentStore.get datastore round-trip for each referenced segment name (lines 184-192). Nothing memoizes entitlement results or segment lookups within a single evaluate_all call. With N flags (up to FLAG_LIST_LIMIT=500) each requiring the same entitlement key and/or referencing segments, one evaluate_all fans out to N billing HTTP calls (threadpool saturation) and N*M segment reads. Reachable by any flags.read holder (POST /api/v1/flags/evaluate with no keys) and by any internal caller (POST /internal/flags/evaluate).
findings.failure_scenario: A caller POSTs /api/v1/flags/evaluate with an empty keys list against a catalogue where 50 flags share requires_entitlement='pro'. Each request issues 50 blocking 10s-timeout billing calls through the threadpool; a burst of such requests exhausts the threadpool and stalls all flag evaluation across the process (the very failure the to_thread offload was meant to avoid, just moved up a level).
findings.fix: Memoize entitlement results per (tenant,key) and segment membership per (segment,attrs) for the duration of one evaluate_all call; consider a short-TTL cache for segment definitions like the flag-definition cache.

findings.title: /flags/evaluate scopes tenant but not user — arbitrary global user ids can be probed
findings.detail: In the evaluate endpoint the tenant is forced to the caller's own tenant for non-platform callers (line 219), but body.user is passed through unchanged (line 220). User overrides and per-user rollout bucketing key on a GLOBAL user id (the code itself notes at lines 180-182 that a user override targets a global user id carrying no tenant). A flags.read holder can therefore evaluate flags as any arbitrary user id and observe the decision and the reason string ('user_override', 'segment_match', 'rule_match', 'variant_rollout').
findings.failure_scenario: A tenant-A operator with flags.read POSTs /api/v1/flags/evaluate {"user":"<a user id belonging to tenant B>"} and reads back reason='user_override' plus the enabled value and variant, learning that a platform-level override exists for that user and what it resolves to — cross-tenant leakage of targeting/experiment state.
findings.fix: Either require the evaluated user to belong to the caller's tenant, or accept that user ids are opaque but suppress override-existence reasons for non-platform callers. At minimum document that user is caller-supplied and unscoped.

findings.title: GET /config/{key} exposes global config to any flags.read holder (no scoping)
findings.detail: GET /api/v1/config/{key} is guarded by _READ (platform.flags OR flags.manage OR flags.read) and returns the full ConfigEntry value with no tenant scoping (config is global/env-scoped, app/core/config_service.py:27-28). If any config key stores sensitive platform values (URLs with tokens, limits, credentials, or PII), a low-privileged flags.read holder in any tenant can read them by key. Severity depends on what operators store in config.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator stores an integration setting containing a secret under config key 'x'. A tenant user with only flags.read GETs /api/v1/config/x and reads the secret. There is no per-tenant or sensitivity gating.
findings.fix: Scope config reads (require platform.flags for global config, or namespace per tenant), and/or mark keys as sensitive and redact on read for non-platform callers.

findings.title: DSAR erasure does not invalidate the flag cache and bypasses CAS
findings.detail: FeatureFlagErasure.erase removes the subject from user_overrides and writes via self._store.put directly (erasure.py:39-44). It does NOT invalidate the FlagService definition cache (flag:<key> / flags:all), so an erased user's override keeps influencing evaluation and remains readable from cache for up to FLAG_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS after the DSAR acks. The direct put also bypasses the version CAS used everywhere else (FlagStore.cas_save), so a concurrent admin override edit and the erasure can clobber each other (last-writer-wins), potentially resurrecting the erased entry.
findings.failure_scenario: compliance-service calls /internal/privacy/erase for a subject. The ack says erased, but for the next cache-TTL window flag evaluations still apply that person's cached user_override, and a concurrent set_override on the same flag can re-add the erased subject (lost update).
findings.fix: Invalidate the flag caches for touched keys after erasure (reuse FlagService._invalidate), and perform the override removal through the CAS-retry mutate path instead of a raw put.

findings.title: ROLLOUT_SALT defaults to a public constant, making rollout buckets predictable
findings.detail: ROLLOUT_SALT defaults to the literal 'base-services' (app/config.py:274). Bucketing is sha256(salt:key:subject) mod 10000 (app/core/rollout.py:14-25) and the flag key is discoverable. With the default salt an attacker can compute, for any subject id they control, whether they fall below the rollout threshold for a given flag key, and can grind user/tenant ids until they land in the enabled bucket.
findings.failure_scenario: A flag with rollout_pct=5 gates early access to a sensitive feature. Knowing the default salt and the flag key, an attacker enumerates candidate user ids offline, finds one whose bucket < 500, and uses it to force themselves into the 5% rollout for the gated capability.
findings.fix: Require ROLLOUT_SALT to be set to a per-deployment secret (fail startup on the default in production), and treat it as a secret rather than a config constant.

findings.title: Cursor pagination tie-breaks on absent 'id' field, causing boundary-row duplication in stale() on postgres
findings.detail: find() encodes the next cursor from last.get('id','') (postgres.py:230, memory.py:84), but the flag/config/segment models have NO 'id' field (app/core/models.py) — only 'key'. The postgres find WHERE tie-break compares (value->field, key) against (cursor_value, cursor_id) where cursor_id is '' (postgres.py:201-213), while ordering/keying is on the real 'key' column. For the boundary row where value->'key' == key == last_key, the comparison (last_key, last_key) > (last_key, '') is TRUE, so the previous page's last row is re-returned on the next page. The in-memory datastore does not exhibit this because its tie-break degenerates identically for both sides. This diverges memory vs postgres and yields duplicate entries in the paginated FlagStore.stale() sweep (app/core/stores.py:70-85).
findings.failure_scenario: On postgres with >500 live flags, GET /api/v1/flags/stale returns the page-boundary flag twice per page turn, inflating and duplicating the cleanup worklist; results differ from the in-memory test/dev backend which is clean, so tests miss it.
findings.fix: Encode the cursor tie-break from the actual key column (r['key']/the sort key), not a non-existent 'id' JSON field, and use a strict boundary comparison so the last returned row is excluded from the next page. Align memory and postgres on the same tie-break field.

findings.title: segment_match forces enabled=True, overriding a targeting rule that would disable
findings.detail: In the precedence chain, a segment match (evaluate.py:72-73) returns decision(True,'segment_match') unconditionally and sits ABOVE targeting rules (line 75) and rollout. A flag whose intent is 'in this audience, evaluate the rule/variant' cannot express 'in this segment but rule says off' — segment membership always forces ON. Combined with cross-tenant segment editability (finding 03), this makes segment membership a hard on-switch.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator adds a segment to a flag expecting it to scope the audience for the rules/rollout below, but every segment member now gets enabled=True regardless of the flag's rules — a gated feature turns on for the whole segment unexpectedly.
findings.fix: Document that segment_match is an on-switch, or let a segment feed into (rather than short-circuit above) rule/rollout evaluation; consider a per-flag flag for segment semantics.

findings.title: DELETE records the audit event BEFORE authorization, so any caller can spray false 'file.deleted' entries for arbitrary file ids / tenants
findings.detail: In `delete()` the write-ahead audit `record('file.deleted', ...)` runs at line 269-271, BEFORE `_load_scoped()` (line 273) authorizes the caller against the file's tenant. This is exactly the bug the team fixed in `signed_url()` (line 254-256 comment: 'Authorize (tenant ownership) BEFORE recording issuance ... recording first logged an issuance that never happened, a false audit entry an attacker could spray by id'). The delete route regressed the same pattern: the mutation is correctly gated by `_load_scoped`, but the audit is not.
findings.failure_scenario: An authenticated user in tenant B (holding files.upload) calls DELETE /api/v1/files/{id} with a file id belonging to tenant A (or a guessed/known id). `_load_scoped` will 404 and nothing is deleted, but a `file.deleted` row for actor=attacker, resource=file:{id} has already been appended to the immutable audit chain. Sprayed at scale this pollutes the append-only log, manufactures deletion evidence for files that were never touched, and can implicate the attacker's own tenant in cross-tenant activity that never happened.
findings.fix: Call `await _load_scoped(svc, file_id, principal)` FIRST, then write the write-ahead audit, then mutate. Mirror the ordering already used in `signed_url()`.

findings.title: Cross-tenant byte download by a platform.files holder through the normal GET /{file_id} route is UNAUDITED
findings.detail: `_load_scoped` (line 81-82) returns any file unscoped when the principal holds `platform.files`. The operator browse routes `/admin/list` and `/admin/{file_id}/metadata` audit ('file.inspected') and the admin metadata route deliberately serves metadata only. But the ordinary `download()` (GET /{file_id}, line 236-247) and `signed_url()` POST route contain NO auditor.record() call at all, yet a platform.files holder reaches them and pulls another tenant's actual bytes (or mints a bearer link to them). So the one cross-tenant action that exposes content, done through the normal route, leaves no audit trail, while the metadata-only admin route is audited.
findings.failure_scenario: A support/platform operator (platform.files) issues GET /api/v1/files/{id} for any tenant's file id and receives the bytes (or a 302 to a presigned bucket URL). No 'file.inspected'/'file.downloaded' record is written. Cross-tenant content access is invisible to a later investigation, defeating the purpose of the audited /admin surface.
findings.fix: Audit the download path when the read crosses tenants (or unconditionally). E.g. in `download()` and `signed_url()`, when `'platform.files' in principal.caps and f.tenant != principal.tenant`, record a 'file.downloaded'/'file.inspected' event with the file's tenant. Better: fold cross-tenant reads through one audited helper.

findings.title: Default posture LARGE_UPLOAD_SCAN=async + SCANNER_DRIVER=none serves large objects unscanned in production; boot guard only blocks 'skip'
findings.detail: `assert_large_scan_ok()` refuses to boot only when LARGE_UPLOAD_SCAN=='skip'. The defaults are LARGE_UPLOAD_SCAN='async' (config.py:281) and SCANNER_DRIVER='none' (config.py:291). With that combination the ScanWorker calls `NoneScanner.scan_stream` which does nothing, so a multi-GB object is promoted to READY and served with NO malware scan, while the operator believes 'async' scanning is in effect. The fail-closed branch in `begin_large_upload` only triggers for scan_policy=='require' (file_service.py:95-99), never for 'async'. So 'async' silently degrades to 'skip' whenever no real scanner is wired.
findings.failure_scenario: Operator deploys to production with the defaults (or sets LARGE_UPLOAD_SCAN=async but forgets SCANNER_DRIVER), passes all boot guards and health checks, and the service becomes a malware-distribution channel: any client uploads an executable via the direct-to-bucket large path, it verifies only by hash, is promoted, deduped and served by short-lived presigned URLs to any tenant that shares the content hash.
findings.fix: Extend the boot guard: in production, LARGE_UPLOAD_SCAN in {'async','require'} with SCANNER_DRIVER=='none' must refuse to start (an async scan with no scanner is skip with a misleading name). Alternatively make 'async'+none fail-closed at begin_large_upload as 'require' does.

findings.title: finalize/upload put-then-incr can race a concurrent last-ref delete, leaving a live FileObject pointing at a deleted blob
findings.detail: The delete-safety invariant relies on 'upload writes the blob before it increments' (delete() comment, line 285-289). But the ordering is put/promote THEN incr_ref, and claim_blob_delete only checks ref==0. Consider content sha S already referenced by one file (ref=1). Concurrent: (A) a fresh large upload of the same content finalizes -> `promote(staging, content_key)` restores/keeps the blob (line 185), THEN `incr_ref(S)` (line 186). (B) delete of the sole existing file -> `decr_ref` 1->0, then `claim_blob_delete(S)` sees ref==0 and deletes the blob. Interleaving A.promote, B.decr(->0), B.claim+store.delete, A.incr(->1) leaves blob_refs[S].count=1 with the object gone. Same shape in the small `upload()` path (put line 251, incr line 252). Round 1 notes flag CAS/concurrency as deferred.
findings.failure_scenario: Under concurrent re-upload and last-reference deletion of the same content hash, a tenant's newly created (deduped/finalized) file references a sha whose bytes were just deleted. Subsequent download 404s / NoSuchKey; the file record survives but the content is permanently gone. Also corrupts erasure receipts (claims bytes removed while a ref row survives, or vice-versa).
findings.fix: Make the increment and the zero-claim mutually exclusive: either incr_ref before promote and re-verify existence (as begin_large_upload's dedup path already does at lines 118-126), or gate blob deletion on a claim that also fails if any incr happened after the decr (version/CAS token), or perform decr+claim+delete and incr+existence-restore under one store-level transaction.

findings.title: Large-upload dedup possession check keys on owner only, not (tenant, owner)
findings.detail: `first_by_owner_sha(owner, sha256)` (file_repository.py:39-48) filters `{owner, sha256}` with no tenant. `begin_large_upload` uses it to short-circuit an upload as 'you already possess this' and to copy the existing file's content_type/size (file_service.py:111-125). Safe only while the JWT `sub` (owner) is globally unique across tenants. `_extract_principal` takes `sub` verbatim (auth.py:31-33); if any issuer ever mints tenant-local/reused subject ids, an attacker in tenant B whose sub collides with a victim in tenant A could claim a reference to the victim's content by declaring its sha256, without ever possessing the bytes.
findings.failure_scenario: Attacker learns/guesses a content sha256 (or reuses one leaked via a dedup timing difference) and, sharing a subject id with the original uploader in another tenant, calls POST /uploads with that sha. The dedup branch creates a FileObject in the attacker's tenant referencing the blob with no upload and no scan, then downloads it — a cross-tenant content disclosure.
findings.fix: Scope the possession query to (tenant, owner, sha256), or bind dedup to a possession proof that cannot be satisfied by naming a hash. At minimum document and enforce the global-uniqueness invariant of `sub` at the token-verifier boundary.

findings.title: Byte-serving download, metadata and signed-url-minting routes carry no rate limit
findings.detail: Only `upload`, `initiate_large_upload`, `list_files`, and the operator routes declare `Depends(rate_limit)`. The GET `download` (line 236), GET `metadata` (line 226), POST `signed_url` (line 250), the public `signed_download` (line 314), and `complete/get/abort` upload routes do not. So an authenticated caller can hammer downloads (each may proxy full bytes for a non-presign store) and spray POST /{id}/signed-url, each of which also appends an audit row (file.signed_url_issued).
findings.failure_scenario: An authenticated user issues thousands of POST /{id}/signed-url per second: mints unbounded bearer links and floods the audit chain, or hammers GET /{id} on a local/memory store to force repeated full-object reads into memory — a self-service DoS and audit-amplification with no throttle.
findings.fix: Add `Depends(rate_limit)` to download, metadata, signed_url, signed_download, and the large-upload complete/status/abort routes, with an appropriate route class/cost.

findings.title: Presigned bucket GET TTL is hardcoded to 300s; PRESIGN_TTL_SECONDS only governs PUT/multipart, not downloads
findings.detail: `download_redirect(f, *, ttl=300)` (file_service.py:292) is called from `download` and `signed_download` with no ttl argument, so every presigned GET is minted for 300s. PRESIGN_TTL_SECONDS (config.py:296-299, default 900) is documented as 'Consumed by the s3 object store when it mints presigned PUT/GET URLs' and is wired only into S3ObjectStore._presign_ttl (used by begin_multipart PUT URLs, s3.py:163). The GET presign path uses the hardcoded 300 instead. An operator setting PRESIGN_TTL_SECONDS to tighten/lengthen download link lifetime has no effect on downloads.
findings.failure_scenario: Operator sets PRESIGN_TTL_SECONDS=60 to minimize the window a leaked bucket URL is usable; downloads keep issuing 300s URLs. The control the operator relied on is silently inert (the advertised-but-unread-knob failure mode).
findings.fix: Thread PRESIGN_TTL_SECONDS into download_redirect (pass it from build_files / the route) rather than a hardcoded 300, or drop the default and require the caller to pass the configured value.

findings.title: SIGNED_URL_SECRET falls back to INTERNAL_SERVICE_TOKEN, so the internal service token can forge share links for any file
findings.detail: The hmac signer is built as `HmacSigner(s.SIGNED_URL_SECRET or s.INTERNAL_SERVICE_TOKEN, ...)` (container.py:141). When SIGNED_URL_SECRET is unset, the same secret that authenticates every /internal caller also signs public share-link tokens. The signer signs only {key,exp} (hmac_signer.py:46-49) and `resolve_signed_file` returns the file for any valid token with no further authz (file_service.py:307-311). Every service in the fleet holds INTERNAL_SERVICE_TOKEN.
findings.failure_scenario: Any component or attacker who obtains the internal service token (a widely-shared secret) can forge a valid /files/signed/{token} for an arbitrary file id and download it without any user JWT or tenant check, for the token TTL. Compromise of the internal token thus also becomes universal file-read.
findings.fix: Require SIGNED_URL_SECRET explicitly for the hmac driver (fail-fast if empty) rather than silently reusing the internal token; keep the two keys distinct so the blast radius of each is bounded.

findings.title: Signed token carries no owner/tenant/IP binding and a valid token minutes-old still yields a fresh 300s bucket redirect
findings.detail: The HMAC token payload is {key,exp} only (hmac_signer.py:47) — no tenant, owner, or client binding — a pure bearer credential. Additionally the effective access window stacks: a token resolved at t just before SIGNED_URL_TTL_SECONDS expiry hands out a bucket presign valid for another ttl (300s, see file-r2-07), and the signer verifies against the previous rotated secret for the whole rotation window (hmac_signer.py:41,56-57). All by design, but it means a link leaked to logs/referrers/proxies is usable by anyone until exp, plus the presign tail.
findings.failure_scenario: A /files/signed/{token} URL captured from an access log, browser history, or an HTTP referrer header is replayable by any party (no IP/tenant binding) until expiry, and the final bucket 302 remains valid ~300s beyond that. For long SIGNED_URL_TTL_SECONDS this is a meaningful exposure window on shared content.
findings.fix: Keep default TTL short (already 300s); consider optionally binding the token to the issuing subject/tenant when minted via the authenticated route, and ensure the bucket-redirect TTL is <= the remaining token lifetime rather than a fresh full window.

findings.title: Magic scanner: overly-broad RIFF signature, no archive-content inspection, and shebang blanket-rejects benign text
findings.detail: `_SIGNATURES['image/webp']=(b'RIFF',)` (magic.py:19) matches any RIFF container (AVI/WAV), so a non-webp RIFF passes strict declared-type validation. Archives ('application/zip' PK header) are accepted without inspecting members, so an MZ/ELF payload inside a permitted zip is stored and served. `_DANGEROUS` includes b'#!' (magic.py:25), which rejects every file that legitimately begins with a shebang or the characters '#!' even when declared text/plain. The scanner only inspects the first 16 bytes (scan_stream keeps a 16-byte header, line 37-44).
findings.failure_scenario: With SCANNER_DRIVER=magic (the lighter option many deployments choose over clamav), an attacker uploads content_type=image/webp whose bytes are a RIFF/AVI (or an executable wrapped in an accepted zip) and it passes; conversely a legitimate script/text upload beginning with '#!' is rejected as 'executable'. Type gating gives false assurance.
findings.fix: Tighten webp to require 'WEBP' at offset 8 after RIFF; recurse into archives or refuse to bless their contents by declared type; scope the shebang rejection to declared executable/script types rather than all content; consider clamav for real malware coverage.

findings.title: Keyset next_cursor id uses value['id'] while the SQL tie-break compares the primary key column, diverging for collections whose key != value id
findings.detail: In postgres `find`, the cursor comparison clause tie-breaks on the primary-key column `key` (postgres.py:217), but `next_cursor` is built from `last.get('id','')` (postgres.py:235). The memory adapter uses `str(r.get('id',''))` for BOTH ordering and cursor (memory.py:84-96). For `file_subjects` rows the datastore key is `link_id` = 'tenant|ref|file_id' while the stored value has no 'id' field (subject_links.py:70-71), so the postgres cursor id degenerates to '' and no longer matches the column it is compared against. Today this is masked because files_for sorts by the unique file_id, but it is a latent correctness gap and a memory/postgres behavioral divergence.
findings.failure_scenario: If a collection ever pages on a non-unique sort value with key != value['id'] (or a future field reuses this path), a page boundary can skip or duplicate rows in postgres but not in memory. In an erasure/subject-links context a skipped row means a file the DSAR believed it erased is actually retained, while the receipt says otherwise.
findings.fix: Make the postgres cursor tie-break and next_cursor both use the same identifier (the primary-key `key`), and make the memory adapter agree, so the two adapters are provably identical. Add a contract test that pages a collection where key != value['id'] with tied sort values.

findings.title: Object-store endpoint, credentials, JWKS and audit URLs are all config-sourced, never caller-influenced (SSRF checked, clean)
findings.detail: Reviewed for SSRF/credential injection: S3 endpoint_url comes only from config (s3.py:38-39 'never from a caller'); credentials require both halves or fall back to the ambient chain (s3.py:69-77); object keys are strictly validated (keys.py validate_key blocks traversal, backslash, NUL, absolute, drive letters, and re-normalizes). Presigned URLs sign only host (request_checksum_calculation=when_required) and force ResponseContentDisposition=attachment (s3.py:185-198), preventing inline HTML rendering. No user input reaches an outbound URL or the object key namespace beyond the content hash / session id. No SSRF finding.
findings.failure_scenario: N/A - documented as a checked dimension with no exploitable path found.
findings.fix: No change required; retain the config-only endpoint invariant and the validate_key gate. Keep the safety:scans / egress-allowlist gates enforcing it.

findings.title: max_candidates cap is ineffective for a single high-frequency term (full posting-list load + one get per candidate)
findings.detail: In _run, `for term in set(terms): postings = await self._index.postings(index, term)` loads the ENTIRE posting list for each term into memory, then merges every doc_id into candidate_tf. The cost guard `if len(candidate_tf) >= cap: break` is only evaluated AFTER a whole term's postings are absorbed. A single very common term whose posting list already exceeds `cap` (SEARCH_MAX_CANDIDATES=10000) blows straight past it: candidate_tf can hold the term's full list (potentially the whole per-index corpus across ALL tenants, since postings are keyed by (index,term) and shared across tenants), and the subsequent ranking loop (line 140) issues ONE datastore get per candidate before the tenant/filter check. The advertised 'documented cost ceiling' does not bound the two most expensive operations (the posting-list read and the per-candidate get) for the exact pathological query it claims to defend against.
findings.failure_scenario: A tenant on a shared index name (e.g. 'products') submits a query containing one term present in most documents (a stopword-surviving common word, or a term the attacker first mass-indexed). BuiltinIndex.postings returns a dict of every doc_id carrying that term across every tenant sharing the index; _run then performs that many datastore.get calls plus an in-memory BM25 rank. At 100 req/min/subject (RATELIMIT_MAX) with cost=1 per request, a handful of subjects drive millions of datastore reads, saturating the connection pool (pool_max default 5) and starving every other request — a self-inflicted DoS the cap was written to prevent.
findings.fix: Bound the work BEFORE materialising a term's full list: cap the number of postings consumed per term and in aggregate (e.g. request/slice postings with a limit, or check the cap inside the inner `for doc_id, tf in postings.items()` loop and break). Also cap total datastore.get calls in the ranking loop. Consider ordering terms by doc_freq ascending so rare (cheap, selective) terms are consumed first.

findings.title: DSAR erasure deletes docs but never invalidates the result cache — erased PII keeps being served for cache_ttl
findings.detail: SearchErasure.erase() calls self._index.delete(...) (the raw index engine) directly and never bumps the per-tenant search generation. Cache invalidation lives ONLY in SearchService._bump(tenant) (search_service.py:42), which is called by SearchService.index/delete but NOT by the erasure path. The search result cache key (search_service.py:96) is keyed by `g` = the tenant generation; if the generation is not bumped, previously-cached result pages that contain the erased subject's documents continue to be returned verbatim (with `cached: True`) until SEARCH_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS (default 30s) expires.
findings.failure_scenario: compliance-service fans out a DSAR to POST /internal/privacy/erase. The subject's documents are removed from the index and the ack reports success, but any query whose result page was cached before the erase keeps returning the person's name/fields for up to 30s afterward. A DSAR that reports 'erased' while the data is still searchable is a PDPL/GDPR compliance failure, and the window is trivially observable.
findings.fix: Have the erasure path bump the tenant's search generation after deletions (inject SearchService or the cache and call the same generation-bump used by index/delete), so cached pages for that tenant are invalidated immediately rather than after TTL.

findings.title: Posting-list read-modify-write is a lost update under concurrent indexing — a document can silently become unsearchable
findings.detail: upsert() updates each term's posting row with a non-atomic read-modify-write: `row = await self._store.get(_POST, pk) or {}; row[doc_id] = tf; await self._store.put(_POST, pk, row)`. Both DataStore adapters make this racy: the memory adapter deep-copies on get/put (memory.py:18-23), and the postgres adapter does a plain SELECT then a separate INSERT..ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE overwriting the whole `value` (postgres.py:113-129). The `await` points between get and put let a concurrent coroutine/request interleave. Two documents indexed concurrently that share a term each read the same posting row, each add only their own doc_id to a stale copy, and the second put overwrites the first — the first document's posting for that term is lost, so it will not match a search for that term.
findings.failure_scenario: Two peer-service index calls (POST /internal/search/index) for docA and docB, both containing the word 'riyadh', are processed concurrently. Both read search_postings['idx:riyadh'] before either writes. docA writes {docA:tf}; docB writes {docB:tf}, clobbering docA. A later search for 'riyadh' never returns docA — a silent correctness/data-integrity loss with no error surfaced.
findings.fix: Make the posting update atomic: a JSONB merge in postgres (e.g. `value = value || $delta` or `jsonb_set` in a single statement), a row-level lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE within a transaction), or a store-level atomic mutate primitive. At minimum serialise writes per (index) or per (index,term).

findings.title: meta counters (n_docs / total_len) drift under concurrent indexing, skewing BM25 relevance
findings.detail: Both _remove_existing (lines 57-60) and upsert (lines 77-81) do read-modify-write on the per-index meta row (n_docs, total_len) with awaits between the get and the put. Concurrent indexing produces lost updates and double counting: two concurrent NEW-doc upserts each read existing=None (skip remove) and each increment n_docs, but the last put wins so one increment is lost — or, symmetrically, concurrent re-indexes double-decrement. n_docs and total_len feed idf() and avg_doc_len in ranking (search_service.py:116-117, ranking.py:16-33), so drift degrades ranking quality for the whole index over time.
findings.failure_scenario: A bulk import runs many concurrent /internal/search/index calls into one index. n_docs settles well below (or above) the true document count; avg_doc_len and idf are computed from wrong totals, so relevance scoring is systematically off and pagination totals reported to callers are inaccurate.
findings.fix: Update meta atomically (single SQL statement doing the arithmetic, or a transaction with row lock), or derive n_docs/total_len from an authoritative count rather than an incrementally maintained counter.

findings.title: suggest() scans a global, non-tenant-scoped row window before filtering by tenant — a tenant's suggestions can be starved to empty
findings.detail: iter_docs() reads up to _SUGGEST_SCAN (10000) rows of the shared search_docs collection filtered only by `index` (r.get('index') == index), and the tenant filter is applied afterward in SearchService.suggest (search_service.py:213). On a hot index shared by many tenants, the first 10000 rows the store returns may belong entirely to OTHER tenants, so the calling tenant receives zero suggestions even though it has matching documents — and the full scan cost is paid regardless on every keystroke. This is the same shared-index shape that the postings DoS (search-r2-01) exploits: cost is not tenant-proportional.
findings.failure_scenario: Tenant B has 50 documents in the 'contacts' index but tenants A and C together have >10000 documents ordered ahead of B's in the store. Every /api/v1/search/suggest call from B scans 10000 of A/C's rows, matches none for B, and returns [] — a broken autocomplete plus a per-keystroke 10000-row read that does no useful work for the caller.
findings.fix: Maintain a per-(tenant,index) document index/collection so suggest reads only the caller's rows, or store postings/terms per-tenant so autocomplete is tenant-scoped and O(tenant rows), not O(scan window).

findings.title: Erasure matches only owner==subject; PII in fields of documents whose owner is unset/different is never erased (silent DSAR no-op)
findings.detail: erase() finds documents with find(_DOCS, {'tenant': tenant, 'owner': subject}). The `owner` field is optional at index time (IndexIn.owner default '', Document.owner default '', search_service.index owner=''). Any document that embeds the subject's PII in its `fields` (name, phone, email) but was indexed without owner set — or with a different owner (e.g. the record's own id) — is not matched, so it is never scrubbed while the ack still reports success (already_absent or a partial count). The service has no way to detect that PII survived.
findings.failure_scenario: A peer indexes an order document with fields={customer_name, customer_phone} and owner left blank (or owner=order_id). A DSAR erases the customer: erase() finds zero owner-matching rows, acks {already_absent: true}, and the customer remains fully searchable by name/phone — a PDPL breach that looks like a successful erasure.
findings.fix: Define and enforce the owner contract for indexed documents that contain personal data (reject/flag PII-bearing docs without an owner), or erase by additionally matching subject identifiers within indexed fields. At minimum document that erasure coverage depends entirely on callers setting owner correctly, and surface it in the ack.

findings.title: Default-open internal route policy + single fleet-wide shared token lets any internal caller read/erase/index ANY tenant
findings.detail: The internal tier authenticates with a shared flat token (INTERNAL_CALLER_DRIVER default 'shared') and authorises via a per-route allow-list that is DEFAULT-OPEN: 'A route with no policy admits any authenticated caller' (require_internal_token, lines 90-91; config INTERNAL_ROUTE_POLICY_JSON default ''). /internal/search/query and /internal/search/suggest take `tenant` from the request body (QueryIn.tenant), and /internal/privacy/erase performs a destructive per-subject deletion for an arbitrary body-supplied tenant. With no INTERNAL_ROUTE_POLICY_JSON configured, any service (or anything) holding the shared token can read every tenant's documents and erase any subject in any tenant, with no per-caller restriction.
findings.failure_scenario: A lower-trust service that legitimately needs to index its own entities holds the same shared INTERNAL_SERVICE_TOKEN (fleet secret). Because the token is shared and the route policy is empty by default, that service (or a compromised pod/leaked token) can POST /internal/search/query for a competitor tenant's data, or POST /internal/privacy/erase to destroy another tenant's indexed documents. Nothing in the default configuration constrains caller-to-tenant.
findings.fix: Ship a non-empty default route policy for the sensitive internal routes (query/suggest/index/bulk/delete/erase) or require per-caller RS256 assertions (static/jwks driver) in production via a boot guard; bind erase/query to the caller's authorised tenant set rather than trusting the body tenant unconditionally.

findings.title: Highlights embed unescaped user field content wrapped in <em> — HTML-injection/XSS if a consumer renders them as HTML
findings.detail: _highlight() builds highlight strings by wrapping matching words as f'{word}' and joining the raw, unescaped words of the field value (lines 191-199). The words come straight from indexed document fields (attacker-controllable via the indexing path). The service returns these as strings in the JSON `highlights` map. If any consumer (operator panel, client app) renders highlight snippets as HTML (the conventional use of highlighting), embedded markup/script in a field value executes.
findings.failure_scenario: A document field contains `` and a searched term. The highlight string returned includes that markup verbatim; a panel that renders search highlights as HTML executes it — stored XSS reaching an operator's session.
findings.fix: HTML-escape each word before wrapping (escape then insert <em> around the escaped match), or document that highlights are HTML and must be sanitised/escaped by the caller. Prefer emitting match offsets rather than pre-marked HTML.

findings.title: Cache generation read/bump fail open silently — a flaky cache can serve stale results after writes
findings.detail: _gen() returns '0' on any cache exception (lines 39-40) and _bump() swallows all exceptions (lines 48-49). If the cache backend (redis) intermittently fails, a write's generation bump can be silently dropped while reads still hit a cached page under the old generation key, serving stale results. The degradation is invisible (no metric/log at the call site).
findings.failure_scenario: During a redis blip, an index update's _bump() throws and is swallowed; subsequent searches read the still-valid cached page (generation unchanged) and return pre-update results with cached:true until TTL. Combined with search-r2-02, a write that should have refreshed results does not.
findings.fix: Distinguish 'cache unavailable' from 'generation 0' (e.g. skip the cache entirely / mark degraded when the backend errors), and emit a metric/log when a bump is dropped so stale-serving windows are observable.

findings.title: Tenantless principals collapse into a shared '__none__' tenant scope
findings.detail: _tenant() returns `p.tenant or '__none__'`. Any authenticated principal whose token carries no tenant/org/tid claim (auth.py:_extract_principal sets tenant=None) is mapped to the literal tenant '__none__'. All such principals share one search scope: they can see each other's documents indexed under tenant '__none__', and cannot be isolated from one another.
findings.failure_scenario: Two different tenantless service/user tokens (misissued without a tenant claim) both search index 'x'; each sees any document indexed with tenant '__none__', because the isolation key collapses them together. Isolation silently degrades to 'all tenantless callers are one tenant' rather than failing closed.
findings.fix: Reject a search from a principal without a resolved tenant (401/403) instead of substituting a shared sentinel, or ensure '__none__' can never be an indexing tenant so the read scope is provably empty.
