findings.title: bulk() is non-atomic and non-idempotent — a mid-batch CrossTenantConflict leaves a partial index and 500s the caller
findings.detail: bulk() loops over docs calling self.index() sequentially with no batch idempotency key and no rollback. If any document triggers BuiltinIndex.CrossTenantConflict (builtin.py:66-69) or any store error mid-batch, earlier documents are already indexed, the exception propagates unhandled (internal.py:112 has no try/except) producing a 500, and the returned count is never sent. A retry re-runs the whole batch. Individual upserts are idempotent, but the meta counters are not (see search-r2-04), so retries compound counter drift.
findings.failure_scenario: A peer submits a 1000-doc bulk where doc #500 shares an (index,id) with another tenant's document. Docs 1-499 are indexed, doc 500 raises, the caller gets a 500 with no result, retries the full batch, and n_docs is inflated by the re-indexed prefix.
findings.fix: Make bulk report per-doc success/failure without aborting the batch (collect errors), or process the batch transactionally; add a batch idempotency key so retries are safe.

findings.title: Internal DeleteIn / QueryIn tenant and id fields lack the length/pattern bounds the user and IndexIn models enforce
findings.detail: DeleteIn (lines 40-43) declares index/id/tenant as bare `str` with no min/max length or pattern, unlike IndexIn (lines 25-32) and SearchIn (search.py:49-56) which constrain index with pattern ^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$ and cap lengths. An internal caller can pass arbitrarily large or oddly-shaped index/id/tenant strings to /internal/search/delete, which become datastore keys (builtin _dk 'index:doc_id'). Not a direct injection (postgres uses parameterised queries), but unbounded key sizes and inconsistent validation across twins are a hardening gap.
findings.failure_scenario: A buggy or hostile internal caller sends a multi-megabyte `id` to /internal/search/delete; it is used unbounded as part of a datastore key with no rejection, inflating storage/index key size and diverging from the validated user-facing contract.
findings.fix: Give DeleteIn (and re-check QueryIn) the same Field(min_length/max_length/pattern) constraints as IndexIn/SearchIn so all twins validate identically.

findings.title: Erasure legal-hold seam reads ALL holds capped at 100 and filters `active` in Python, with no completeness guard — an active hold beyond page 100 is missed and held data is erased
findings.detail: erase() is documented as 'the single seam every erase path funnels through' for hold enforcement. But it calls self._store.find(_HOLDS, {"tenant": tenant, "subject": subject}, limit=100, sort=("placed_at","asc")) and then filters active_holds in Python (lines 55-56). This fetches active AND inactive/released holds into the same 100-row budget, unlike HoldStore.active_for() which pushes {"active": True} down to the store, and unlike HoldStore.active_in_tenant() which returns a completeness flag. release_hold() only sets active=False (compliance_service.py:52) and never deletes the row; retention does not purge the legal_holds collection. Released holds therefore accumulate forever. The cursor returned by find() is discarded, so truncation is silent.
findings.failure_scenario: A litigious subject accrues 100+ historical (released) holds over the years. A new active hold is placed today (newest placed_at). find() sorts placed_at ASC and returns the oldest 100 rows — all released — and the active hold falls beyond the page. active_holds is empty, erase() proceeds, deletes the consent rows and pseudonymises the proof for a subject who is CURRENTLY under litigation hold. This is spoliation of evidence, reached through the very seam that exists to prevent it, and via the direct /internal/privacy/erase caller it bypasses the upstream DsarService.process hold check entirely.
findings.fix: Push {"active": True} into the find (reuse HoldStore.active_for), and treat a non-None cursor as INCOMPLETE — fail CLOSED (refuse the erase, do not pseudonymise) when the hold answer may be truncated, exactly as active_in_tenant()/held_refs() already do. Never decide 'no hold' from a page that could be truncated.

findings.title: A 200 response carrying `blocked_by_legal_hold` is classified ACKED, so a target that RETAINED data under hold flips the DSAR target to complete
findings.detail: erasure.py:57-67 deliberately returns HTTP 200 with {"erased": [], "already_absent": False, "blocked_by_legal_hold": True} when the subject is held in THAT target's own jurisdiction. HttpPrivacyTransport.erase() only special-cases unrecognized_subject_kind and truncated before falling through to ACKED (lines 75-90). blocked_by_legal_hold is not recognised, so the outcome is ACKED, PrivacyDispatcher._attempt sets dsar.targets[key]=True (privacy_dispatcher.py:105), and completion is derived as done. Reached whenever compliance-service (or any peer that adopts the same blocked-ack shape) is a target of another service's DSAR fan-out and holds its own hold on that subject.
findings.failure_scenario: Shop A files an erasure DSAR for a subject via the orchestrating service; compliance-service is a data-map target. compliance-service has an active local legal hold, so its /internal/privacy/erase returns 200 + blocked_by_legal_hold. The dispatcher marks the compliance target ACKED; once the other targets ack, the DSAR is derived COMPLETED and reported to the regulator as fully erased — while compliance-service lawfully retained the data. A false 'she was erased', the exact lie the service's own comments say must never happen.
findings.fix: Classify a 200 ack carrying blocked_by_legal_hold (or an empty erased[] with a retained legal_hold basis) as FAILED/non-ack, mirroring the unrecognized_subject_kind handling, so the target stays unacked and the DSAR stays open and visible rather than closing over retained data.

findings.title: erase() never touches consent_proof_seq, whose row key embeds the RAW subject — the raw identifier survives erasure and is exported in backups
findings.detail: add_proof (stores.py:177) keys the per-subject sequence counter as seq_key = f"{p.tenant}::{p.subject}" with the RAW subject. erase() deletes _CONSENT, pseudonymises _PROOF and reads _HOLDS, but never deletes or renames the _PROOF_SEQ row (grep confirms the only writers are add_proof and _rebuild_proof_seq). backup_manifest.py:46 includes consent_proof_seq in the sealed archive. pii.py is explicit that erasure must 'delete the mutable PII and destroy the LINKAGE'; here a store KEY containing the raw subject identifier persists indefinitely after erasure.
findings.failure_scenario: A subject (identified by e.g. email/phone/user-id as `subject`) requests erasure. Every consent row is deleted and every proof pseudonymised, and the DSAR closes COMPLETED. Yet consent_proof_seq still holds a row keyed 'tenant::alice@example.com'. A regulator inspection, a backup export, or a database dump reveals the raw personal identifier of a person the platform swore it had erased.
findings.fix: In erase(), after pseudonymising proofs, delete the consent_proof_seq row for (tenant, raw subject) — the counter is derived and self-heals from proof ids via _rebuild_proof_seq — or re-key it under subject_ref. Add consent_proof_seq to the erase fan-out and to an erasure-completeness test.

findings.title: Consent deletion in erase() is capped at limit=1000 with no pagination; survivors past the cap are left while the ack reports only the deleted count
findings.detail: erase() reads consent rows with self._store.find(_CONSENT, {...}, limit=1000, sort=("updated_at","asc")) and deletes them, but unlike the proof loop directly below it (lines 87-96, which paginates with a cursor) it never pages. If a subject has more than 1000 consent rows, only the first 1000 are seen and deleted. `erased` reports the true deleted count and already_absent=not erased, so the caller/regulator receives a success ack with no signal that rows remain.
findings.failure_scenario: A high-volume subject (or an abusive tenant that granted thousands of per-purpose consents) has >1000 consent rows. erase() deletes 1000, the DSAR target acks, the DSAR completes, and hundreds of consent records for the 'erased' subject silently remain in the store.
findings.fix: Paginate the consent deletion with the same after-cursor loop already used for proofs, or assert the page was not truncated and fail the ack (not already_absent) if it was, so incompleteness is loud rather than silent.

findings.title: grant()/withdraw() persist the consent row and bump the cache AFTER add_proof; if add_proof raises, consent state changes with no immutable proof and no cache invalidation
findings.detail: grant() calls self._store.put(c) (line 100), then add_proof (101-104), then _bump (105). withdraw() is the same shape (116-120). add_proof retries CAS 64 times and raises RuntimeError('could not allocate a consent-proof sequence under contention') on exhaustion (stores.py:189-190), and any store error there also propagates. Because the consent row is already written and _bump happens only after add_proof, an exception leaves: (grant) a granted consent with NO ConsentProof — the 'prove they consented' evidence is missing for processing that is now permitted; (withdraw) a withdrawn row whose cache generation was never bumped, so check() keeps answering the cached 'allowed' until TTL, i.e. withdrawal is NOT immediate.
findings.failure_scenario: Under heavy concurrent consent writes for one subject (or a flaky datastore), add_proof exhausts its 64 CAS attempts. The withdrawal is stored but the generation is not bumped; a hot-path check() served from cache continues to return allowed:true for up to CONSENT_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS — processing continues against a subject who withdrew consent.
findings.fix: Bump the generation and/or write the proof before (or transactionally with) the consent mutation, or on add_proof failure roll back the consent write and surface the error. At minimum bump the cache in a finally so a persisted withdrawal always invalidates cached allows.

findings.title: erase() is not serialized against a concurrent grant(): a grant landing after the scan re-creates an un-erased consent row and a proof carrying the RAW subject
findings.detail: erase() reads-then-deletes consent (69-83) and reads-then-pseudonymises proofs page by page (87-96). There is no lock, no re-check, and no generation guard against a ConsentService.grant()/withdraw() running concurrently. A grant that commits after erase() has passed a given page adds (a) a fresh consent row that erase() will not revisit and (b) a ConsentProof whose subject field is the RAW subject, which the pseudonymisation pass already walked past.
findings.failure_scenario: A subject requests erasure at the same moment an ingest pipeline records a late consent/withdrawal for them (e.g. a queued webhook). The DSAR completes COMPLETED, but a live consent row and a proof containing the raw subject identifier remain for the 'erased' person.
findings.fix: Bump the consent generation at the start of erase and re-scan until a pass deletes/pseudonymises nothing, or gate consent writes for a subject with an active erasure DSAR (the ERASURE_GRACE / hold machinery could carry an 'erasing' flag). Treat erase as needing a fixed-point, not a single pass.

findings.category: retention vs legal-hold bypass / evidence destruction
findings.title: RetentionEnforcer._is_held checks holds by the row's `subject`, but pseudonymised proof rows carry subject_ref while holds are keyed by the raw subject — a held proof can be age-purged
findings.detail: _is_held(row) calls self._holds.active_for(row['tenant'], row['subject']) (line 88). A pseudonymised consent_proof row has subject == subject_ref (an HMAC, set by erase()), whereas LegalHold rows store the RAW subject. active_for on a subject_ref matches no hold, so _is_held returns False and the proof is eligible for deletion. The shipped RETENTION_RULES example (config.py:372) is literally 'dsar=365,breaches=1825,consent_proof=2555', i.e. consent_proof IS an intended retention collection, and append-only evidence is being age-purged at all. _purge also scans with limit=max_per_run and pages nothing, so a large collection is only partially considered per run.
findings.failure_scenario: A subject's consent proof was pseudonymised by an earlier erasure; later a legal hold is placed (holds can be placed on any subject id). The nightly retention run sees the proof older than 2555 days, cannot match the hold (ref vs raw), and deletes evidence that is under active legal hold — spoliation via the retention path.
findings.fix: Resolve holds against BOTH the raw subject and its subject_ref when evaluating retention on pseudonymised collections, or exclude append-only evidence (consent_proof) from age-based purge entirely; document that proof retention, if allowed, must honour holds keyed by ref.

findings.title: Cross-tenant open-DSAR officer view returns each request's raw `subject` and full `payload`, broader than needed for discovery
findings.detail: list_all_open() maps every tenant's open DSAR through d.public(), which strips only verification_token (models.py:205-208). The returned item includes the raw `subject` and the entire `payload` dict, which for correction/export DSARs can carry personal data (correction values, export-bundle contents). The platform.compliance cross-tenant read is legitimate-by-design and audited, but the discovery view needs identifiers and status, not payload bodies for every shop.
findings.failure_scenario: A platform compliance officer (or a compromised platform.compliance token) lists all open DSARs and receives, for every tenant on the platform, the raw subject identifiers and correction/export payloads — a single call that aggregates cross-tenant PII well beyond 'which requests exist'.
findings.fix: Return a discovery projection for the cross-tenant view (id, tenant, type, status, deadline, overdue, subject_ref) and require an explicit per-DSAR fetch (already tenant-scopable) to see payload/subject. Keep the full payload out of the aggregate list.

findings.title: erase() evaluates hold state with wall-clock time.time() instead of the injected clock used everywhere else
findings.detail: erase() does 'import time as _time; now = _time.time()' (lines 51-52) and uses it to evaluate hold expiry. Every other core path (DsarService, dispatcher, sweepers, ComplianceService, retention) takes an injected clock, which is how manual/test clocks and any deterministic time control work. This single hard-wired wall clock diverges from the rest of the system and cannot be advanced by the ManualClock the tests and any time-travel operations rely on.
findings.failure_scenario: A test (or an operational time-skew scenario) advances the injected clock to simulate a hold expiring; erase() ignores it and reads the host wall clock, so its hold-expiry decision disagrees with DsarService.process and with the ManualClock — masking or manufacturing a divergence that only appears in production.
findings.fix: Inject the container clock into ComplianceErasure and use clock.now() for the hold-time evaluation, consistent with every other module.

findings.title: erase() hold-expiry branch references h['expires_at'], a field LegalHold does not define — the documented time-based hold expiry is non-functional
findings.detail: The active-hold filter is `[h for h in all_holds if h.get('active', True) and (not h.get('expires_at') or now < h['expires_at'])]` (lines 55-56). The LegalHold model (models.py:216-223) has no expires_at field — only active/placed_at/released_at. h.get('expires_at') is therefore always falsy, so the expiry clause is dead: holds only ever end via the active flag. This is harmless today (it fails safe toward 'held') but the code advertises a time-expiry capability that does not exist, inviting a future caller to rely on it.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator sets an expires_at on a hold expecting it to auto-lift (the code appears to support it); nothing populates the field on the model, so the branch never fires and the behaviour silently differs from the apparent contract.
findings.fix: Either add expires_at to LegalHold and honour it consistently in HoldStore.active_for / active_in_tenant / hold_check, or remove the dead expires_at clause from erase() so the only hold-ending mechanism (active flag + release) is the one the code shows.

findings.title: release_hold scopes to the caller's own tenant and ignores any tenant selector, so a platform officer cannot release a cross-tenant hold they discovered; audit tenant also mismatches the scoped tenant
findings.detail: Unlike verify_dsar/process_dsar (which take a tenant query param and pass _tenant(principal, tenant)), release_hold() calls release_hold(hold_id, tenant=_tenant(principal)) with no selector — a platform.compliance operator is pinned to their own reserved tenant and release returns 404 for any real shop's hold. Separately, the write-ahead audit records tenant=principal.tenant (line 387) while the scope uses _tenant(principal); for a platform op these can differ, so the audit row's tenant does not name the tenant actually acted on.
findings.failure_scenario: A platform compliance officer discovers an active hold via the cross-tenant list view, then cannot release it (404) — or the operation is inconsistent with place_hold, which DOES honour a body tenant. The asymmetry either blocks a legitimate release or, if later 'fixed' carelessly, opens a cross-tenant release; and the audit trail attributes the release to the wrong tenant.
findings.fix: Give release_hold the same tenant selector honoured only for platform.compliance (as verify/process do), pass the same scoped tenant to both the audit record and release_hold, and keep tenant-admin values ignored so cross-tenant release stays platform-only and correctly recorded.

findings.title: Concurrent _stop double-releases the concurrency reservation -> per-tenant/global cap can be breached
findings.detail: _stop() guards idempotency with `if sess.is_terminal: return sess` (line 317) but the LIVE->terminal transition is a non-atomic read-modify-write: sess is loaded, status is set in memory (line 337) and persisted with `self._sessions.save(sess)` (line 339) which is a plain put() (SessionStore.save -> store.put, last-writer-wins) NOT a CAS. Two callers that each load the same still-LIVE session both pass the is_terminal guard and both run `_release_quota(self._release_map(), sess)` (line 342), decrementing the tenant and global counters TWICE for a single session teardown. _decr() floors at 0 but that does not help: a live session's slot is freed while OTHER sessions are still live, so the counted `live` value under-counts real live sessions by 1 per race, and the next start_session sees room below cap that does not exist.
findings.failure_scenario: Concurrent paths: (a) user POST /sessions/{id}/stop and the CronJob POST /internal/stream/sweep enforce_and_reconcile() reaching the same session in the same window; or (b) two racing user stop/kill calls; or (c) a guard-breach stop in the sweep loop plus a reconcile-dead stop in the same run for a session that is both. Each double-decrement permanently lowers the tenant counter by 1 relative to reality. Repeating the race N times lets a tenant hold cap+N concurrent sessions, defeating STREAM_MAX_CONCURRENT_SESSIONS_PER_TENANT and STREAM_MAX_CONCURRENT_SESSIONS_GLOBAL (resource-exhaustion / cost DoS). This is the exact TOCTOU class the round-1 reservation code set out to close, reopened on the release side.
findings.fix: Make the LIVE->terminal transition atomic and release exactly once only for the caller that wins it. E.g. CAS the session status (store.cas on the session row's version) and release the quota only when the CAS succeeds; a loser returns the already-terminal session without touching counters. Alternatively key the reservation to the session id and make _release idempotent per session (delete-if-present of a per-session reservation marker before decrementing).

findings.title: ONVIF PTZ connects to the stored host with no re-validation and no IP pinning (DNS-rebinding SSRF with camera credentials)
findings.detail: _default_factory() builds `ONVIFCamera(onvif.get('host'), int(onvif.get('port',80)), user, password)` (lines 21-24) straight from the stored source dict, and _ptz() (line 35) then opens ONVIF/media/PTZ services against it. The ONVIF host is SSRF-validated ONLY once, at register_source (stream_service.py:95-99). Nothing re-validates or pins the host at PTZ time. move()/stop()/presets()/goto()/capability() are all reached via /api/v1/sources/{id}/ptz/* (api/v1/stream.py:288-329) using src.onvif from _ptz_source(). The source URL path was hardened with re-validate + _pin_url at start_session; the ONVIF host path was not.
findings.failure_scenario: Attacker (a stream.manage caller) registers a source whose onvif.host is a domain they control resolving to a public IP (passes register-time _check_ssrf). After registration they repoint DNS to 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata) or an internal 10.x/172.16.x host. An operator (or the attacker) issues POST /sources/{id}/ptz/move; ONVIFCamera re-resolves the hostname at connect and the SOAP requests (carrying any configured camera credentials) hit the internal/metadata endpoint -> the service becomes an authenticated proxy into the cluster / cloud metadata (CWE-918).
findings.fix: Re-run _check_ssrf on the ONVIF host at every PTZ/capability call and pin the connection to the validated IP (pass the resolved IP to ONVIFCamera instead of the hostname, mirroring _pin_url for the source URL). If python-onvif-zeep cannot accept a pinned IP with the original Host header, resolve+pin at the socket layer or reject hostnames that resolve to more than the validated address.

findings.title: probe_source validates then connects by hostname (unpinned) — DNS-rebinding window, violating the code's own pinning rule
findings.detail: probe_source() unseals the URL, calls self._check_ssrf(url) (line 115), then passes the ORIGINAL url to self._engine.probe(url, transport=...) (line 116). It does NOT use the resolved/pinned IP. _check_ssrf's own docstring (lines 446-449) states: 'Callers that connect (start_session) MUST use the pinned IP, or ffmpeg re-resolves the hostname and a DNS-rebinding attacker swaps in an internal IP after validation.' probe_source is a connecting caller and breaks this contract; start_session correctly pins via _pin_url (line 128) but probe does not.
findings.failure_scenario: Attacker registers a source at http(s)/rtsp://attacker-domain/... resolving to a benign public IP. They call POST /api/v1/sources/{id}/probe; between _check_ssrf's getaddrinfo and ffprobe's own resolution the domain is rebound to 169.254.169.254 or an internal service. ffprobe connects to the internal target (CWE-918), and probe metadata/errors can leak internal responses.
findings.fix: Return the Resolved from _check_ssrf and probe the pinned IP: `resolved = self._check_ssrf(url); await self._engine.probe(self._pin_url(url, resolved.ip), transport=src.transport)`, exactly as start_session does.

findings.title: Reservation release uses CURRENT config, not what was actually reserved — a cap toggle leaks or steals slots
findings.detail: _release_map() (lines 398-402) reconstructs 'what a live session holds' from the CURRENT StreamConfig (max_concurrent_per_tenant, max_concurrent_global, one_session_per_source) rather than from the `taken` map recorded at reservation time. _reserve_quota only increments a dimension when its cap was truthy at start (lines 373-384: `if cap and ...`). If config changes between a session's start and its stop, the release no longer matches the reservation.
findings.failure_scenario: Cap raised 0 -> N (or one_session_per_source false -> true) after sessions were started: those sessions took NO tenant/source reservation, but _stop now sees the dimension enabled and calls _decr, decrementing a counter this session never incremented — stealing a live slot from another session and letting the cap be BREACHED. Cap lowered N -> 0 (feature disabled): sessions that DID reserve are stopped with _release_map returning false, so _decr is never called and the counter permanently retains phantom `live` counts; re-enabling the cap leaves every tenant with a reduced effective ceiling (self-DoS). Config changes are routine (redeploys/panel edits), so this is not exotic.
findings.fix: Persist the `taken` map on the session (e.g. sess.placement['reserved'] or a dedicated field) at start_session and release exactly that set in _stop, instead of recomputing from live config. Reservations must be released against what was taken, not against present configuration.

findings.title: Reservation leaks when session-row creation fails after placement (create is outside the rollback try/except)
findings.detail: In start_session the try/except BaseException (lines 144-157) wraps ONLY self._placer.start(); the reservation rollback _release_quota(reserved, sess) fires only if placer.start raises. The subsequent self._sessions.create(sess) (line 161) is OUTSIDE that block. If create() fails (datastore error, pool exhaustion), the exception propagates with the quota already reserved AND the engine already placed, but NO session row exists.
findings.failure_scenario: Datastore hiccup at line 161: tenant/global counters stay incremented (and the source claim held) with no session row. The reaper's placer.reconcile(seen) will kill the orphan engine handle (killed_orphans), but nothing ever calls _stop for a non-existent session, so the reservation is never released -> permanent slot consumption. Repeated occurrences erode the tenant/global cap toward zero.
findings.fix: Extend the rollback to cover session creation: put _sessions.create inside the try, or wrap reserve+place+create so any failure runs _release_quota(reserved, sess). Also stop the placement on create failure to avoid the orphan engine.

findings.title: Playback HMAC key falls back to INTERNAL_SERVICE_TOKEN with no production boot guard — internal token holders can forge cross-tenant playback tokens
findings.detail: _playback_secret() returns `s.PLAYBACK_SIGNING_SECRET or s.INTERNAL_SERVICE_TOKEN` (container.py:204-205). PLAYBACK_SIGNING_SECRET defaults to '' (config.py:479) and assert_stream_config_ok (config.py:534-544) has NO guard requiring it in production (unlike SEAL_KEY at line 539). HmacSignedPlayback.sign is a deterministic HMAC over {tenant,session,output,exp} (signed_playback.py:33-38). When the fallback is used, the service-to-service auth secret doubles as the media-token signing key.
findings.failure_scenario: In a production deployment where PLAYBACK_SIGNING_SECRET is left unset, any party that knows INTERNAL_SERVICE_TOKEN (every peer service authorized to call /internal/*, plus anything that logs/leaks it) can locally compute a valid playback token for ANY tenant+session+output and pull live HLS/snapshot media, bypassing tenant isolation on the media plane. Blast radius couples S2S auth compromise to media-access forgery.
findings.fix: Require a dedicated PLAYBACK_SIGNING_SECRET in production (add to assert_stream_config_ok) and refuse the INTERNAL_SERVICE_TOKEN fallback outside dev/test, matching the SEAL_KEY posture.

findings.title: Playback tokens are stateless with no revocation — media stays fetchable after a session is stopped or erased for the full TTL
findings.detail: verify() only checks signature + exp (lines 45-53); there is no binding to session liveness. _playback (stream_service.py:474-489) issues tokens with ttl = PLAYBACK_URL_TTL_SECONDS. Once minted, a token remains valid until exp regardless of stop_session / erase / retention delete. TTL defaults to 60s but is operator-configurable to larger values.
findings.failure_scenario: A session is stopped (user or guard) or its footage erased for a privacy request; a token already handed to a viewer keeps working until exp. With a raised PLAYBACK_URL_TTL_SECONDS the exposure window widens accordingly. Combined with stream-r2-06 (forgeable tokens) the window is unbounded.
findings.fix: Keep the TTL short and documented as the hard revocation ceiling; if stronger revocation is needed, have the media origin check the session is still LIVE (or maintain a short deny-list of stopped session ids) before serving. At minimum, cap PLAYBACK_URL_TTL_SECONDS in config validation.

findings.title: SSRF metadata/loopback checks may be bypassed by an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address on allow_private deployments
findings.detail: The block list is a string-exact _METADATA set plus addr.is_loopback/is_link_local/is_private checks (lines 58-65). A resolver returning an IPv4-mapped IPv6 form such as ::ffff:169.254.169.254 will not string-match '169.254.169.254', and Python's ipaddress classifiers for IPv6 do not consistently delegate to the embedded IPv4 for is_link_local. On an on-prem deployment with STREAM_ALLOW_PRIVATE=true, the is_private branch (the only one that would catch the mapped range) is skipped, leaving link-local/metadata reachable via the mapped form.
findings.failure_scenario: Attacker-controlled DNS returns ::ffff:169.254.169.254 (or a mapped link-local) for a registered source/ONVIF host on an allow_private deployment; validation passes and ffmpeg/ffprobe connects to metadata/link-local. Requires the resolver/getaddrinfo to yield the mapped form, so exploitability is environment-dependent.
findings.fix: Normalize each resolved address before classification: if addr is an IPv6Address with .ipv4_mapped, re-check the embedded IPv4 against all rules (metadata set, loopback, link-local, private). Reject mapped forms outright unless explicitly needed.

findings.title: Hard crash between _incr and session-row creation leaks a reservation the reaper can never reclaim
findings.detail: _incr (lines 404-420) documents that the reservation counter is deliberately NOT reconciled against live session rows, because during a start burst the rows do not exist yet. Reservations are bumped before _sessions.create (line 161) and are only ever released on a session's LIVE->non-LIVE transition via _stop. If the process is killed (OOM, SIGKILL, node loss) after _incr commits but before/without a session row, there is no row for the reaper to _stop and no reconcile path -> the counted slot is orphaned permanently.
findings.failure_scenario: Under memory pressure or rolling restarts, starts that were mid-flight at kill time each leak one tenant+global slot. Because postgres persists the stream_quota counters across restarts, the leak survives the restart and accumulates, slowly starving the tenant/global concurrency caps until legitimate starts get 429. No operator-visible signal ties the drift to the cause.
findings.fix: Add a bounded, off-request reconciliation that (safely) rebuilds the reservation counters from the authoritative live-session count during a quiescent sweep window, or attach a short TTL/heartbeat to reservation rows so an orphaned reservation with no corresponding session row expires. Emit a metric for counter-vs-live drift.

findings.title: heartbeat has no session-ownership binding — any authorized internal caller can refresh any session's lease and inject arbitrary stats
findings.detail: POST /internal/stream/sessions/{session_id}/heartbeat (internal.py:102-108) is guarded only by require_internal_token and passes session_id + attacker-supplied stats straight into StreamService.heartbeat (stream_service.py:181-193), which loads the session by id with NO tenant/source/engine-identity check. heartbeat resets lease_expires_at (line 188) and stores stats verbatim (line 187).
findings.failure_scenario: A compromised or over-broadly-scoped internal caller (the internal tier is default-open per require_internal_token unless a per-route policy is configured) can (a) indefinitely refresh the lease of any session id, defeating the missed-heartbeat zombie-reaping backstop in _guard_breached (line 259), and (b) inject arbitrary stats including bytes_out to force a spurious max_size stop (line 191-192) of another tenant's session. Session ids are random UUIDs, so this needs a known/leaked id, bounding severity.
findings.fix: Bind the heartbeat to the placement/engine identity for that session (e.g. verify a per-session engine token or the placement handle id) and/or scope it by tenant. Constrain the internal-tier policy so only the media/engine caller may reach the heartbeat route.

findings.title: playback() and heartbeat()/motion save the full session via last-writer-wins put, clobbering concurrent field updates
findings.detail: SessionStore.save() is a plain store.put of the whole session row (stores.py:67-71), not a field-level or CAS update. playback() sets last_viewer_at then save() (stream_service.py:177-178); heartbeat() sets lease/stats then save() (188-193); poll_motion sets stats then save() (286-287). Concurrent calls load-modify-write the entire row, so overlapping updates lose each other's fields.
findings.failure_scenario: A viewer poll (updating last_viewer_at) racing an engine heartbeat (updating lease_expires_at/stats) each read the same snapshot and write back their whole copy; the later write drops the other's change. E.g. a heartbeat's fresh lease is overwritten by a slightly older playback save that carried a stale lease, making a live session look lease-expired and get reaped early — or an idle-timeout viewer bump is lost so an active session is stopped as idle. Not a direct security breach but affects the guard/quota correctness the round-1 work depends on.
findings.fix: Apply targeted CAS/field updates for the hot mutable fields (last_viewer_at, lease_expires_at, stats) instead of whole-row put, or serialize per-session mutations, so concurrent heartbeat/playback/motion updates compose rather than clobber.

findings.title: Raw principal.subject written as audit `actor` into the immutable hash-chained audit log on every ticket route
findings.detail: Every user-facing ticket route calls request.app.state.auditor.record(..., actor=principal.subject, ...) with the RAW JWT `sub` claim (an email or user id — auth.py:32 `subject=str(claims.get("sub",""))`). Auditor.record (app/core/audit.py:68-103) does NOT pseudonymize `actor`; it stores it verbatim in the AuditEvent (audit.py:79) which is emitted into an append-only, hash-chained sink. This directly contradicts (a) the project rule captured in memory ('audit resource= takes subject_ref not a raw person'), (b) operator.py which carefully pseudonymizes with _actor() (operator.py:50-56) before every operator.* audit call, and (c) internal.py grantee routes which audit with the pseudonymous gref. Affected calls: ticket.created (tickets.py:118), ticket.replied (199), ticket.status_changed (323), ticket.escalated (347), ticket.assigned (363).
findings.failure_scenario: A customer opens a ticket. Their email (JWT sub) is written raw into the immutable audit chain as the actor of ticket.created. Because the chain is tamper-evident, the value can never be redacted without breaking verify(). A later DSAR erase (internal.py:85 -> erasure.py) only touches the `tickets` and `ticket_events` collections and matches by pseudonym, so the raw email persists in the audit log forever — an un-erasable PII record and a GDPR/PDPL right-to-erasure failure.
findings.fix: Pseudonymize before auditing exactly as operator.py does: pass actor=subject_ref(PII_SALT, tenant, principal.subject) (or a shared helper) for every auditor.record call in tickets.py. Alternatively make Auditor.record pseudonymize actor centrally, but the per-call helper keeps the pattern uniform with operator.py/internal.py.

findings.title: Operator raw identity stored in the immutable ticket_events.actor_ref (reply/transition/escalate/assign)
findings.detail: In reply() `actor_ref = author if is_operator else self.pseudonym(...)` (ticket_service.py:92); transition() `actor_ref = actor if is_operator else ...` (line 129); escalate() same (line 152); assign() appends actor_ref=actor raw (line 167). For operator actions the RAW principal.subject is persisted into ticket_events, an append-only 'HISTORY IS THE TRUTH' log. The TicketEvent model doc claims actor_ref is 'pseudonym of who acted (raiser or operator)' (models.py:111) — the code violates its own contract. DSAR erasure (erasure.py:64) redacts event bodies only where actor_ref == subject_ref(...) i.e. a pseudonym, so a raw operator id is never matched and never redacted.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator (agent email in JWT sub) replies to and resolves a ticket. Their raw email is written into ticket_events.actor_ref for the replied/status_changed events. If that operator later exercises their own erasure right, erasure.erase() computes their pseudonym and matches zero events, returning already_absent while their raw email remains in the immutable log.
findings.fix: Always pseudonymize the actor into actor_ref for the log (operator identities included), keeping a separate non-PII role label (the existing `by`/is_operator flag) for KPI classification. If an operator's real handle must be shown in an operator UI, resolve it at read time from a reversible store, never persist it raw in the event log.

findings.title: assign/tag/rate/escalate use plain save() and clobber a concurrent CAS status transition
findings.detail: Round 1 made transition() atomic via cas_save (ticket_service.py:133, TicketStore.cas_save stores version-pinned). But assign() (line 165), tag() (line 174), rate() (line 187) and escalate() (line 154) all call self._tickets.save(t) -> DataStore.put (stores.py:21-23), an unconditional upsert that writes the whole row (including the stale status and the stale version read before the mutation). put ignores the optimistic-lock version entirely.
findings.failure_scenario: Concurrent paths: operator A POSTs /tickets/{id}/status open->resolved (cas succeeds, row now version N+1, status=resolved); operator B POSTs /tickets/{id}/assign at the same time, having fetched the row at version N/status=open. B sets assignee and calls save()->put, overwriting the row with status=open, no resolution, and version=N. The status_changed event still exists in the log but the projection every read uses has silently reverted to open — the ticket looks un-resolved, and the version counter is rolled back so a subsequent stale CAS could also misfire. The atomicity round 1 added is defeated by any sibling mutator.
findings.fix: Route all mutations that persist the ticket row through the same CAS-retry loop transition() uses (fetch -> mutate -> cas_save -> retry on False), or restrict save() to inserts only and make every projection update version-checked.

findings.title: Inbound thread-grouping index is get-then-put (TOCTOU) — concurrent messages open duplicate tickets for one customer
findings.detail: The external-id idempotency claim is atomic (cas on _INGESTED, inbound_bridge.py:83), but the per-customer thread GROUPING is not: idx = await self._store.get(_THREAD, tkey) (line 92), then on a miss open() a ticket and self._store.put(_THREAD, tkey, {ticket_id}) (line 103). There is no CAS/lock on the thread key. Two DISTINCT external_ids from the same (tenant, channel, sender) each pass their own idempotency claim and race this read-modify-write.
findings.failure_scenario: Concurrent paths: a scheduled poll batch (ingest_batch) plus a retry, or two pods, process two different inbound messages from the same phone number within the same window. Both call get(_THREAD, tkey) -> empty, both call svc.open(), producing TWO open tickets, then both put the thread index (last writer wins). The documented invariant 'one open ticket per customer per channel' (module docstring, lines 12-14) is violated, and one of the two tickets is orphaned from the thread index so future replies never append to it.
findings.fix: Reserve the thread slot atomically: cas(_THREAD, tkey, 0, {"ticket_id": placeholder}) as an insert-if-absent before opening, then update it with the real ticket_id; the loser of the race re-reads and appends to the winner's ticket. Alternatively serialize per (tenant,channel,sender).

findings.title: Shared-tickets list pages the ENTIRE tenant when the grant scope is narrow (O(tenant rows) per request)
findings.detail: list_shared_tickets loops `while len(covered) <= cap:` calling tickets.find(tenant=tenant, limit=cap+1, after=cursor) and post-filtering with grant.covers, breaking only when cap+1 covered rows are found OR the tenant is exhausted (internal.py:320-326). The comment acknowledges this was chosen over a single page to fix an under-read, but it converts a bounded read into a scan of the whole tenant whenever the grant's scope matches few tickets.
findings.failure_scenario: A tenant with 1,000,000 tickets grants a partner a scope of {"type":["vip"]} that matches 3 tickets. Each GET /internal/tickets?tenant&grantee pages through all ~1M rows (≈5000 find() round trips at cap=200) before returning. A grantee (or an internal caller holding the shared token) can repeat this cheaply, exhausting the DB pool (postgres pool_max is small, postgres.py:75) and starving every other request — a request-path amplification/DoS.
findings.fix: Cap total pages scanned per request (e.g. a max_pages / max_rows budget) and return `truncated=true` with a continuation cursor when the budget is hit, so the read stays O(budget). Better: push the scope filter (type/status allowlists) into the find() where-clause so the datastore returns only covered rows.

findings.title: Inbound idempotency key is not tenant-scoped
findings.detail: ikey = f"{msg.channel}:{msg.external_id}" (inbound_bridge.py:77) keys the dedupe claim on channel+external_id only, omitting tenant — despite the thread key being carefully length-prefixed with tenant (line 54) and the project's own 'tenant-scoped idempotency' lesson ('a global key = cross-tenant unbilled usage'). external_id is trusted to be globally unique (a WhatsApp wamid is), but the primitive is documented as channel-agnostic ('any channel tomorrow'), and a channel whose external ids are only unique PER tenant (an incrementing per-account id, a per-shop reference) would collide.
findings.failure_scenario: A future/second inbound channel issues sender-scoped or tenant-scoped message ids. Tenant A ingests message id 42 (claims 'chan:42'). Tenant B legitimately receives its own message id 42; ingest() finds the claim present and returns 'skipped', silently dropping tenant B's customer message — a cross-tenant message loss and a support gap.
findings.fix: Length-prefix the tenant into ikey exactly as _thread_key does: f"{len(tenant)}:{tenant}|{channel}:{external_id}".

findings.title: Grantee write routes bypass the per-type reply_capability enforcement
findings.detail: Round 1 added reply-capability enforcement — but only in the user-facing route (tickets.py:194-197 checks svc.reply_capability_for(t.type) for non-operators). TicketService.reply() itself performs no capability check (ticket_service.py:88-102). The internal grantee reply route (internal.py:447 reply_as_grantee -> svc.reply) and grantee open (internal.py:415) call the core directly with is_operator=False and never consult reply_capability_for. Enforcement therefore lives in the route, not the core, contradicting the service docstring's claim that rules are 'ENFORCED here, in the core, not trusted from the client' (ticket_service.py:2-7).
findings.failure_scenario: A tenant configures a ticket type with reply_capability set to a restricted capability (e.g. 'billing.agent'). A write-consented grantee replies via POST /internal/tickets/{id}/replies; the reply is accepted regardless of the type's reply_capability because only the grant's write flag is checked. The consent model (write) is the intended authority here, so impact is limited, but the per-type reply restriction is silently unenforced for grantees and any future non-HTTP caller.
findings.fix: Move the reply_capability check into TicketService.reply (accept the caller's capability set / class) so every path — HTTP, grantee, inbound — is judged by the same core rule, or explicitly document that grant.write supersedes reply_capability and assert that intent in a test.

findings.title: Consent share grants never expire by default
findings.detail: TICKET_SHARE_DEFAULT_TTL_SECONDS defaults to 0 (config.py:191). grant_share computes expires_at = (time.time()+ttl) if ttl>0 else 0.0 (internal.py:263,269), and ShareGrant.is_active treats expires_at==0 as 'never' (share.py:82-84). So unless a caller explicitly passes ttl_seconds, a grant is perpetual — contradicting the share.py module doc that consent is 'time-boxed by nature' (share.py:16-17).
findings.failure_scenario: A platform records a partner share without specifying a TTL (the easy default). The partner retains scoped read/write access to the tenant's tickets indefinitely, surviving until someone remembers to explicitly revoke. Consent that outlives its purpose is a privacy-minimization failure.
findings.fix: Ship a non-zero default TTL (e.g. 90 days) or refuse a grant with no effective expiry, so 'forever' is an explicit, audited choice rather than the default.

findings.title: is_subject_ref self-fold lets a subject shaped like a pseudonym be stored unpseudonymized
findings.detail: subject_ref() returns the input unchanged when is_subject_ref(subject) is true (pii.py:51-52), i.e. any string starting with 'sub_' and exactly 36 chars long (pii.py:59-61). The idempotence is intended so erasure can re-hash a ref without double-wrapping, but it means a raw subject that happens to match that shape is persisted verbatim as if it were already a pseudonym.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller-controlled identifier that reaches pseudonym()/subject_ref — a grantee handle (_grantee_ref folds 'grantee:<handle>' which won't match, so safe), or a token `sub` claim, or a future channel sender — that is literally 'sub_' + 32 hex chars would be stored as-is in raiser_ref/actor_ref, defeating pseudonymization for that record and making it non-erasable (erasure recomputes a different hash). Low likelihood given current inputs (phone numbers, emails, uuid subs), hence speculative.
findings.fix: Only treat a value as an existing pseudonym when the caller asserts it is one (a typed wrapper or an explicit already_ref flag), rather than inferring from a guessable prefix+length shape; or namespace the pseudonym prefix with a per-product secret component.

findings.title: Erasure does not clear ticket tags or event data that may carry derived content
findings.detail: erase() redacts ticket subject/meta/ref.id (erasure.py:44-49) and event body (line 68), but leaves ticket `tags` and event `data` intact. The suggester can auto-tag tickets from message content (referenced in tickets.py:48-50 SUGGEST_AUTOTAG_MIN_CONFIDENCE; tag() persists tags), so a tag string could echo a fragment of what the person wrote.
findings.failure_scenario: An AI auto-tag derived from a customer message body (e.g. a tag containing an order number, a name, or a quoted phrase) survives a DSAR erase because tags are never redacted. Whether any current suggester actually emits content-bearing tags was not confirmed in this pass, hence speculative.
findings.fix: If auto-tags can embed submitted content, clear tags (or a designated content-derived subset) during erase alongside subject/meta; confirm the suggester's tag vocabulary is a closed, non-PII set and document it.

findings.title: Event ordering seq is a per-process global; multi-pod/postgres appends order only by wall clock
findings.detail: seq_now() maintains a module-global _last_seq seeded from time.time_ns() and forced strictly increasing within one process (models.py:22-37). History reads sort by seq (stores.py:93-96). In the memory adapter (single process, tests) ordering is perfectly total. Under postgres with multiple pods, each process has its own _last_seq, so cross-pod ordering falls back to unsynchronized wall clocks; two events appended on different pods within the same tick (or under clock skew) can read back in the wrong relative order.
findings.failure_scenario: Two operators on two pods act on the same ticket near-simultaneously (a reply and a status change). Their events get seq values from independent clocks; the history/KPI derivation (first_response_at, resolution) may order them incorrectly, mis-stating 'who did what and when' — the exact property the log promises (models.py:3-6). Impact is a subtle KPI/ordering inaccuracy, not access control, hence low/speculative.
findings.fix: Use a datastore-side monotonic sequence (a per-ticket append counter via CAS, or a DB sequence/serial column) so ordering is globally total independent of pod-local state and wall-clock skew.

findings.title: allocate_slot number-idempotency not atomic: concurrent same-number finalize mints two ICVs
findings.detail: Atomic guard (create) is on icv:: only; number idempotency is a by_number() read + plain put on num:: (:180). Distinct-ICV guaranteed, not one-ICV-per-number.
findings.failure_scenario: Two concurrent finalize for the same number both pass by_number->None; A claims icv N, B claims N+1; two invoice rows for one number; the orphan is pending so the sweep signs+submits it -> same number filed twice under two ICVs.
findings.fix: Make num::{tenant}::{number} the atomicity authority: create() it first; on failure re-read and return the existing invoice before claiming any ICV.

findings.title: mark_signed saves the signed body before the CAS check and _sign ignores its False return -> concurrent double-sign forks chain + mutates a signed invoice
findings.detail: mark_signed does await self.save(inv) unconditionally, THEN the head-cas loop; a losing sign has already overwritten signed_xml/hash and returns False, but zatca_service.py:153 discards the return and still _submits.
findings.failure_scenario: Two overlapping sweep runs (or sweep vs resubmit) sign the same due invoice; non-deterministic SDK hash -> winner sets signed head=hashA, loser save() overwrites the stored invoice with hashB; successor binds PIH=hashA while ICV N stores hashB -> verify_chain pih_mismatch; both submitted to ZATCA; an already-signed invoice mutated.
findings.fix: Sign only if still pending (status CAS); do the head-CAS BEFORE persisting the signed body; have _sign honor a False mark_signed return (defer, do not submit).

findings.title: one permanently-unsignable ICV bricks every higher ICV for the tenant
findings.detail: Strict contiguous signing: ICV N defers until N-1 signed. If N-1 can never sign, N..inf defer then cap to terminal failed; a failed row leaves the swept set and resubmit cannot re-sign it -> head never advances, no recovery.
findings.failure_scenario: Invoice #500 has a bad qty (never signs); #501..#999 (valid) defer every sweep then cap to failed one by one -> a whole day of valid invoices lost behind one bad one.
findings.fix: Operator quarantine/re-slot for a stuck predecessor; keep failed invoices re-signable; alert when the contiguous head lags the reserved head.

findings.title: due_for_retry sort mixes None and float -> TypeError crashes the sweep on the memory adapter
findings.detail: sort=('next_retry_at','asc') over a swept set that legitimately holds both None (fresh pending / signed-before-schedule / post-crash) and float rows; memory adapter sort key mixes '' (str) and float -> Python 3 TypeError in find(); postgres orders jsonb null first and does not raise.
findings.failure_scenario: Any swept collection containing a None next_retry_at row crashes sweep() on the memory adapter (tests/dev), while postgres limps -> adapter divergence the port claims not to have.
findings.fix: In cursor._key coerce numeric sort fields to a numeric sentinel (inf/-inf) or normalize None to match jsonb-null ordering so both adapters agree.

findings.title: input validation narrower than build_ubl: bad qty/issued_at burns an ICV and 500s
findings.detail: _validate_invoice_input checks currency + amount_minor but not qty or issued_at; build_ubl int()-coerces both (ubl.py:58,83) AFTER allocate_slot burns the ICV.
findings.failure_scenario: Payload with qty:'x' passes validation, burns an ICV, then build_ubl raises ValueError -> uncaught 500; the burned unbuildable pending row then stalls the chain tail (see r2-03), re-raising forever.
findings.fix: Validate qty and issued_at (every field build_ubl coerces) in _validate_invoice_input, and/or wrap build_ubl so a build error is a 422 that never consumes the slot.

findings.title: resubmit cannot re-sign a sign-capped failed invoice; submits an empty signed_xml
findings.detail: resubmit re-signs only status in (none,pending); a 'failed' row capped while awaiting signing has no signed_xml, so resubmit skips signing and submits '' -> rejected (terminal).
findings.failure_scenario: An invoice capped to failed during sign-deferral is unrecoverable: resubmit submits an empty document the gateway rejects.
findings.fix: In resubmit, re-sign whenever not inv.signed_xml (or status in {none,pending,failed} and unsigned).

findings.title: crash mid-allocate_slot orphans an icv:: claim -> permanent unrecoverable ICV gap
findings.detail: icv:: claim, invoice save, and num:: write are three non-transactional steps; a crash after the claim leaves icv::N with no invoice; a later finalize skips past it -> permanent gap at N -> verify_chain icv_gap forever.
findings.failure_scenario: Crash between the create(icv) and save(invoice) leaves an orphan ICV claim; the chain gaps and never reconciles.
findings.fix: Allocate the invoice row and ICV claim in one transaction, or have the sweep reconcile/reclaim an icv:: claim with no invoice.

findings.title: classify marks an empty/partial 2xx as success -> a standard invoice cleared with no cleared XML
findings.detail: accepted = status in (CLEARED,REPORTED) OR (2xx and no NOT_ and no errors); an empty-body 2xx satisfies the second clause; for a standard invoice clearedInvoice is None so cleared_xml='' yet status='cleared' (terminal).
findings.failure_scenario: A body-less 2xx from the gateway marks a clearance invoice cleared with no stamped legal document, never retried -> silently non-compliant record.
findings.fix: For clearance, require clearanceStatus==CLEARED AND a non-empty clearedInvoice; treat a body-less 2xx as transient (pending).

findings.title: standard-invoice QR taken from the pre-clearance sign response, not the ZATCA-stamped cleared response
findings.detail: inv.qr = signed.get('qrBase64') at sign time; cleared_xml arrives later at :188 and the QR is never re-derived from it.
findings.failure_scenario: A B2B standard invoice may print a pre-clearance QR lacking ZATCA's clearance stamp. Needs SDK QR-semantics domain review.
findings.fix: For standard invoices, extract/replace the QR from the cleared response after successful clearance.

findings.title: unseal swallows all errors -> a wrong/rotated seal key silently strands every invoice as 'not onboarded'
findings.detail: unseal except: return None; load_secrets returns None on any decrypt failure; finalize/sweep treat None identically to never-onboarded.
findings.failure_scenario: A rotated/misconfigured seal_key or corrupted CSID bytes is indistinguishable from 'not onboarded'; every invoice defers indefinitely with a misleading message, no alarm.
findings.fix: Distinguish 'no CSID stored' from 'CSID present but undecryptable'; log/raise loudly on decrypt failure.

findings.title: finalize 500s (not 422) on a missing number, before validation
findings.detail: by_number(str(invoice_in['number'])) raises KeyError if 'number' absent -> unhandled 500; no ICV burned (precedes allocate_slot).
findings.failure_scenario: A payload without number 500s instead of a clean 422.
findings.fix: Validate presence of number in _validate_invoice_input and guard the lookup.

findings.title: Auth, capability and rate-limit decisions use the non-normalized inbound path while the upstream receives the httpx-normalized (dot-segment-collapsed) path
findings.detail: handle() decides routing (self._routes.match(path)), auth mode, capabilities (holds_any) and the rate-limit class (policy.classify(path)) from request.url.path, which uvicorn/httptools does NOT collapse of '..' or decoded '%2e%2e'. build_url() (app/core/models.py:45) then appends the raw remainder to the fixed upstream and hands it to HttpxForwarder, and httpx.AsyncClient normalizes RFC-3986 dot-segments before sending. Verified: Route(prefix='/public').build_url('/public/../admin/secret') => 'http://up:8000/../admin/secret', and httpx.URL(...) collapses it to 'http://up:8000/admin/secret'. So the gateway authorizes the request as if it were '/public/...' (auth=none, no caps, default/loose rate-limit class) but the upstream actually serves '/admin/secret'. Test suites miss this because the httpx-based Starlette TestClient normalizes the URL client-side before it ever reaches the app.
findings.failure_scenario: Operator maps two prefixes on one service to differing policy, e.g. route {'/api/v1/shop' auth=none} and {'/api/v1/shop/admin' auth=required caps=[shop.admin]}, both -> http://shop:8000. An anonymous attacker requests GET /api/v1/shop/..%2fadmin/orders (or /api/v1/shop/../admin/orders). The gateway matches the auth=none route, skips the JWT/caps check, forwards, and httpx delivers /admin/orders to the shop service with the trusted X-Internal-Token but NO identity headers. Separately, a brute-force attacker dodges the strict login rate-limit class: /somepublic/../api/v1/auth/login is classified under the loose default class because it does not startswith '/api/v1/auth', yet is delivered to the auth login upstream. The internal tier itself stays protected (the 'internal' segment survives in the pre-normalization string that _targets_internal inspects), but every other cross-prefix policy boundary on a shared upstream is bypassable.
findings.fix: Normalize/reject dot-segments BEFORE any routing/auth/rate-limit decision: collapse '.'/'..' and reject any path that escapes (contains '..' after decode) with 400, and reject raw '%2e'/'%2f' encoded separators. Apply the exact same normalized path to match(), classify(), the auth check AND build_url() so the authorized path and the forwarded path are byte-identical. A canonicalization helper run once at the top of handle() (and used to build the forward URL) closes the divergence.

findings.title: Response cache (default memory driver) has no size bound or proactive eviction; attacker-varied query strings grow it without limit
findings.detail: MemoryCache._data is a plain dict; entries are only removed lazily when that exact key is read again (_expired) or on close(). The gateway cache key is 'gw:{method}:{path}?{query}' (app/core/gateway.py:128) and an anonymous GET on any auth!=required route with cache_ttl>0 is stored (lines 150-151). CACHE_DRIVER defaults to 'memory'.
findings.failure_scenario: On a deployment that enables a cache_ttl for a public GET route, an unauthenticated attacker issues GET /public/thing?x=<random> with a unique query string on every request. Each distinct key is stored for the full TTL with the full response body base64-encoded in RAM, and nothing evicts keys except a later hit on the same (never-repeated) key. The process RSS climbs until OOM-kill — a single-source memory-exhaustion DoS that needs no auth.
findings.fix: Bound the memory cache (max entries + LRU eviction, or a periodic sweep of expired keys), and/or refuse to cache when the query string is present/over a length. At minimum cap entry count and evict oldest. Same lazy-only-eviction issue affects MemoryRateLimiter._tats (app/adapters/rate_limiter/memory.py) — see r2-06.

findings.title: Only 4 client headers are stripped before forwarding; client-supplied X-Forwarded-For / X-Real-IP / Forwarded pass through to upstreams
findings.detail: _forward_headers() drops only _HOP_BY_HOP + _STRIP_FROM_CLIENT ({x-internal-token, x-user-id, x-tenant-id, x-caps}). Every other client header, including X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP, Forwarded, X-Original-URL, X-Rewrite-URL, is copied verbatim to the upstream. The gateway itself reads XFF correctly via trusted_proxy_hops, but it does not sanitize or overwrite XFF on the way out.
findings.failure_scenario: An upstream service that trusts X-Forwarded-For / X-Real-IP for its own rate-limiting, audit 'ip' field, or IP allow-listing receives whatever the client forged, because the gateway forwarded the client's value unchanged. An attacker sets X-Forwarded-For: <trusted-internal-IP> or spoofs the source IP recorded in a downstream audit log. Also X-Original-URL/X-Rewrite-URL can confuse some frameworks' routing.
findings.fix: After computing the real client IP, set a canonical X-Forwarded-For (append the real peer) and X-Real-IP yourself and strip inbound copies; add X-Forwarded-Proto/Host from the gateway's view. Consider an allowlist of forwardable headers rather than a denylist so a new sensitive header is safe by default.

findings.title: Shared anonymous response cache keyed only on method+path+query ignores Accept/Accept-Language and other representation-selecting request headers
findings.detail: cacheable responses are keyed as 'gw:{method}:{path}?{query}'. _is_storable() refuses responses carrying Vary, Set-Cookie, or no-store/private/no-cache, which mitigates the classic case. But an upstream that content-negotiates (returns JSON vs HTML by Accept, or localized bodies by Accept-Language) WITHOUT emitting a Vary header will have the first anonymous representation cached and replayed to every subsequent anonymous caller regardless of their request headers.
findings.failure_scenario: Anonymous client A requests a public endpoint with Accept-Language: ar and the upstream (not emitting Vary) returns Arabic. It is cached. Anonymous client B with Accept-Language: en receives the cached Arabic body for the TTL. Not a data-leak (anonymous only) but a correctness/cache-poisoning issue; an attacker can also 'pin' an unusual representation for all users by racing the first request.
findings.fix: Include the negotiated request headers the gateway is willing to serve from cache in the cache key (or refuse to cache unless the upstream sets an explicit public Cache-Control). Given the gateway cannot know the upstream's Vary intent, defaulting to cache only when upstream explicitly opts in (public/max-age present) is safer than caching on absence of directives.

findings.title: Upstream responses are fully buffered into memory (resp.content); no response-size cap
findings.detail: HttpxForwarder.forward returns resp.content, reading the entire upstream body into RAM, and the gateway then builds Response(content=resp_body). BODY_LIMIT_BYTES caps the REQUEST body but nothing caps the RESPONSE. follow_redirects=False is good (prevents redirect-driven SSRF). The upstream is config-fixed and generally trusted, hence low severity.
findings.failure_scenario: A compromised or buggy upstream, or an upstream endpoint that streams a very large/unbounded body (e.g. an export), makes the gateway buffer the whole payload per concurrent request; enough concurrent large responses exhaust gateway memory. Also negates streaming for large legitimate downloads.
findings.fix: Stream the upstream response (httpx stream + StreamingResponse) and enforce a max response size, aborting with 502 when exceeded; only buffer when caching a small response.

findings.title: MemoryRateLimiter._tats grows unbounded with distinct keys (no eviction of expired TATs)
findings.detail: _tats maps every seen key to its TAT and is only pruned on reset(); expired keys are never swept. Keys are composite (class|subject/ip/tenant). This is also the fallback used by the redis driver during a Redis outage.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker able to generate many distinct key components (distinct subjects via many tokens, or distinct IPs when GATEWAY_TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS>0 and XFF is attacker-influenced within the untrusted left portion — though the trusted index mitigates) grows the dict without bound. More realistically, over a long uptime with many legitimate subjects the dict only grows. Memory pressure over time / during a Redis outage when the local fallback absorbs the whole fleet's key space.
findings.fix: Add TTL-based eviction (drop a key once its TAT is in the past) via a periodic sweep or an OrderedDict/LRU with a max-entries cap; this matches the redis driver's self-evicting PX TTL.

findings.title: Internal-tier per-route caller policy is default-OPEN and token fallback is default-ON
findings.detail: require_internal_token() authorizes a caller against INTERNAL_ROUTE_POLICY_JSON, but a route absent from that map 'admits any authenticated caller (default-open)' (config.py:135-138), and INTERNAL_CALLER_ALLOW_TOKEN_FALLBACK defaults True so a request with only the shared flat token (no signed assertion) is accepted as an unnamed peer even under the static/jwks drivers. This is a documented migration posture, but it means the strongest per-caller controls are opt-in and the default trusts anyone holding the one shared token.
findings.failure_scenario: If the shared INTERNAL_SERVICE_TOKEN leaks (it is injected into every forwarded upstream request as X-Internal-Token, so it is present on a very wide blast radius), any party holding it reaches every /internal route on the gateway (e.g. POST /internal/privacy/erase, GET /internal/routes revealing the full upstream map) because no per-route allow-list is configured by default and no per-caller assertion is required. Defense-in-depth degrades to a single shared secret.
findings.fix: Ship a default-deny INTERNAL_ROUTE_POLICY for sensitive routes (privacy/erase, routes, assistant-catalog) and plan to flip INTERNAL_CALLER_ALLOW_TOKEN_FALLBACK off once callers sign; document the flip as a hardening milestone, not an option.

findings.title: TimeoutMiddleware (BaseHTTPMiddleware + asyncio.wait_for) cancels the handler but the in-flight upstream request may keep running
findings.detail: TimeoutMiddleware wraps call_next in asyncio.wait_for. On timeout it returns 408, cancelling the downstream task. With BaseHTTPMiddleware, cancellation of a task blocked in the httpx upstream call is not guaranteed to promptly release the upstream connection, and BaseHTTPMiddleware has known interactions with cancellation/anyio task groups that can surface as secondary errors. REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS (30s) is also larger than UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT_SECONDS (15s), so normally the forwarder times out first (good), but a slow limiter/verify path under the 30s budget can still be cut mid-flight.
findings.failure_scenario: Under load with slow upstreams, requests that hit the 30s wall-clock are cancelled at the middleware while the httpx request continues to completion in the background, transiently holding upstream connections/pool slots beyond the client-visible 408; repeated, this amplifies connection pressure during exactly the incident the timeout exists to contain.
findings.fix: Rely on the forwarder's own timeout as the primary control and/or implement the wall-clock timeout as pure-ASGI with explicit cancellation of the upstream request; ensure UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT_SECONDS < REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS (currently true) is asserted at boot.

findings.title: /metrics is exposed with no authentication
findings.detail: The /metrics route serves the full Prometheus registry (including prometheus_fastapi_instrumentator RED metrics grouped by route template) with no token or network guard at the app layer. Comment explicitly states 'public, no auth'.
findings.failure_scenario: If the gateway's /metrics is reachable from outside the cluster (misconfigured ingress/NetworkPolicy), an attacker enumerates route templates, request volumes, latency and error patterns — operational reconnaissance (which endpoints exist, which are failing/under attack). Typically mitigated by NetworkPolicy, but the app provides no defense of its own.
findings.fix: Bind /metrics to the internal tier (require X-Internal-Token) or a separate admin port, or document a hard NetworkPolicy requirement that scrapers are the only reachable clients.

findings.title: _targets_internal is case-sensitive and matches only the literal segment 'internal'
findings.detail: _targets_internal('/Internal/audit') returns False (verified). The guard relies on downstream services mounting the internal tier at lowercase '/internal' and on HTTP path case-sensitivity, which holds for the current fleet (Starlette/FastAPI route matching is case-sensitive, so an upstream would not serve '/Internal/...' either). No exploit found, but the guard's safety depends on an assumption about every present and future upstream's path-matching being case-sensitive.
findings.failure_scenario: A future or third-party upstream (a customer's own product service added via ADMIN_SERVICES / route table) that matches paths case-insensitively, or normalizes case, could serve its internal tier for a '/Internal/...' request that this guard let through as a non-internal path. No such upstream exists today.
findings.fix: Lower-case the path before the segment test (p.lower()), and treat any segment equal to 'internal' case-insensitively; cheap and removes the dependence on upstream case behavior.

findings.title: undo() is not a true rollback: rows the restore INSERTED are never removed
findings.detail: A restore takes a whole-service pre-restore snapshot (_snapshot, tenant="") of the target's CURRENT state, then calls import_archive. import_archive INSERTS any archived row whose id is absent from the target (backup.py:161-164, `inserted`). undo()/_undo_one (restore.py:278-301) rolls back by re-importing that snapshot with overwrite=True. import_archive only put()s keys that exist in the snapshot body; it has no delete path. Therefore any row the restore inserted (a key that did NOT exist before the restore, so it is absent from the snapshot) is left in place after undo. The docstrings claim undo 'put[s] back exactly what was there before' (restore.py:250) and that restore is 'undoable' (restore.py:15-17), which is false whenever the restored archive contained rows newer/absent than the live target.
findings.failure_scenario: Operator restores run R into a service to recover from a bad deploy. The archive holds 10k rows the live target no longer has; import reports inserted=10k. The restore turns out wrong, operator clicks undo. undo re-applies the pre-restore snapshot (overwrite) but the 10k inserted rows remain, because they are not keys in the snapshot. The service is left in a state that is neither pre- nor post-restore, and the 'safety net' silently failed. In the into_tenant clone case this leaves an unbounded set of foreign rows under the destination tenant that undo cannot reach.
findings.fix: Make undo authoritative: capture the exact set of keys import_archive wrote (return inserted keys, or diff snapshot-vs-current) and have undo delete keys that were inserted by the restore in addition to overwriting snapshot keys. Alternatively snapshot the full key set and, on undo, delete any live key in the affected collections that is absent from the snapshot. Do not advertise 'undoable' until inserts are reversible.

findings.title: Global-collection export silently TRUNCATES at scan_cap instead of failing; incomplete archive still passes checksum, verify and drill
findings.detail: _read_collection's non-tenant path returns `await datastore.scan_all(name, scan_cap)` and the docstring/comment claims it is 'Bounded by scan_cap so a runaway collection fails the backup rather than exhausting memory' (backup.py:58-60). But scan_all in BOTH adapters truncates silently with no signal: MemoryDataStore.scan_all returns `rows[:limit]` (memory.py:73-76) and PostgresDataStore.scan_all runs `... ORDER BY key LIMIT $2` returning at most `limit` rows (postgres.py:209-222). Nothing raises when the collection exceeds scan_cap (default BACKUP_MAX_ROWS_PER_COLLECTION=5_000_000, config.py:162). The archive is then sealed over only the truncated rows, the checksum matches, verify_restore round-trips the truncated set (checked==expected because expected is computed from the truncated body), and the drill re-verifies the same truncated bytes. Every honesty mechanism reports OK over a backup that is missing rows.
findings.failure_scenario: A global (tenant_scoped:false) collection grows past 5,000,000 rows. The nightly backup captures only the first 5,000,000 by key order; the run is marked ok+verified, health is green, the drill passes. At restore time the archive faithfully restores an incomplete dataset and the rows past the cap are gone forever, discovered only when data is missing in production. The exact 'we have backups' lie the phase claims to kill.
findings.fix: Detect truncation: read scan_cap+1 (or have scan_all report whether more rows exist) and FAIL the target's export with a clear error when the cap is hit, exactly as the docstring promises. Never seal a knowingly-truncated collection. Same treatment needed for the per-tenant path (see backup-r2-05).

findings.title: HTTP redirects are auto-followed, bypassing the egress allowlist and leaking the internal token + resolved operator secret
findings.detail: post_json validates only the INITIAL url against EGRESS_ALLOWED_HOSTS and the metadata-host blocklist (_check_host, internal_http.py:33-53), then calls urllib.request.urlopen(req, ...) with the DEFAULT opener (internal_http.py:67). The default opener installs HTTPRedirectHandler, which auto-follows 3xx responses. The redirect target is NEVER re-checked by _check_host, and urllib carries custom headers across the redirect: X-Internal-Token (the shared fleet internal-tier secret) and X-Internal-Assertion, plus any operator secret resolved into an outbound header (assertion_headers_for_url / token_ref -> secret_store.get). Python's cross-host header stripping only covers Authorization/Cookie, not these custom headers. Every outbound path is affected: orchestrator export/verify, restore import, drill verify, snapshot export, and undo import.
findings.failure_scenario: A registered target (first- or third-party) is compromised or malicious. On /internal/backup/export it answers 302 Location: http://169.254.169.254/latest/... or http://attacker.example/collect. backup-service follows the redirect, re-sending X-Internal-Token and the target's resolved operator secret to the attacker/metadata endpoint. The attacker harvests the shared internal token (full internal-tier pivot across the fleet) and cloud credentials, all while the destination never appeared on EGRESS_ALLOWED_HOSTS. The metadata blocklist in _check_host is useless because it only sees the first hop.
findings.fix: Disable redirect following for these token-bearing calls: build an opener with a no-op/rejecting HTTPRedirectHandler (redirect_request returns None -> raise), or treat any 3xx as TargetUnreachable. If redirects must be supported, re-run _check_host (host allowlist + metadata block) on every redirect target and strip the X-Internal-Token/assertion/secret headers on any cross-host hop.

findings.title: into_tenant remaps EVERY tenant's rows in a whole-service archive into one tenant, with no single-tenant guard
findings.detail: import_archive applies `if into_tenant and "tenant" in row: row = {**row, "tenant": into_tenant}` to every row of every collection (backup.py:157-159). There is no check that the archive represents a single tenant. Restore/plan expose into_tenant directly (operator.py:242, internal.py:129) and the restore always applies the WHOLE stored archive (restore.py comment 196-198 states import has no tenant filter; the `tenant` arg does NOT scope the restore). A run captured whole-service (tenant="") contains every customer's rows, so restore-as-clone into_tenant=X collapses ALL customers' data under tenant X.
findings.failure_scenario: Support wants to stand up customer A's data in a sandbox tenant. They restore the latest (whole-service) run with into_tenant="sandbox". Instead of only A, every tenant's rows are rewritten with tenant="sandbox" and inserted, mixing all customers' PII/records under one accessible tenant — a cross-tenant disclosure created by the tool meant for isolation. With overwrite=True and colliding ids it also clobbers existing sandbox rows.
findings.fix: Refuse into_tenant unless the archive is single-tenant (body["tenant"] non-empty, or all remapped rows share one source tenant). For selective clone, require the source archive to have been captured per-tenant, or add a source-tenant filter to import so only that tenant's rows are remapped.

findings.title: Per-tenant export accumulates the entire tenant into memory with no scan_cap
findings.detail: The tenant-scoped branch of _read_collection pages with find() but appends every page into `out` and returns the whole list (backup.py:50-57); scan_cap is applied ONLY to the global scan_all branch (backup.py:60). export() then holds all collections' full row lists in `payload`, computes tenants_covered over them, and json.dumps the entire structure before sealing (backup.py:73-95). A single large tenant is fully materialised twice (list + serialised string) in one request.
findings.failure_scenario: A tenant with millions of rows triggers a per-tenant backup (or a pre-restore snapshot, which calls export). The service loads the entire tenant into RAM plus the serialised JSON copy, spiking memory and risking OOM/eventloop stalls on the backup pod — a self-inflicted DoS with no configured ceiling, in contrast to the (silently-truncating) global path which at least caps rows.
findings.fix: Apply a bound to the tenant path too (cap total rows and fail loudly when exceeded, like backup-r2-02 recommends), and/or stream the archive to the object store instead of building the whole sealed body in memory.

findings.title: RunStore.recent() returns the OLDEST 10k runs when run count exceeds _RECENT_SCAN, so 'latest run' can be stale
findings.detail: recent() does `rows = await scan_all(_COLL, _RECENT_SCAN=10_000)` then sorts newest-first and slices (runs.py:36-37). scan_all returns key-ASCENDING first N (memory.py:73-76 insertion-order-ish / postgres.py ORDER BY key), and run ids are `run_<timestamp>_...`, so the first 10k by key are the OLDEST runs. If more than 10k run records exist, the newest runs are never read; recent(1) then yields the newest of the OLDEST 10k — a stale run. tenant-coverage (internal.py:295 uses recent(1) as 'the latest run') and health/drill would reason over stale data.
findings.failure_scenario: Retention is disabled or the prune cron stalls (both possible: BACKUP_RETENTION_MAX_AGE_SECONDS default 0 = age-based off; prune is cron-driven). Runs accumulate past 10,000. A dispute-defense query GET /internal/backup/tenant-coverage answers 'covered/verified' against an ancient run while recent runs (which may show the tenant MISSED) are invisible — a confidently wrong compliance answer.
findings.fix: Have scan_all support a newest-first read (ORDER BY key DESC) for these control logs, or key the log so the DB can return the most recent N directly; alternatively raise if the scan hits _RECENT_SCAN so the truncation is observable rather than silently wrong.

findings.title: Pre-restore snapshots are never pruned
findings.detail: RetentionSweeper.prune only deletes objects listed as `archive_key` inside run results (retention.py:74-81).
