Pre-restore snapshots are stored under `{restore_id}/pre/{service}.json` (restore.py:240) and are referenced only from restore records (backup_restores), never from run results, so no code path ever deletes them.
findings.failure_scenario: Over months of restores/drills, snapshot objects accumulate unbounded in the object store, growing cost and, for the local adapter, disk until the store fills and future backups fail to store (orchestrator marks targets FAILED).
findings.fix: Add snapshot pruning tied to restore-record retention (delete snapshot_key objects when their restore record ages out), or a max-age sweep over the `*/pre/` prefix.

findings.title: Stored archive not bound to its run; an object-store writer can substitute an older valid same-service archive undetected
findings.detail: Integrity rests on _checksum over the `sealed` field and AES-GCM (backup.py:40-41,265-300). Neither binds the archive to its run_id or the recorded taken_at (taken_at lives inside the sealed body but is never compared to the run record on restore/drill). The stored object at `{run_id}/{service}.json` (orchestrator.py:115-117) is read back by key on restore (restore.py:208) and drill (drill.py:106) and accepted if checksum+unseal succeed.
findings.failure_scenario: An actor with write access to the object store (but without BACKUP_KEK) overwrites run R's archive for a service with that service's OWN older valid archive from run R-10. Checksum passes, GCM decrypts, verify/drill pass, and a restore from R silently restores stale data — a rollback attack the self-verifying design does not detect.
findings.fix: Bind the stored object to its run: include run_id in the sealed body and verify it matches the run record on restore/drill, or store the expected checksum in the run record and compare against the re-read object before trusting it.

findings.title: verify_restore passes archives with duplicate row ids that real import cannot faithfully restore
findings.detail: verify_restore writes each row into ns keyed by id then immediately reads it back and compares (backup.py:226-240). If a collection contains two rows sharing an id, each is written-then-read in its own iteration so both compare equal and count toward `checked`, and `verified` becomes true. But import_archive keys on id and (without overwrite) SKIPS the second, or (with overwrite) keeps only the last — so a real restore loses one of the duplicates. verify therefore reports an archive as faithfully restorable when it is not.
findings.failure_scenario: A target's export emits two rows with the same id (a schema/serialisation quirk). The archive verifies OK and drills green, but a real restore silently drops or overwrites one of the two rows, and the loss is never surfaced.
findings.fix: Detect duplicate ids per collection during verify_restore (and/or in verify/import) and fail the archive, since idempotent id-keyed restore is exactly the invariant the archive relies on.

findings.title: No response-size cap on target replies; a compromised target can OOM the orchestrator
findings.detail: post_json does `resp.read()` with no size limit (internal_http.py:68) and _parse json-loads the whole body. Export/verify responses are expected to be large, but there is no ceiling, so a hostile or buggy target can return an arbitrarily large body.
findings.failure_scenario: A compromised target answers /internal/backup/export with a multi-gigabyte body; backup-service reads it entirely into memory (the read runs in a worker thread via asyncio.to_thread, so it does not block the loop but does consume heap), risking OOM of the backup pod during a routine run.
findings.fix: Cap the read (Content-Length check plus a bounded read that aborts past a configured max archive size) and treat oversize responses as a failed target.

findings.title: Tenant row writes use full-object put() with NO optimistic concurrency (CAS) — lifecycle state silently reverts
findings.detail: create() atomically reserves the slug/domain indexes with cas() (round-1 fix), but EVERY mutation of the tenant row itself goes through repo.update()/tombstone() which call self._store.put(_TENANTS, tenant.id, tenant.to_dict()) (repository.py:63, :109) — a blind whole-record overwrite. There is no version field on the tenant row and no compare-and-set. Each API route (tenants.py) independently _load()s a fresh snapshot, mutates its in-memory copy, then puts the ENTIRE object back, so two overlapping writers each clobber the other's fields, not just the one they intended to change.
findings.failure_scenario: Operator POST /api/v1/tenants/{id}/suspend and the tenant's own PUT /api/v1/tenant/config run concurrently. Both _load the tenant while status=='active'. suspend() puts status='suspended'. update_config() (which already passed _require_active on its stale active snapshot) then puts its copy with status=='active' — the suspension is silently reverted and the abusive tenant stays live. The same race lets a concurrent update_config/set_branding wipe a close() (dropping status='suspended' and the config._close schedule), so an owner-requested close never gets swept.
findings.fix: Give the tenant row a monotonic version and route all lifecycle/config writes through store.cas() with the loaded version, retrying (re-load + re-apply) on a CAS miss; or apply status transitions as a store-side conditional update rather than read-modify-put of the whole document.

findings.title: suspend()/reactivate() have no terminal-state guard — a DELETED tombstone can be flipped back to suspended/active, defeating the tombstone and resurrecting the tenant for fail-open peers
findings.detail: suspend() (line 146) sets status='suspended' unconditionally and reactivate() (line 152) sets status='active' unconditionally; neither rejects a tenant already in the terminal DELETED state. update_config/set_branding/rename are protected by _require_active (raises TenantInactive), but the lifecycle transitions are not. The admin routes POST /{id}/suspend and /{id}/reactivate (tenants.py:132,155) load the tombstone row (status=='deleted') and call straight through.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator issues POST /api/v1/tenants/{id}/suspend against an id that was already deleted (fat-finger, stale UI, replayed request). _load returns the tombstone; suspend() overwrites status 'deleted' -> 'suspended' via a full put. GET /internal/tenants/{id} now answers status='suspended' instead of 'deleted', so every peer that missed the at-most-once tenant.deleted event — the exact case the tombstone exists to cover — fails OPEN and resumes accepting writes to an erased company. reactivate() is worse: it sets status='active' AND pops config._close, producing an ACTIVE tenant with slug=='' and no domain index (a zombie the erasure already stripped of its data).
findings.fix: In suspend()/reactivate() (and ideally a single _transition helper) reject when tenant.status == DELETED (raise TenantInactive/terminal), the same way _require_active guards config writes. Deletion must be a one-way terminal state.

findings.title: close_sweep erases on a STALE snapshot — a reactivate racing the sweep either loses a live tenant or resurrects a tombstone
findings.detail: close_sweep() (lines 190-210) pages iter_suspended(), and for each row whose config._close.grace_until <= now_iso calls self.delete(Tenant.from_dict(r)) at line 206 using the row as read at the top of the page. It never re-reads or re-checks the tenant's current status/schedule immediately before deleting, and delete()/tombstone() do not CAS on state.
findings.failure_scenario: During the grace window an owner calls POST /api/v1/tenant/reactivate (sets status='active', pops config._close). If reactivate lands AFTER iter_suspended snapshotted the row but BEFORE line 206's delete, the sweep tombstones a tenant that is now live again — the owner's shop is erased despite a valid take-back. If the two land in the other order, reactivate's blind put (finding -01) can re-write the just-tombstoned row back to a full ACTIVE record, resurrecting an erased tenant. Either interleaving corrupts the close/reactivate contract the round-1 rework was meant to make safe.
findings.fix: Make the erase conditional: re-load the tenant (or use a CAS/conditional delete) immediately before tombstoning and skip it unless status is still SUSPENDED and config._close.grace_until <= now. Pair with the version/CAS scheme from -01 so reactivate and sweep cannot both win.

findings.title: scope() ignores the tenant's stored isolation_mode and always returns the globally-configured strategy; provision accepts an unvalidated isolation_mode
findings.detail: provision() stores a PER-TENANT isolation_mode (line 91), accepted verbatim from the request body with no allowlist check (tenants.py:47 / internal.py:165 -> tenant_service.py:80-91). But scope() (line 242) returns self._isolation.scope(...) where self._isolation is the SINGLE global strategy chosen by ISOLATION_DRIVER in the container (container.py:229 — one instance, not a per-mode map). The stored isolation_mode is never mapped to a strategy. _internal_view() (internal.py:89) then hands scope() to peers as authoritative 'data scoping'.
findings.failure_scenario: Platform runs ISOLATION_DRIVER=shared-row but provisions a high-compliance customer with isolation_mode='db' (or 'schema'), trusting the per-tenant field the API exposes. GET /internal/tenants/{id} returns isolation={'mode':'shared-row','namespace':<id>} instead of a dedicated DSN/schema, so every peer places that customer's data in the shared row store — a silent isolation-guarantee violation. Because isolation_mode is also never validated, junk values ('db ', 'DB', 'garbage') are persisted and would break any future per-tenant dispatch.
findings.fix: Either drop the per-tenant isolation_mode field entirely (make isolation a service-global decision and stop advertising a knob nothing reads), or build a per-mode strategy map and have scope() dispatch on tenant.isolation_mode; in both cases validate isolation_mode against the _ISOLATION allowlist at provision time (400 on unknown).

findings.title: update_config/provision accept reserved underscore keys — a tenant can inject config._close and weaponise the close-sweep
findings.detail: update_config() does tenant.config.update(config) (line 119) with no filtering of service-internal keys, and provision() does config.update(config_overrides or {}) (line 88) likewise. The close-sweep's erase trigger is entirely driven by config._close.grace_until (tenant_service.py:203-205). _internal_view strips underscore keys on the way OUT to peers (internal.py:86) but the sweep reads the raw stored config, so nothing prevents a caller from writing _close IN.
findings.failure_scenario: A tenant.manage self-service user (or the platform via config_overrides) PUT /api/v1/tenant/config with {"_close": {"grace_until": "2000-01-01T00:00:00+00:00"}} while ACTIVE (allowed — _require_active passes). The tenant stays active, so the sweep (SUSPENDED-only) ignores it for now. Later an operator SUSPENDS the tenant for investigation (a plain suspend, not a close). The next close_sweep finds a suspended tenant carrying a _close with a past grace_until and ERASES it — destroying the tenant and any evidence, from an admin action that was never a close request. Also lets an owner pre-arm self-destruction.
findings.fix: Reject or strip keys beginning with '_' (and any other reserved namespace) in update_config and provision config_overrides before merging; keep the close schedule in a dedicated field the public config API cannot write.

findings.title: close_sweep aborts the entire run on the first tenant whose delete() raises — later due tenants in that run are skipped
findings.detail: The per-row loop (lines 202-207) calls await self.delete(...) with no try/except. delete()/tombstone() perform several store writes (put marker, delete slug, delete each domain). Any transient failure on ONE tenant (store hiccup, a domain key error) propagates out of close_sweep and terminates the whole sweep call; every remaining row in the current page and all subsequent pages go unprocessed for that run.
findings.failure_scenario: A scheduled sweep has 500 due tenants; tenant #7's tombstone write hits a momentary datastore error. The exception unwinds close_sweep, so tenants #8..#500 are not erased on this run and the returned {scanned,erased} counts understate the backlog. The FOCUS invariant 'never skip a tenant' is violated within a run; it is only self-healing because the next scheduled run re-queries SUSPENDED — but a persistently-failing single tenant permanently blocks the whole tail behind it.
findings.fix: Wrap the per-tenant delete in try/except, count and log failures, continue the loop, and surface a 'failed' tally in the result so a stuck tenant is observable rather than silently blocking the rest.

findings.title: DSAR erase() does read-modify-put of the whole tenant row and can resurrect a concurrently tombstoned/suspended tenant
findings.detail: erase() gets the full tenant row (line 40), mutates branding, and puts the ENTIRE row back (line 51). The inline comment asserts it is 'not a concurrent request path', but it shares the same collection/key as every lifecycle and config write and has no CAS. Like finding -01 this is a blind whole-record overwrite.
findings.failure_scenario: A subject erasure runs while the tenant is deleted (tombstone drops name/branding/config/domains and sets status='deleted') — or while an operator suspends it. erase() read the full pre-delete row, so its put() writes that full row back: status flips from 'deleted' to the old 'active', the name/branding/domains the tombstone erased reappear, and the PII the DSAR was clearing is re-persisted. Requires overlapping timing and (for the branding path) a branding hit, hence SPECULATIVE, but the outcome is an un-erased, un-deleted tenant.
findings.fix: Perform the branding scrub as a CAS/conditional update (or a field-scoped store operation), and refuse to write when the row is a tombstone (status==DELETED); never round-trip the whole document from a stale read on a shared key.

findings.title: iter_suspended sorts by a non-existent field 'created' (model field is created_at) — sweep ordering claim is false and the postgres ordering index is bypassed
findings.detail: iter_suspended() passes sort=('created','asc') (line 76), but Tenant.to_dict() has no 'created' key — it stores 'created_at' (models.py:32,44). In the memory adapter r.get('created') is None for every row; in postgres COALESCE(value->'created','null'::jsonb) is JSON null for every row. Both adapters therefore fall back to the id/key tie-break (which is total, so pagination does NOT skip — the round-1 completeness fix survives), but the intended 'oldest-closing-first' ordering does not happen and the kv_created_desc btree cannot serve the ORDER BY.
findings.failure_scenario: Not a data-loss bug (id tie-break keeps the page total-ordered), but the sweep does not process due tenants in close order as documented, and on a large SUSPENDED set postgres orders by a constant-null expression then key, so the '(created) DESC, key' index is not the intended match — degrading the very O(page) property the index comment claims. A future change that relied on created ordering would silently misbehave.
findings.fix: Change the sort field to 'created_at' (matching the model and the kv_created_at_desc index) or add a real 'created' field; add a test asserting iter_suspended returns oldest-first.

findings.title: Crash between slug CAS reservation and tenant-row put leaves an orphaned slug reservation that 409s forever
findings.detail: create() reserves the slug with cas(_SLUGS,...) at line 30, then reserves domains, then puts the tenant row LAST (line 40). The three steps are not atomic across a process crash. If the pod dies after the slug (and/or domain) reservation but before the _TENANTS put, the index rows persist with no backing tenant.
findings.failure_scenario: Provision reserves slug 'acme' (tenant_slugs row written), then the process is killed before line 40. get_by_slug('acme') resolves the index to an id whose _TENANTS row does not exist and returns None (repository.py:47-49), yet a retry of provision('acme') hits cas() and raises SlugTaken -> 409 forever. The slug is permanently un-provisionable and invisible, with no live tenant to delete to release it.
findings.fix: Write the tenant row first (or within the same transaction as the index reservations), or add a reconciliation/self-heal that releases an index row whose target _TENANTS row is absent; on postgres, wrap create in a single transaction.

findings.title: _reindex_tenants after restore is bounded by scan_cap and never removes stale index rows
findings.detail: _reindex_tenants() (lines 313-332) rebuilds slug/domain lookups by scan_all('tenants', scan_cap) — bounded by BACKUP_MAX_ROWS_PER_COLLECTION (default 5,000,000) — and only PUTs derived rows; it never deletes pre-existing index entries. It also skips slug-less tombstones correctly, but does not reconcile an index pointing at a now-absent or reassigned target.
findings.failure_scenario: If the restored registry exceeds scan_cap, tenants beyond the cap get no slug/domain row and answer 404 on host/slug resolution despite existing in the registry. And if a slug/domain was reassigned to a different tenant after the backup, a non-overwrite restore leaves the live index pointing one way while the reindex (over restored rows) may point another, or a stale mapping to a tenant not in the restore survives — host resolution then routes to the wrong or a missing tenant.
findings.fix: Reindex over the full registry (page rather than a single capped scan_all) and rebuild the index collections from scratch (clear-then-fill) so stale/removed mappings cannot survive a restore.

findings.title: at-least-once tail page is re-delivered on every poll forever (terminal/empty cursor is unackable)
findings.detail: In at_least_once mode records are intentionally NOT reserved (line 144 gates reserve behind `if not at_least_once`), and the watermark advances ONLY when a subsequent pull echoes a non-empty ack_cursor (line 109 `if ack_cursor and ...` ignores empty). The final page of a resource returns `next_cursor=""` (line 173 `next_cursor = page.next_cursor or ""`), so `out["cursor"]=""` (line 192). The consumer's next pull passes ack_cursor="", which line 109 skips, so the watermark stays at the previous cursor Cn-1. fetch(cursor=Cn-1) returns the same tail page again. Default mode survives this because the per-record reserve (line 145) skips already-seen records; at_least_once has no such gate.
findings.failure_scenario: Resource has 2 pages. Pull1(alo,ack=""): wm=W0, fetch W0 -> page1, returns cursor=C1. Pull2(alo,ack=C1): wm->C1, fetch C1 -> page2, next_cursor="" returns cursor="". Pull3(alo,ack=""): empty ack ignored, wm stays C1, fetch C1 -> page2 AGAIN. Every subsequent poll re-delivers the entire last page. Steady-state = continuous duplicate delivery; the consumer must retain the dedup key-set for that page indefinitely, and the watermark can NEVER advance to the tail once caught up. A busy connector re-emits its newest batch on every scheduler tick.
findings.fix: Advance the watermark on a terminal fetch even in at_least_once mode once the batch has been returned+acked, OR treat an empty returned cursor as 'ack of the last non-empty cursor' (carry a monotonic delivered-cursor so the consumer can ack the tail). Alternatively keep a lightweight per-record delivered-mark in alo mode that is cleared on ack, so a re-poll of an already-delivered-but-unacked tail does not re-emit records the consumer has not yet had a chance to ack.

findings.title: at-least-once poison record is re-dead-lettered on every re-delivery (reserve is set but never checked in alo mode)
findings.detail: On a mapping failure in at_least_once mode the code reserves the key (line 155-156 `if at_least_once: await self._seen.reserve(key)`) and DLQs the record (line 157). The comments at lines 152-154 and 161-162 claim the reservation prevents a re-fetch from re-DLQ'ing the same record ('the poison-pill stall'). But the reserve CHECK that would skip the record on re-delivery is guarded by `if not at_least_once` (line 144), so in alo mode it is NEVER consulted. On the next re-delivery of the same un-acked batch the poison record is re-mapped, fails again, `reserve(key)` returns False (ignored), and `self._dlq.add(...)` runs AGAIN, appending a NEW dlq_ row each time.
findings.failure_scenario: A batch's newest page contains one unmappable record. Because of connector-r2-01 the tail page is re-fetched on every poll; each poll re-DLQs the poison record with a fresh id (new_id('dlq_')). The sync_dlq collection grows by one row per poison record per poll, unbounded, until the batch is acked (which for a tail page never happens). Dead-letter counts become meaningless, operator alerting floods, and the DLQ store fills. If the consumer never fully processes the batch (e.g. downstream keeps failing) growth is truly unbounded.
findings.fix: In at_least_once mode consult the reservation before mapping/DLQ: `if await self._seen.seen(key): continue` for records already durably dead-lettered (a poison marker), OR key the DLQ row by idempotency_key (put(_DLQ, key, ...)) so re-DLQ is an idempotent overwrite rather than an append. Make the code match the comment.

findings.category: input validation / data loss / ack contract
findings.title: ack_cursor is trusted blindly — watermark set to any caller-supplied string with no proof it was ever issued
findings.detail: `if ack_cursor and conn.watermarks.get(resource, "") != ack_cursor: conn.watermarks[resource] = ack_cursor` (lines 109-111). The ack value is accepted verbatim from the request body (internal.py:36 `ack_cursor: str = Field(default="", max_length=1024)`) and written straight into the durable watermark. There is no check that ack_cursor equals the `cursor` the service actually returned on a prior pull, no monotonicity check, and no binding to a run id. Whoever holds the internal token (job-service, or any caller that can reach /internal/connectors/sync) can move the watermark to an arbitrary position.
findings.failure_scenario: For providers with human-legible cursors (HubSpot timestamp `after`, Salesforce SystemModstamp) a caller (buggy scheduler, replayed/duplicated job, or a compromised internal peer) sends ack_cursor far in the future. The watermark jumps forward and every record between the real position and that cursor is never fetched — silent, unrecoverable data loss for that resource. A stale/duplicated job could equally move it backward, forcing a full re-scan and duplicate processing.
findings.fix: Bind the ack to something the service issued: persist the last delivered cursor per (connection,resource) at pull time and reject/ignore an ack_cursor that does not match it; or make ack a distinct step that references the run id whose cursor is being acknowledged. At minimum reject an ack_cursor the service has no record of having returned.

findings.title: SeenStore (sync_seen) grows without bound — one permanent row per record, no TTL or pruning
findings.detail: Every default-mode pull record (sync_engine.py:145 reserve) and every push record (sync_engine.py:224 reserve) inserts a row into the `sync_seen` collection (stores.py:104 cas insert-if-absent). Rows are only ever deleted by release() on a failed push (line 109). Successfully processed records' reservations are kept forever (by design, for idempotency), and there is no TTL, watermark-based compaction, or sweeper. The rows also carry no tenant field (value is `{"k": key}`), so backup/erasure cannot scope or prune them.
findings.failure_scenario: A connector syncing 1M records/day accrues ~365M permanent sync_seen rows/year. On the memory datastore this is an unbounded process-memory leak (OOM); on postgres it is unbounded table growth that eventually degrades cas latency on the sync hot path and inflates every backup. There is no operational lever to reclaim the space.
findings.fix: Prune reservations below the durable watermark (once the watermark has advanced past a record, its idempotency key can never be re-fetched), or attach a TTL to sync_seen rows sized to the max provider re-delivery window. Add a tenant field so erasure/backup can scope them.

findings.title: connection read-modify-write is not CAS-guarded — concurrent runs lose circuit-breaker and counter updates
findings.detail: Each pull/push loads `conn` once (`self._conns.get`, line 99/199) and later persists mutations with a plain `save()` (ConnectionStore.save -> DataStore.put, an unconditional overwrite; stores.py:18-19). `_record_failure` (line 67-74) reads `conn.consecutive_failures` from that snapshot, computes new circuit state, and saves; `_record_success` (line 76-81) resets it. cas() exists on the datastore but is NOT used for connection saves. Two runs on the same connection (scheduler tick overlapping a slow run, or user /sync concurrent with internal /sync) each hold their own snapshot.
findings.failure_scenario: Run A and Run B both load conn with consecutive_failures=4 (threshold=5). Both fail: each computes 5 and saves 5 (not 6); last-writer-wins, so two failures count as one and the breaker trips a cycle late. Worse: Run A records a failure (sets opened_at/state) while Run B records a success on its stale snapshot and saves last, erasing A's trip so a dead provider keeps consuming workers. sync_count/failure_count/watermark updates from the losing writer are also dropped.
findings.fix: Persist connection state mutations via cas() with a version check and retry on conflict, or serialize per-connection run execution (advisory lock / single-flight keyed by connection_id) so counters and circuit state are read-modify-written atomically.

findings.category: PII / secret leakage at rest and in API
findings.title: DLQ stores the full raw provider record and the dead-letters endpoint returns it verbatim
findings.detail: Both pull (line 157 `record=rec`) and push (line 242 `record=rec`) dead-letter the complete, unredacted provider payload. `GET /api/v1/connectors/dead-letters` (connectors.py:253-256) returns `DlqStore.list(...)` rows to any caller with connectors.read, and each row includes `record` (SyncRecord.to_dict). Provider records routinely contain PII (contact emails, phones, names) and can contain secrets. This data sits at rest in sync_dlq (retained until manually removed) and is exposed through a read API.
findings.failure_scenario: A HubSpot/Salesforce contact fails mapping and is dead-lettered with its full PII body. A connectors.read principal (or a leaked read token) pulls /dead-letters and harvests every failed record's PII across the tenant. Because DLQ rows have no per-subject index, the /internal/privacy/erase path (erasure over text_keys) may also miss them, leaving PII after an erasure request.
findings.fix: Store only what reprocessing needs (idempotency_key + a sealed/pointer reference to the payload, or a redacted projection), seal the record body at rest, and redact/omit `record` from the dead-letters read response (return counts + keys + error, fetch the body only via an audited admin path). Ensure DLQ payloads are in erasure scope.

findings.title: process-wide _LOCKS dict grows one asyncio.Lock per connection id, never evicted
findings.detail: `_LOCKS: dict[str, asyncio.Lock] = {}` (line 31) is populated by `_LOCKS.setdefault(conn.id, asyncio.Lock())` (line 114) on every refresh path and never cleaned, even on disconnect. Over the lifetime of a long-running process every connection that ever refreshed retains a Lock object.
findings.failure_scenario: A tenant that churns through many short-lived connections (connect/disconnect cycles, or many connections over months) slowly grows _LOCKS unbounded, a small but permanent memory leak. Not exploitable, but unbounded.
findings.fix: Evict the lock on disconnect, or use a bounded/weak mapping (e.g. keyed cleanup when a connection is revoked) so the lock table tracks live connections.

findings.title: user-facing /sync cannot opt into at-least-once — user pulls are at-most-once with silent loss on a dropped response
findings.detail: The v1 SyncIn model (connectors.py:102-106) has no at_least_once / ack_cursor fields, and the pull call (line 241-242) never passes them, so user-driven pulls always run the default at-most-once path. As the pull() docstring warns (sync_engine.py:89-98), if the HTTP response carrying the batch is lost in transit the watermark has already advanced and those records are never re-fetched. Only the internal tier (internal.py:35-36, 88-90) can request at-least-once.
findings.failure_scenario: A tenant integration calls POST /api/v1/connectors/sync (pull); the connection succeeds, the watermark advances, but the response is lost (client timeout, LB reset). The caller retries, gets the NEXT batch, and the first batch is silently gone. The safer delivery mode exists but is unreachable to the user-facing caller.
findings.fix: Expose at_least_once/ack_cursor on the v1 SyncIn (or document that user pulls must be treated as at-most-once and steer integrators to the internal/scheduled path). Even a returned cursor the caller could re-submit would let a user integration recover a dropped response.

findings.title: single-flight refresh is per-process only; two replicas can both refresh and one rotated refresh token is lost
findings.detail: The refresh lock is a module-global keyed by conn.id (line 31, 114), so single-flight holds only within one process. The comment (lines 28-30, 139-149) acknowledges cross-replica races and relies on the CredentialInvalid recovery (re-read latest conn) to heal. But if the provider permits brief refresh-token reuse, replica B's concurrent refresh with the OLD refresh token can SUCCEED and return a different rotated token (RT3), which store_tokens overwrites A's RT2 with. Whether the connection survives depends entirely on provider-side reuse tolerance and timing.
findings.failure_scenario: Replica A and B both see the token expiring and refresh concurrently against a provider that rotates refresh tokens. A stores RT2; B (using RT1 within a reuse window) stores RT3, invalidating RT2. If the provider then rejects RT3 (or a further refresh uses the now-dead RT2 from a stale cache), the connection lands in NEEDS_REAUTH — a spurious re-auth for a healthy integration under load.
findings.fix: Add a cross-process guard for refresh (a short datastore/redis lock keyed by connection_id, or a cas on a 'refreshing' marker) so only one replica refreshes; keep the existing re-read recovery as the fallback.

findings.title: reclaim() blind non-CAS save can resurrect a job that a concurrent ack/nack/cancel already finished (re-execution)
findings.detail: claim() moves QUEUED->LEASED through cas_save() with an optimistic-lock version (line 94) precisely so two writers cannot both win. reclaim() does NOT: after get() (line 175) it mutates the in-memory Job and calls the plain save() (line 193) with no version check and no re-read. There are multiple `await` points between the get() and the save() (unindex_leased at line 185, etc.), so on the single asyncio loop another coroutine can run to completion in that window. _held() (line 118-119) checks only status==LEASED and token match; it does NOT check lease_expires, so a worker whose lease has just expired can still successfully ack/nack.
findings.failure_scenario: Job J is LEASED, lease expired. Worker W (lease expired but still alive) sends ack(J, token). reclaim() runs concurrently: it get()s J (still LEASED/expired), passes its guards, then awaits unindex_leased. During that await the ack coroutine runs fully: J -> DONE, save, unindex_leased, unique_clear, emit job.done. reclaim() then resumes with its stale in-memory J (still LEASED), sets attempt+=1, status=QUEUED, next_run_at=now, and save()s -> the DONE job is overwritten back to QUEUED and re-indexed as due. A worker claims and RE-EXECUTES an already-completed job (double side effects: duplicate email/charge). The mirror case (reclaim lands first) is safe because the token is cleared, but the interleaving above is not.
findings.fix: Make reclaim() transition through cas_save(job, expected_version) exactly like claim(), skipping the candidate when the CAS loses; and/or re-check job.status==LEASED and lease_expires<=now immediately before the save. Also make ack/nack/heartbeat reject an expired lease in _held() (compare lease_expires to clock.now()) so a worker that has lost the race cannot mutate at all.

findings.title: GET /api/v1/jobs/stats scans the ENTIRE job table (scan_all up to 50k) per request, despite the code claiming it is timer-only
findings.detail: stats() (line 236-246) calls counts() (stores.py line 79) which does scan_all(_JOBS, _INDEX_MAX=50_000) over EVERY job ever enqueued and aggregates in Python, plus a second full scan of due_index (line 240). The stores.counts() comment asserts 'Not on any request path - the metrics endpoint calls it on a timer', but the /stats route (api/v1/jobs.py line 143-147) is reachable by any holder of jobs.read / jobs.manage / platform.jobs and invokes it synchronously on the request.
findings.failure_scenario: A tenant reader with jobs.read repeatedly calls GET /api/v1/jobs/stats. Each call reads up to 50,000 job rows from the datastore (a full JSONB table scan on postgres, no WHERE), deserializes and aggregates them in Python inside the request. A handful of concurrent callers, or one caller in a loop, saturates the DB pool and event loop -> latency spike / DoS for the whole service, including the claim/ack hot path.
findings.fix: Serve status counts from maintained counters or a cheap indexed aggregate rather than a full scan on the request; or move /stats behind platform.jobs only and rate-limit it; at minimum stop asserting in the comment that counts() is off the request path when it is not.

findings.title: claim() reads and Python-sorts the WHOLE due-index (up to 50k) on every poll, not 'bounded by batch' as documented
findings.detail: The module docstring (lines 13-14) states 'claim reads the small due-index (bounded by batch), never the whole job table.' In fact claim() calls due_index() (stores.py line 99 -> scan_all(_DUE, 50_000)), materializes ALL claimable rows, list-filters them, then _order() sorts the full list up to twice (job_service.py line 104 and 113) on EVERY claim call, regardless of batch. The bound is the index size (50k), not batch.
findings.failure_scenario: One tenant enqueues tens of thousands of immediately-due jobs. Every worker's claim poll (many workers, high frequency) now reads all ~50k due rows and sorts them in Python just to lease 1. CPU and DB egress scale with the backlog, not with the work leased -> claim latency collapses fleet-wide and one tenant's flood degrades every other tenant's claims (a cross-tenant DoS the fairness sort cannot help with because the cost is paid before fairness is applied).
findings.fix: Push the due query into the datastore with ORDER BY (queue, priority, next_run_at) LIMIT (batch * small_factor) and a WHERE next_run_at<=now, so claim reads O(batch) rows, not the whole index. Correct the docstring to match reality.

findings.title: Job.public() returns the full payload and result to any jobs.read holder; results are known to hold personal data outright
findings.detail: Job.public() (line 43-46) strips only lease_token and returns everything else, including payload and result. GET /api/v1/jobs/{id}, GET /api/v1/jobs (list) and GET /api/v1/jobs/dead-letters all return .public() to any holder of the broad jobs.read cap (api/v1/jobs.py lines 104, 111, 162). The erasure module's own docstring (core/erasure.py lines 4-5) states a payload 'holds the recipient's address' and 'the result of an export job may hold their data outright' - i.e. payload/result routinely carry PII and can carry secrets (API tokens, callback credentials) passed by enqueuers.
findings.failure_scenario: A low-privilege support user granted jobs.read to triage failures opens GET /api/v1/jobs/{id} or the DLQ listing and reads the raw payload/result of an export or 'send credential' job - full personal data or a secret token - even though their role only needed status/error/attempt to decide a replay. Scoping is per-tenant only, so it is an intra-tenant over-exposure, not cross-tenant.
findings.fix: Add a redacted projection for read endpoints (status, attempts, error, type, timestamps; payload/result omitted or key-masked) and gate raw payload/result behind a stronger cap (jobs.manage or platform.jobs) or a dedicated jobs.read.payload cap. The get_job docstring should stop advertising payload as part of the ordinary read.

findings.title: Delivery is at-least-once (visibility-timeout reclaim), but the docstring advertises 'no double-execution'
findings.detail: The module docstring (line 3-10) claims 'no double-execution'. The CAS fencing genuinely prevents two workers both winning the CLAIM and prevents a lost-lease worker from MUTATING the job. It does not prevent duplicate SIDE EFFECTS: reclaim() (line 169-196) returns an expired-lease job to the queue immediately (next_run_at=now, line 192) while the original worker may still be executing its handler. Two handlers then run the same job body concurrently; only the DB write of the loser is rejected by fencing. There is no execution-dedup key that a handler can consult to make its side effect idempotent.
findings.failure_scenario: A slow handler exceeds LEASE_SECONDS (default 60s). reclaim() requeues the job; a second worker claims and runs it. Both send the email / call the payment gateway. The first worker's eventual ack fails fencing, but the external side effect already happened twice. Callers that trusted the 'no double-execution' wording built non-idempotent handlers.
findings.fix: Document the real guarantee (at-least-once; handlers must be idempotent) prominently, and/or expose a per-attempt execution token workers can use for downstream idempotency. Consider not resetting next_run_at to now on reclaim without a small grace so a briefly-overrunning worker can still heartbeat.

findings.title: enqueue() can orphan one reservation and temporarily break idempotency when idempotency_key wins but unique_key loses (or vice versa)
findings.detail: enqueue() reserves BOTH idempotency_key and unique_key in a loop (lines 58-63) before save() (line 64). If the first key (idempotency_key) is reserved successfully but the second (unique_key) loses to a concurrent enqueue, the function returns the existing job (line 63) and NEVER saves the new job - but the idempotency_key reservation created at line 59 now points at job.id that was never persisted. unique_get later returns that id, get() returns None, so the (key==idempotency_key) branch's `existing and ...` guard is False and the code falls through to create yet another job, re-reserving over the orphan only if TTL expired.
findings.failure_scenario: Two enqueues share unique_key U but have distinct idempotency_key I1/I2. Enqueue A reserves I1 then loses U to B; A returns B's job without saving. I1 now maps to a non-existent job id for the whole UNIQUE_DEDUPE_TTL window. A genuine idempotent retry with I1 no longer dedupes to a real job -> a duplicate job is created, defeating the idempotency guarantee for I1 until TTL expiry.
findings.fix: Reserve both keys, and if any reservation loses, release the reservations THIS call created (unique_clear on the ones it won) before returning the existing job, so no key is left pointing at an unsaved job id.

findings.title: reclaim() double-counts attempts / duplicates work if two reclaim sweepers run concurrently (non-CAS)
findings.detail: reclaim() reads leased_index and blind-save()s each requeue (lines 182-194) with no version check. Two concurrent reclaim invocations (two pods, or an operator manual /internal/scheduler-style trigger plus the cron) both read the same expired-lease row, both increment attempt from the same base, and both index_due -> the attempt counter advances by only 1 while two due-index writes occur (idempotent on key), or, combined with finding job-r2-01, a save races an ack.
findings.failure_scenario: Two reclaimer instances tick simultaneously. A job near max_attempts is evaluated by both from attempt=N; both compute N+1; the dead-letter decision (line 186) is taken on stale state, so a job that should dead-letter is instead requeued once more, or attempt accounting drifts. Low likelihood with a single cron, higher with HA reclaimers.
findings.fix: Route reclaim's requeue/dead-letter transition through cas_save(expected_version) so only one sweeper wins per job, matching claim().

findings.title: Internal /jobs/enqueue does not bound payload size, priority, delay_seconds, or max_attempts
findings.detail: EnqueueIn (lines 26-35) caps only type/unique_key/idempotency_key string lengths. payload is an unbounded dict, priority an unbounded int, delay_seconds an unbounded float, max_attempts an unbounded int. A buggy or compromised peer holding the internal token can enqueue multi-megabyte payloads (stored verbatim in JSONB and returned by every read/backup), a priority that starves all fairness tiers, or a delay far in the future that pins a due-index/leased row.
findings.failure_scenario: A peer service with a bug posts a 10MB payload per job in a loop; the job table and every backup archive balloon, scan-based paths (stats/counts/due_index) slow, and memory spikes on reads. Trusted-tier, so severity is low, but there is no server-side guard.
findings.fix: Add max payload byte-size, a bounded priority range, and sane ceilings on delay_seconds/max_attempts in EnqueueIn (or in enqueue()).

findings.title: No SSRF surface inside job-service: it stores callback/HTTP targets in payloads but never dereferences them
findings.detail: The FOCUS hint asked about SSRF on job callback/HTTP targets. job-service is a queue/scheduler: enqueue stores payload verbatim, claim hands it to external workers, and there is no code path in this service that fetches a URL taken from a job payload. The only outbound HTTP is the audit sink (adapters/audit_sink/http.py) and the internal client, both configured from settings, not from job payloads. SSRF, if any, lives in the WORKER services that execute jobs, which are out of this audit's scope.
findings.failure_scenario: N/A - documented as no-finding so a future reviewer does not re-open it; the risk, if realized, is in job executors elsewhere, which should be audited to validate/allow-list any URL they take from a payload.
findings.fix: No change in job-service. Ensure worker services that consume payloads apply egress allow-listing / SSRF guards on any URL fields.

findings.title: release() is the only mutating op with no _claim guard -> concurrent double-release under-counts held and raids other holds' reserved money
findings.detail: confirm() and settle_withdrawal() take an atomic claim; release() does not. The _mutate CAS prevents lost updates but BOTH signed held_delta still apply, and the new_held<0 -> 0 clamp masks the corruption.
findings.failure_scenario: funds cash:200, holds H1(cash:100) H2(cash:50), held=150. Two concurrent release(H1) both read ACTIVE; A held 150->50; B reads 50, 50-100=-50 clamped to 0 -> held={}. available now 200 but H2 still reserves 50; a spend drains all 200 and H2.confirm fails INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS. Also release racing sweep_holds.
findings.fix: Guard release with _claim(tenant,'release',hold_id) and re-read the hold under the claim (mirror confirm); same claim around the per-hold decrement in sweep_holds.

findings.title: reclaim() claim keyed on caller source (not grant) + stale pre-claim state read -> two distinct-source concurrent reclaims double-credit (mint)
findings.detail: reclaim keys _claim on source (RECLAIM, src) and never re-reads grant.state under the claim (unlike confirm). refund deliberately keys on spend:{seq} to avoid exactly this.
findings.failure_scenario: dormant grant swept=100; two flows source=jobA and jobB fire concurrently; different claim keys both win; both see stale state='dormant'; both _mutate +100 -> 200 credited for a 100 dormant balance.
findings.fix: Key the claim on the grant (f'reclaim:{grant.id}' always) and re-read grant state under the claim before mutating.

findings.title: idempotency is TTL-bounded (24h) so any money op replayed after the TTL re-executes: double-credit/refund(mint)/payout/reverse
findings.detail: _claim replays only while row.expires_at>now; after the finalized result TTL lapses the key is re-claimed and the mutation re-runs. refund's 'one refund per spend' cap only holds 24h; the spend ledger row is immutable so a later refund reverses again.
findings.failure_scenario: refund(tenant,seq=N) replayed >24h later (re-processed chargeback / retried batch / delayed webhook) -> funds credited twice for one spend. Same window for credit/withdraw/settle(paid=False).
findings.fix: For once-only money events make idempotency durable on the source object (a refunded/reclaimed flag on the ledger row/grant checked before mutating), independent of the idempotency TTL.

findings.title: overlapping sweep_grants runs double-debit an expiring grant (no per-grant claim)
findings.detail: sweep_grants _mutate(funds_delta -remaining) per grant then sets state, with no _claim on the expiry transition (contrast confirm/settle).
findings.failure_scenario: cron interval < slow sweep, or manual sweep during the scheduled one: two runs both read grant active+expired, both debit; for forfeit that over-claws (customer loses more than the grant); for dormant it debits twice while reclaim restores once -> net customer loss.
findings.fix: Claim on f'sweep:{grant.id}' (or CAS grant state active->expired/dormant) before the debit; a lost claim = already swept.

findings.title: idempotency claim lease (60s) can lapse mid-mutation, letting a duplicate execute a second time
findings.detail: A winner whose mutation outlives the 60s lease (heavy CAS contention CAS_MAX_RETRIES=20 with jitter + DB/audit latency) lets a concurrent duplicate re-claim and both run.
findings.failure_scenario: Two redelivered settlement webhooks for the same credit(source=X); winner stalls >60s; loser's retry re-claims and credits a second time before the winner finalizes.
findings.fix: Renew the lease during long mutations, or make finalize refuse if the pending claim it started no longer matches (version/owner token).

findings.title: reclaimed-then-swept over-claw across grants sharing a fund
findings.detail: _reserved_for_other_grants queries only state='active'; a dormant->reclaimed grant's money credited back into the shared fund is not protected, so a forfeit grant on the same fund can claw it.
findings.failure_scenario: fund cash: grant A (reclaimed 100 back) + grant B (forfeit, amount 100); B expires: spare=200 reserved=0 claimable=min(200,100)=100 -> claws the just-reclaimed money.
findings.fix: Also reserve dormant/reclaimed grants' preserved amounts, or track per-grant consumption.

findings.title: refund() reads the ledger row without _flush; a just-crashed spend's pending row is invisible and the claim sits pending for the lease
findings.detail: refund reads _LEDGER directly (unlike ledger()/reconcile() which _flush first); if the spend is the latest op and the process died between its CAS and ledger put, refund raises LEDGER_ENTRY_NOT_FOUND after taking the spend:{seq} claim, blocking a legit retry for the 60s lease.
findings.failure_scenario: Fail-safe (never over-refunds) but a spurious refusal + blocked retry.
findings.fix: _flush the wallet before the ledger read in refund.

findings.title: backup import_archive into_tenant same-store clone skips grants/holds (key template {id} not tenant-qualified)
findings.detail: grants/holds use key {id}; into_tenant remaps tenant field but not id, so the rebuilt key finds the source row -> skipped; a same-store clone gets wallet+ledger but no grants/holds.
findings.failure_scenario: Operator clone within one store diverges on expiry/clawback/reservations. Operator tooling only, not a production money path.
findings.fix: Give grants/holds a tenant-qualified key template, or namespace clones into a distinct store.

findings.title: internal route policy is default-open; money-moving /internal/wallet/* reachable by any token-passing caller absent an allow-list
findings.detail: resolve_internal_policy.permits returns allow for any route absent from INTERNAL_ROUTE_POLICY_JSON (documented default-open).
findings.failure_scenario: Within the internal trust boundary, but credit/withdraw/refund/reclaim would be safer fail-closed per-route.
findings.fix: Ship a restrictive default policy for the mutation routes.

findings.category: privacy/erasure-ineffective (CWE-212 improper removal of sensitive info)
findings.title: DSAR erasure of inbound events writes the redacted copy under the WRONG key, leaving the original PII row intact
findings.detail: `_redact_row` persists with `await self._store.put(collection, row["id"], row)`. For the `events` and `deliveries` collections the store key equals `row["id"]`, so the redacted row overwrites the original. But inbound events are NOT keyed by id: InboundStore stores them under the composite key `f"{source}::{provider_event_id}"` (app/core/stores.py:216-217,230,242) while `row["id"]` is the surrogate `in_<uuid>` (app/core/models.py:113). So for the `inbound` collection, erasure reads the row (via scan_all), redacts it in memory, then PUTs the redacted copy under a brand-new key `in_<uuid>` and never touches the original `stripe::evt_123` row. The original inbound payload — described in erasure.py:6-7 as 'a third party's raw body (Stripe, GitHub), routinely full of PII' — survives forever, yet the DSAR ack reports `inbound:N` in `erased` and returns success. The unit test misses this because its fake store keys by `id` (tests/unit/test_erasure.py:108 `r["id"] == key`) and its inbound fixture has no source/provider fields (test line 144), i.e. a memory-fake-vs-real-store divergence.
findings.failure_scenario: A customer files a right-to-erasure request. Operator calls POST /internal/privacy/erase {tenant, subject}. The service returns {"erased": ["inbound:3", ...], "already_absent": false} — a clean success. The person's email/name/card metadata inside the three Stripe/gateway inbound payloads is still in the datastore under keys `stripe::evt_...`, plus three orphan duplicate rows now exist under `in_...`. The org has certified an erasure that did not happen (PDPL/GDPR Art.17 violation) and doubled the stored PII.
findings.fix: Persist inbound redactions under the SAME key the row was read at, not row["id"]. Either have scan_all/find surface the storage key and put back under it, or add a store method that rewrites in place. At minimum, InboundEvent redaction must recompute `f"{source}::{provider_event_id}"` from the row and put under that. Add a test that exercises the real memory adapter (not a fake keyed by id) with a genuinely stored inbound event.

findings.title: Sweep `due()` reads EVERY queued/failed delivery each tick; only status is pushed down, next_retry_at is filtered in Python
findings.detail: `due()` pages the whole `{status: [queued, failed]}` set in _SWEEP_PAGE(500) chunks and filters `next_retry_at <= now` in Python, looping `while len(out) < limit`. When the backlog contains many not-yet-due rows (large retry_max_seconds=21600s ceiling means a failing endpoint's deliveries sit FAILED with a future next_retry_at for hours), each sweep drains the entire cursor before it can collect `limit` due rows, reading all queued+failed rows every tick. The next_retry_at predicate is never pushed to the datastore, so the read is O(open backlog), not O(due backlog). deliver() also re-defers disabled/circuit-open endpoints by pushing next_retry_at forward (webhook_service.py:173,183) which keeps them in the queued/failed set, inflating the scanned volume.
findings.failure_scenario: One tenant registers 5k endpoints that all start 5xx-ing. Each event fans out 5k FAILED deliveries with next_retry_at hours in the future. Every /internal/webhooks/sweep tick now paginates through tens of thousands of not-due rows to find a handful of due ones, saturating the DB connection and the worker; healthy tenants' due deliveries are delayed behind the scan.
findings.fix: Push the due-time predicate into the datastore query (`next_retry_at <= now` as an indexed range filter combined with status), or maintain a due-index sorted by next_retry_at so the scan is proportional to the DUE backlog. Cap total rows scanned per sweep and record when the cap is hit.

findings.title: Inbound dedupe re-accept after TTL uses a non-atomic get+put, re-opening the double-publish window reserve() was built to close
findings.detail: reserve() first does an atomic cas(expected=0) insert-if-absent (correct). But the TTL-lapsed branch (lines 244-248) does `get()` then, if the existing row aged past ttl, `put()` (a plain overwrite) and returns True. Two concurrent duplicates arriving after the dedupe window has lapsed both hit the cas (fails, row exists), both get() the aged row, both put() and both return True -> InboundService.ingest publishes the event to the bus TWICE. There is no compare-and-set on this overwrite, unlike the first-seen path. The doc comment claims 'exactly one wins', which holds for the fresh-insert path but not the re-accept path.
findings.failure_scenario: A provider re-sends a webhook with the same provider_event_id more than INBOUND_DEDUPE_TTL_SECONDS (24h default) after the first, and its retry logic fires two near-simultaneous copies (common: provider timeout + retry). Both pass signature verification, both re-accept, both publish `inbound.<source>` — downstream subscribers process the event twice (e.g. double credit / double fulfilment) despite the dedupe guarantee.
findings.fix: Make the re-accept atomic: use a cas keyed on the aged row's version (or a conditional put-if-received_ts-unchanged) so only one caller replaces the lapsed row and publishes. On cas failure, treat as duplicate.

findings.title: Keyset cursor tie-break uses row['id'] but Postgres ORDER BY/compare uses the primary key `key`; they differ for inbound rows
findings.detail: find() orders and compares on `(value->'<field>', key)` where `key` is the PK (postgres.py:219,226), but the emitted cursor encodes `str(last.get('id',''))` (postgres.py:237), and the next-page WHERE compares that encoded id against `key` (line 219). For every collection where key==row['id'] (endpoints/events/deliveries) this is fine. For the `inbound` collection key is `source::provider_event_id` while row['id'] is `in_<uuid>` — so the tie-break value in the cursor is compared against a totally different string domain than the column being ordered. When two inbound rows share the same `received` value at a page boundary, rows can be skipped or duplicated. The memory adapter instead orders AND tie-breaks on `str(r.get('id'))` (memory.py:73,79), so the two backends page inbound listings differently — a divergence tests using the memory store cannot catch.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator pages the cross-source inbound feed (InboundStore.list with a source filter -> find, sort received desc) on Postgres. At a page boundary where several events share a received timestamp, some inbound events silently never appear in any page, hiding events from an investigation; the same query on memory (tests/dev) returns them, so the gap is invisible until production.
findings.fix: Encode and compare the actual ordering key (the PK `key`) in the cursor, not row['id'] — or make the two consistent for every collection. Align the memory adapter to tie-break on the same field so a contract test can assert identical paging across backends.

findings.title: Endpoint circuit-breaker/counter state is saved with save_state() (no CAS), so concurrent deliveries lose failure counts
findings.detail: The delivery row transition is CAS-protected (claim_delivering), but the ENDPOINT state written after each attempt (consecutive_failures, circuit_state, opened_at, success/failure counts) goes through EndpointStore.save_state -> plain put (stores.py:74-78), a read-modify-write with no version guard. Two deliveries to the same endpoint finishing concurrently both read ep, both mutate counters, last write wins.
findings.failure_scenario: An endpoint starts failing under high fan-out; N concurrent deliveries each read consecutive_failures=k and write k+1, so the counter advances by 1 instead of N. The circuit threshold (default 5) is reached far later than intended, letting many more doomed attempts hammer a dead receiver (and burn worker time) before the breaker opens.
findings.fix: Apply the counters as atomic increments (or a versioned CAS with retry) rather than a whole-object put, so concurrent attempts accumulate rather than overwrite.

findings.title: Tenantless principals collapse to a shared '__none__' bucket, mixing endpoints/deliveries across such callers
findings.detail: _tenant() and _owned() fall back to `p.tenant or '__none__'` for a non-platform principal whose verified token carries no tenant/org/tid claim (auth.py:30 leaves tenant=None when absent). Every such principal shares the literal tenant '__none__', so they read/replay each other's endpoints, events, deliveries and dead-letters. This is safe only if the deployment guarantees every non-platform token carries a tenant claim — which is an unenforced assumption, not a checked invariant.
findings.failure_scenario: A deployment (or a misconfigured issuer) mints user tokens without a tenant claim for two different real customers. Both authenticate, both resolve to tenant '__none__', and customer A lists/replays customer B's webhook deliveries and dead-letters — a cross-tenant IDOR that no ownership check catches because both truly share the bucket.
findings.fix: Refuse (403) a non-platform principal with no tenant claim rather than assigning a shared sentinel, or require a tenant claim at authentication for any tenant-scoped route.

findings.title: Inbound-secret resolution reads at most 200 secret rows with no paging; sources beyond the 200th (by name) are silently untrusted
findings.detail: InboundSecretPool._resolve() enumerates stored secrets via store.list_info(tenant='') which does find(_COLL, {'tenant': ''}, limit=200, sort=('name','asc')) with NO cursor loop (secret_store.py:185). A deployment with >200 operator-entered INBOUND_SECRET:* rows only ever resolves the first 200 by name; any source whose secret sorts after that is absent from the pool and every genuine callback for it is rejected as UNKNOWN_SOURCE (inbound_service.py:44-45). Fail-closed (good — no forged acceptance) but a silent, name-order-dependent availability cliff.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator onboards the 201st inbound source; its stored secret is never loaded, so that provider's real signed callbacks all return 400 while the panel shows the secret set correctly. Diagnosis is hard because it depends on alphabetical name ordering, not on the source just added.
findings.fix: Page through all INBOUND_SECRET:* rows (cursor loop) or raise/alert when the row count reaches the read cap, so the resolution is complete or loudly incomplete rather than silently truncated.

findings.title: Inbound verification implements ONLY the service's own Stripe-style HMAC; no per-gateway scheme (Tap/Geidea/PayPal/Stripe-native) is supported
findings.detail: The audit scope names per-gateway inbound schemes, but this service verifies exactly one format: `X-Webhook-Signature: t=<unix>,v1=<hmac_sha256(ts.body)>` (signing.py, inbound.py:35). Real payment gateways sign differently (PayPal transmits a cert-chain + CRC over headers; Tap/Geidea use their own field digests; native Stripe uses this exact scheme but its own header name `Stripe-Signature`). Pointing a real gateway at /inbound/{source} would fail verification for every callback because the header name and/or algorithm do not match. This is a functional/coverage gap (gateway-specific verification lives in payment-service per project notes), not an authentication weakness — the generic scheme fails closed.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator, expecting 'webhook-service handles inbound webhooks', points a live Tap or PayPal webhook at /inbound/tap. Tap signs with its own scheme under its own header; the service's HMAC-on-X-Webhook-Signature check always fails, so every legitimate gateway callback is rejected (400) and the provider eventually stops retrying — lost payment events.
findings.fix: Either document explicitly that inbound is the platform's own HMAC contract only (and route gateway callbacks to payment-service), or add a per-source verifier strategy (header name + algorithm) so a source can declare which gateway scheme applies.

findings.title: verify() compares every secret against every parsed v* signature with no cap on signature count
findings.detail: parse() collects an unbounded list of signatures for any header part whose key starts with 'v' (signing.py:37-38), and verify() does a nested loop secrets x sigs of hmac.compare_digest (lines 51-57). An attacker who can reach /inbound/{source} for a KNOWN source can send a header packed with thousands of v1=... values, forcing len(secrets) * N constant-time SHA-256 comparisons per request. Bounded by the HTTP header size limit, so impact is modest, but it is attacker-controlled CPU on the hot path before any dedupe.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker floods /inbound/stripe with requests carrying maximally long X-Webhook-Signature headers full of bogus v1 entries; each request burns CPU on futile HMAC compares (all rejected on the timestamp/secret check anyway), amplifying a request flood into a CPU flood on the single-worker event loop.
findings.fix: Cap the number of accepted signatures parsed from the header (e.g. first 4) and short-circuit once the timestamp tolerance check fails (already done) — reject before iterating an oversized sig list.

findings.title: Multi-tenant mint does not strip platform.*/* from caps (the '_safe_caps' last door is missing on the tenant path)
findings.detail: The single-tenant mint applies AuthService._safe_caps (auth_service.py:295), which strips '*' and 'platform.*' from a token whose tenant is not PLATFORM_TENANT. Its own docstring calls this 'THE LAST DOOR', because 'a capability that ended up on a User by ANY route became platform authority on login', and the gateway honours '*' as a wildcard matching every capability check. service_accounts.py:230 (token_claims) and grantable_caps() also apply _strip_platform, and service_accounts.py:80 explicitly states it holds 'the same last door AuthService._safe_caps holds for humans'. But the multi-tenant HUMAN mint (auth_service.issue_tenant_tokens, line 680) builds claims via tenancy.claims_for(), which returns {'caps': list(membership.caps if caps is None else caps)} (tenancy.py:65-69) with NO platform stripping. The resolver path is no safer: AuthzCaps.resolve/MembershipCaps.resolve UNION the membership's direct caps into the result (caps_resolver/authz.py:121, caps_resolver/membership.py:18), and neither strips. So a membership row on a customer tenant that carries 'platform.*' or '*' mints a customer-tenant access token that carries platform-wide authority verbatim — exactly the class of bug _safe_caps exists to close, reintroduced on the primary multi-tenant login/switch/refresh path.
findings.failure_scenario: IDENTITY_MULTI_TENANT=on, PLATFORM_TENANT='platform'. A membership for person P on customer tenant 'acme' ends up with caps=['members:write','*'] (or 'platform.admin'). Origin is legitimate-looking: seed_owner / POST /internal/tenancy/seed-owner passes caps through add_member with granter_caps=None (the internal-bootstrap exemption, caps_grant.check() no-ops), so an orchestrator or a fat-fingered provisioning call can write any cap onto the first owner; alternatively any granter whose OWN unstripped multi-tenant token already holds '*' can grant it under the subset policy. P logs in and selects 'acme'. issue_tenant_tokens -> claims_for mints an access token {tenant:'acme', caps:[...,'*']} with no stripping. At the gateway '*' matches every capability check across all 16 services -> full cross-tenant platform compromise from a customer-tenant token. The identical account on the single-tenant path (issue_tokens) would have had '*'/'platform.*' removed.
findings.fix: Apply the same platform-boundary filter on the multi-tenant mint. Either have claims_for() take platform_tenant and strip '*'/'platform.' when membership.tenant != platform_tenant, or filter in issue_tenant_tokens after caps resolution (mirror _safe_caps). Add a safety test asserting a membership with '*'/'platform.admin' on a non-platform tenant yields a token without them, matching the single-tenant and service-account paths.

findings.title: Concurrent use of the same refresh token both succeed — rotation revoke is not an atomic compare-and-swap, defeating theft detection
findings.detail: refresh() reads state = await self._refresh.status(jti) (line 720) and only if state=='active' proceeds to revoke(jti) (line 731) and mint a new family. Reuse detection depends on the SECOND use of a jti observing state=='revoked' (line 722) to trigger revoke_family. But status() (refresh_store.py:44) and revoke() (refresh_store.py:58) are separate get/put operations with no CAS. Two requests presenting the SAME refresh token concurrently can both read 'active' before either revoke lands; both then revoke (idempotent) and both mint fresh, independent token families. Neither is detected as reuse. The refresh_store.revoke comment ('there is no competing writer to lose to') reasons only about the same jti being written once at mint then revoked; it does not account for two concurrent ROTATIONS of the same jti, which is precisely the stolen-token-vs-legitimate-token interleaving the reuse defense targets.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker steals refresh token R. The victim's client and the attacker both POST /api/v1/auth/refresh with R within the same tick. Both calls read status(R)=='active', both revoke(R), both call issue_tenant_tokens minting two live refresh families. The 'REUSED token -> revoke_family' branch never fires because neither call saw 'revoked'. The attacker now holds a self-sustaining session that survives, instead of tripping family revocation on the second use as designed (CWE-613/CWE-384).
findings.fix: Make rotation atomic: revoke should be a compare-and-swap that only succeeds when the row is currently active (e.g. store.cas on a version, or a conditional 'UPDATE ... SET revoked=true WHERE revoked=false'), and refresh() must treat a FAILED conditional revoke as a reuse/race signal (drop the mint, and on a losing CAS where the row is already revoked, trigger revoke_family). Only the winner of the CAS mints the new family.

findings.title: Sole-owner guard is check-then-act, so concurrent owner removals can strand a tenant with zero owners
findings.detail: _guard_last_owner (line 495) calls has_other_active_owner() (membership.py:189, a paged read) and then the caller performs revoke()/grant() as a separate write. There is no lock or CAS spanning the read and the write. delete_self (line 565), remove_member (line 529), update_member_roles (line 600) and set_member_status (line 631) all share this pattern. Two concurrent operations on the last two owners each observe the OTHER as an active owner and both proceed, removing/de-owning/suspending both. The invariant these guards exist to hold ('never leave a tenant with zero owners') is defeated under interleaving, leaving the tenant unmanageable and recoverable only by a manual datastore write (the exact outcome the guards' docstrings promise to prevent).
findings.failure_scenario: Tenant 'acme' has exactly two active owners, A and B. A calls DELETE /api/v1/auth/me (delete_self) while B is removed via DELETE /api/v1/tenancy/members/{B} concurrently. delete_self checks has_other_active_owner(acme, A) -> sees B -> proceeds; remove_member checks has_other_active_owner(acme, B) -> sees A -> proceeds. Both revoke. 'acme' now has no active owner: nobody can manage members, billing, or the tenant. Same result from two concurrent update_member_roles calls each dropping 'owner', or two set_member_status suspensions.
findings.fix: Serialize owner-count-changing writes per tenant, or make them conditional: perform the demotion/removal under a CAS and re-verify the owner count inside the same atomic step, rolling back (raise SoleOwnerError) if the write would drop the active-owner count to zero. An owner-count row updated by CAS is one option.

findings.title: Multi-tenant person login has no per-account lockout — only per-(source-IP, identifier), so distributed credential stuffing is unthrottled
findings.detail: Single-tenant authenticate() keys the lockout on (tenant, username) (line 221/227), i.e. PER ACCOUNT, so N failures from ANY source lock that account. Multi-tenant authenticate_person() keys the lockout on (source, ident) where source is the caller IP (line 329, 341; api/v1/tenancy.py _source() returns request.client.host). The T5 comment justifies not keying on the person alone (to avoid a DoS that locks a consultant out of all clients), but the chosen key means an attacker credential-stuffing one account from many IPs never trips the per-account counter — there is none. The only remaining control is the route-level generic rate_limit (per IP/subject), which the login_attempts.py module docstring itself says 'does NOT stop an attacker credential-stuffing a single account from many IPs'. So the primary login path in the multi-tenant deployment is materially weaker against distributed brute force than the legacy path.
findings.failure_scenario: A botnet with 5,000 IPs targets victim@example.com on POST /api/v1/auth/person/login (or /auth/tenant with credentials). Each IP submits a handful of guesses; per-(IP, identifier) lockout never fires because each source stays under LOGIN_MAX_ATTEMPTS, and no per-account counter exists. Over time the 6-8 char password space is ground down with no account-level lockout ever engaging.
findings.fix: Add an account-scoped failure counter with a distinct, higher threshold and a graduated response (e.g. lock the ACCOUNT after M failures across all sources within a window, in ADDITION to the per-source counter), or require step-up/CAPTCHA once global failures for an identifier spike. Keep the per-source key to preserve the T5 availability property, but do not let it be the only per-account signal.

findings.title: Platform-cap stripping (_safe_caps) is disabled by default because PLATFORM_TENANT defaults to empty
findings.detail: _safe_caps returns caps unfiltered when platform_tenant is empty (line 173-176), and config.py:409 sets PLATFORM_TENANT: str = '' by default. So even the single-tenant 'last door' is OFF unless an operator sets PLATFORM_TENANT. Combined with identity-r2-01 (the multi-tenant path never strips at all), a default deployment provides NO platform-authority containment: any '*'/'platform.*' cap that reaches a user/membership row is minted into a token. The code logs the disablement at boot (a decision, not a silence), which is why this is low rather than high on its own, but it makes r2-01 exploitable in a stock configuration.
findings.failure_scenario: Operator enables multi-tenancy and RBAC but never sets PLATFORM_TENANT (the default). Every mint path emits caps verbatim; a stray 'platform.support' or '*' cap on any membership becomes cross-tenant authority with nothing to catch it.
findings.fix: Fail closed or loud: refuse to boot the multi-tenant/RBAC configuration without an explicit PLATFORM_TENANT (or an explicit opt-out flag), and always strip '*'/'platform.*' from any non-platform-tenant token regardless of whether PLATFORM_TENANT names the platform, deriving the platform identity from a required setting.

findings.title: _extract_principal accepts org/tid as a tenant fallback while the mint gate reads only 'tenant'
findings.detail: _extract_principal (line 30) sets principal.tenant = claims.get('tenant') or claims.get('org') or claims.get('tid'), but tenancy.tenant_of() (tenancy.py:99) reads ONLY 'tenant' and fails closed if absent. principal.tenant feeds audit actor scoping and the subject_ref pseudonym in delete_me/change_password/mfa_enroll (auth/v1/auth.py:403,422,499) and the service-account _actor()/_caller_tenant() (service_accounts route:58,74). Identity itself only ever mints tokens carrying 'tenant', so this is not exploitable via identity-issued tokens; but if this verifier is ever pointed at an external IdP (JWKS driver) whose tokens carry 'org'/'tid' but no 'tenant', the two code paths disagree about which tenant the caller is in — the capability/mint gate says 'no tenant' while principal.tenant is populated from org/tid, which could mis-scope a service-account ownership check or a pseudonym.
findings.failure_scenario: A JWKS-verified upstream token carries {sub, org:'acme', caps:['svc.write']} and no 'tenant'. GET service-accounts flows via _caller_tenant use principal.tenant='acme' (from org) and operate on acme's machine identities, while a route that goes through tenant_of() would have rejected the same token with NO_TENANT. The two surfaces treat the same token differently.
findings.fix: Make the tenant source consistent: either have _extract_principal read only 'tenant' (matching the mint gate) or have tenant_of/authorization consult the same fallback set. Pick one canonical tenant claim across principal extraction, tenant_of, and service-account ownership checks.

findings.title: POST /api/v1/otp/request delivers a code to any identifier, including unregistered numbers, throttled only per-identifier
findings.detail: request_otp (line 57) issues and DELIVERS an OTP to body.identifier without any existence check (correctly, to avoid an enumeration oracle), rate-limited only PER identifier via OtpService (resend cooldown + max_per_hour, otp_service.py:75-80) plus the route rate_limit. Because the throttle is per-identifier, an attacker can fan out low-volume requests across thousands of distinct phone numbers/emails, each staying under the per-identifier cap, and cause the platform to send (and pay for) SMS/WhatsApp messages to arbitrary destinations — an SMS-pumping / toll-fraud and reputation vector. No global per-source or per-tenant delivery ceiling is enforced here.
findings.failure_scenario: Attacker scripts POST /api/v1/otp/request with purpose=reset over a list of 50,000 phone numbers, one request each. Per-identifier limits never trip (one message per number); the notifier dispatches 50,000 paid SMS to numbers the attacker chose (SMS pumping), driving cost and getting the sender number/brand flagged.
findings.fix: Add a per-source (IP) and per-tenant delivery budget in addition to the per-identifier cap, and/or gate OTP delivery for reset/login to identifiers that resolve to a known account (delivering nothing but still returning the uniform response, so no oracle is created). Consider a global circuit breaker on notifier send volume.

findings.title: Internal route policy is default-open and token-fallback is on by default, so a leaked flat internal token reaches every /internal route
findings.detail: InternalRoutePolicy.permits returns True for any route with no declared entry (default-open, internal_policy.py:35), and INTERNAL_CALLER_DRIVER defaults to 'shared' with INTERNAL_CALLER_ALLOW_TOKEN_FALLBACK=True (config.py:125,134). This is the documented non-breaking migration posture, but the practical consequence is that in a stock deployment a single shared INTERNAL_SERVICE_TOKEN authenticates an unnamed peer (caller='') that is admitted to EVERY /internal route — including high-impact ones: POST /internal/tenancy/seed-owner (can mint a first owner with arbitrary caps — see r2-01's origin), POST /internal/privacy/erase (erase any subject), POST /internal/signing-key/rotate, and POST /internal/backup/import (restore/remap tenants). There is no least-privilege separation until an operator hand-writes INTERNAL_ROUTE_POLICY_JSON per route.
findings.failure_scenario: The flat INTERNAL_SERVICE_TOKEN leaks (a mis-scoped k8s secret, a log, a compromised low-value peer that legitimately holds it). With default-open policy the holder can call /internal/tenancy/seed-owner to seed themselves as owner (with platform caps, which r2-01 then fails to strip), /internal/privacy/erase to delete accounts, or /internal/backup/import to overwrite tenant data — none of it gated by a per-caller allow-list because none is declared.
findings.fix: Ship a default DENY-by-default (or at least a restrictive default allow-list) for the destructive internal routes (seed-owner, privacy/erase, signing-key/rotate, backup/import), requiring named assertion-proven callers; and document turning INTERNAL_CALLER_ALLOW_TOKEN_FALLBACK off once callers sign. At minimum, provide a shipped INTERNAL_ROUTE_POLICY_JSON template that closes the destructive routes.

findings.title: Concurrent /provision runs are unserialized: one request's compensation can tear down resources another request confirmed
findings.detail: ProvisioningService.provision() (and the /onboarding/provision route, onboarding.py:118) take no lock or dedup on (tenant, subject). Two concurrent calls for the same signup both run the Saga forward. Every step key is derived (prv_ hash of tenant|subject|kind), so downstream services dedupe: the second create returns 409/EXISTS which ProvisionResult.ok treats as success (ports/provisioner.py:52). Nothing coordinates the two sagas or their compensations.
findings.failure_scenario: Customer double-clicks Provision (or a client retries on timeout). Request A: create tenant -> ref T (ok); create membership -> transient downstream 500 -> A begins compensation, DELETEs membership then DELETEs tenant T. Request B, interleaved: create tenant -> 409 EXISTS ref T (ok); create membership -> succeeds; B returns HTTP 200 {ok:true}. But A's rollback has already deleted tenant T. The customer is told provisioning succeeded while the tenant (and the just-created membership hanging off it) has been destroyed. No error surfaces to B.
findings.fix: Serialize provisioning per (tenant, subject): take an advisory lock / row lock on the provisioning_runs id for the duration of the saga, or make provision() a no-op short-circuit when a prior run with ok=true and no unfinished work already exists. At minimum treat a run as a single-writer critical section so a rollback cannot race a concurrent forward run.

findings.title: provisioning_runs record is blind-overwritten: a later clean run erases an earlier run's unfinished/residue cleanup queue
findings.detail: provision() writes the run record with self._store.put('provisioning_runs', record['id'], record) using the fixed _run_key(tenant, subject). The write is a full replace, not a merge. resume() (line 127) treats record['unfinished'] as THE cleanup queue.
findings.failure_scenario: Run A fails mid-saga and records unfinished=[{step:'tenant', reference:T, error:...}] (wallet-service was down during rollback).
