Before an operator resumes, run B (a retry) executes, its forward steps all return EXISTS, ok=true, unfinished=[], and put() overwrites A's record. resume()/admin/resume now finds nothing outstanding and returns 'nothing to resume', while resource T is still orphaned and the queue that would have cleaned it is gone. The self-healing invariant the file is built around ('the unfinished list IS the queue') is silently defeated.
findings.fix: Merge rather than replace: when writing a run record, union any pre-existing unfinished/residue entries not addressed by this run, or refuse to overwrite a record that still has unfinished work. Alternatively key runs by attempt and aggregate outstanding work across attempts.

findings.title: identity_lookup is never wired, so every once_per=verified_identity grant is permanently REFUSED (the headline welcome credit can never issue)
findings.detail: Container.identity_lookup defaults to None (container.py:147) and build_container() never assigns it (it sets clock, local_facts, grant_ledger at 251-253 but no identity_lookup). claim_grant builds GrantService with identity_lookup=c.identity_lookup (=None) and calls issue() WITHOUT claim_ref. In grants._uniqueness_key, once_per=='verified_identity' -> ref = claim_ref('') or _lookup_identity(); _lookup_identity returns '' because self._identity is None (grants.py:147-148) -> key None -> GrantOutcome REFUSED (grants.py:82-87).
findings.failure_scenario: The shipped b2b_self_serve flow's welcome_credit uses once_per='verified_identity' (onboarding_flows.py:106). In any real deployment every /claim-grant for it returns status=REFUSED ('no verified identity is on record') even for a fully business-verified tenant. The flagship gift never pays out, AND the once-per-verified-identity anti-abuse mechanism the whole grants.py module exists for is dead/untested code in production. Fail-closed for money, but the strongest control in the design is not actually exercised.
findings.fix: Wire an identity_lookup adapter (verification-service claim_ref_for) into build_container and pass it through, OR have claim_grant/evaluator supply claim_ref from the verification requirement's answer so _uniqueness_key can key on the verified identity.

findings.title: Grant issuance is check-then-act on a non-atomic ledger; the 'one grant when raced' guarantee is fully delegated to the backend
findings.detail: GrantService.issue does existing = await ledger.find(key) (91) then, if absent, entitlement.issue() then ledger.record() (114). find/record are separate store ops with no compare-and-set or unique-insert. The route docstring (onboarding.py:92) and grants.py header claim racing yields one grant, but onboarding's own ledger provides NO such guarantee. The only real dedup is the entitlement backend's idempotency on source=key. WalletEntitlement relies on wallet-service deduping on source (wallet.py:53); NullEntitlement/any future 'trial'|'plan' backend (config.py:173 lists these) may not.
findings.failure_scenario: ONBOARDING_ENTITLEMENT is later pointed at a non-idempotent grant backend. Two concurrent /claim-grant calls (same key) both find() empty, both call entitlement.issue(), both succeed -> the customer is granted twice. Even with wallet, if wallet's dedup window or source handling ever changes, onboarding has no second line of defense.
findings.fix: Make the ledger the authority: insert the ledger row with a unique-key/CAS BEFORE calling the backend (reserve-then-issue), or use an atomic put-if-absent so a concurrent second caller sees ALREADY without reaching the backend. Do not depend solely on downstream idempotency for a money control.

findings.title: /provision has no self-idempotency; safety rests entirely on every downstream create being idempotent on the derived key
findings.detail: The route re-runs the full forward saga on every call with no check that a prior run already completed successfully (contrast provisioning_run/resume which DO read the record). The docstring 'Safe to call twice' is true only because HttpProvisioner maps 409->EXISTS on the downstream's dedup of the prv_ key (provisioner/http.py:40).
findings.failure_scenario: A provisioner kind is added whose downstream does NOT dedupe on idempotency_key (or ignores the key), or a downstream that returns 200+new-id instead of 409 on replay. Re-pressing Provision then creates a second tenant/membership/resource, the exact orphan/duplication class the module was built to prevent, with no guard in onboarding itself.
findings.fix: Before running the saga, load the run record; if a prior run is ok=true with no unfinished work, return it as a no-op. Keep the derived-key downstream dedup as defense-in-depth, not the sole mechanism.

findings.title: Flow-declared provisioning attributes are spread into the request body after the fixed identity keys and can override them
findings.detail: create() builds body = {'tenant': request.tenant, 'subject': request.subject, 'idempotency_key': request.key, **request.attributes}. Because **attributes is spread LAST, an attributes entry named tenant/subject/idempotency_key silently overrides the caller-derived values. attributes come from flow config (onboarding_flows.py provisions[].attributes), which is deployment-trusted, but there is no guard.
findings.failure_scenario: A flow author (or a compromised/mistyped flow declaration) sets provisions:[{kind:'tenant', attributes:{tenant:'victim', idempotency_key:'fixed'}}]. Every customer's tenant creation is then sent with tenant='victim' or a constant idempotency key, collapsing all customers onto one downstream record or targeting another tenant. Blast radius is limited to whoever can edit flow config, but the identity keys should not be silently overridable.
findings.fix: Build attributes first and overlay the fixed keys last, or reject attributes keys that collide with tenant/subject/idempotency_key at flow validation time (flows.validate).

findings.title: A grant declared without once_per is silently REFUSED at issue, contradicting the validator that permits it as a 'granted every time' case
findings.detail: flows.validate (flows.py:70-74) treats grants-without-once_per as a non-fatal WARNING, documenting that a platform may legitimately grant something on every flow (tutorial flag, welcome email). But claim_grant passes once_per=spec.get('once_per','') and _uniqueness_key returns None for any once_per not in {verified_identity, tenant, subject} (grants.py:144), so issue() returns REFUSED. Such a grant can therefore NEVER be issued.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator declares a repeatable tutorial-flag grant relying on the validator's stated allowance. The flow boots (only a warning), onboarding reports the grant REFUSED on every claim, and the intended per-flow grant is never delivered while every check looks green.
findings.fix: Either make 'granted every time' explicit (e.g. once_per='none' producing a per-call key) and honor it in _uniqueness_key, or make the validator reject grants without once_per so the behavior matches the documentation.

findings.title: Irreversible-step residue records only the step name, not the created resource reference, so operators cannot locate the orphan
findings.detail: In _compensate, an undo-less step appends residue = {step: name, why: reason} but omits step.result (the created resource id). By contrast the unfinished branch (line 127) correctly carries reference=step.result. An irreversible step that nevertheless created something (e.g. an emitted external resource) leaves the operator its NAME but not its id.
findings.failure_scenario: A signup includes an irreversible step that produced a resource with an id. The saga fails later, residue lists the step but not the reference. An operator reading /admin/provisioning/{subject} sees 'residue: [that step]' with no id, and cannot find or manually reconcile the created artifact.
findings.fix: Include reference=step.result (and irreversible_reason) in the residue dict, mirroring the unfinished entry, so operators can locate what the world is still carrying.

findings.title: resolve() settles with a plain put(), not a CAS — a late/concurrent callback overwrites a settled REFUSED with VERIFIED
findings.detail: Round 1 made decide() and remember() atomic via cas_put/cas, but resolve() was NOT converted. resolve() reads the record, checks `record.verdict != PENDING` (lines 130-131), then writes with `await self._store.put(record)` (lines 139 and 147) — a version-blind overwrite. The PENDING guard is a read that is not atomic with the write. Two writers that both observed PENDING both proceed and last-writer-wins. The verify() creation path also uses put() (line 75), which is fine (create), but every SETTLEMENT via resolve bypasses the optimistic lock the rest of the service now relies on.
findings.failure_scenario: A record is PENDING (async Nafath prompt). Reviewer refuses it through ReviewService.decide() which cas_puts verdict=REFUSED and bumps version. Concurrently (or slightly earlier, having already read the row as PENDING) a provider/attacker callback hits POST /internal/verification/resolve with verified=true; resolve() had read verdict==PENDING, builds a VERIFIED outcome and put()s it, clobbering the refusal with no version check. The result is the exact 'a replay overwrote a refusal with an approval' outcome resolve()'s own docstring (lines 121-126) claims to prevent. The same race applies resolve-vs-resolve (one verified, one refused -> nondeterministic settle) and resolve-vs-sweep_pending (sweep put()s EXPIRED, resolve put()s VERIFIED — either can win and stomp the other).
findings.fix: Make resolve() and sweep_pending() use store.cas_put() with a bounded refetch/retry loop exactly like ReviewService.decide(): on a lost CAS, refetch and re-evaluate (a record no longer PENDING must abort and return unchanged). Never settle a verdict with a version-blind put().

findings.category: spoofed callback / broken authentication of async resolve
findings.title: resolve callback is authenticated only as 'some internal caller' — it never binds the callback to the provider/correlation token stored in provider_state, and is not tenant-scoped
findings.detail: When a provider answers PENDING, HttpVerifier stores state={"reference": reference} and VerificationService._apply copies it into record.provider_state (verification_service.py:108). resolve() (lines 119-149) accepts verification_id + verified + reference + detail and moves any still-PENDING record to VERIFIED/REFUSED WITHOUT ever comparing body.reference against record.provider_state['reference'] or otherwise proving the caller is the provider that owns this prompt. The comment 'the correlation token has done its job' (line 146) clears provider_state but the token is never actually checked. The /internal/verification/resolve route has no per-verification and no tenant check, and INTERNAL_ROUTE_POLICY_JSON defaults to empty => default-open for any authenticated internal caller (internal.py:55, config.py:138).
findings.failure_scenario: Any caller that can reach the internal tier (a compromised/over-broad internal peer, an SSRF pivot, or a misconfigured allow-list) marks ANY pending verification VERIFIED by supplying its verification_id — which is handed to the end user in the submit_claim response (record.public() includes `id`). A user submits an async individual claim, never approves on their phone, then (or a colluding service) calls resolve(verification_id, verified=true) and is verified without Nafath ever confirming. No tenant scoping means it works cross-tenant.
findings.fix: Bind the callback to the prompt: require the provider's correlation token/reference and compare it in constant time against record.provider_state before settling; reject a mismatch as 404/401. Preferably also verify per-caller identity (INTERNAL_CALLER_DRIVER=static/jwks) and add /internal/verification/resolve to INTERNAL_ROUTE_POLICY_JSON so only the provider-integration service may call it.

findings.title: Manual-review approvals never write identity_seen — the day-one default verification path defeats once-per-identity anti-abuse
findings.detail: VerificationService._announce writes the anti-abuse row via registry.remember() only on its own VERIFIED path (verification_service.py:194-203). ReviewService (review.py) has NO registry: __init__ takes none (lines 43-49), build_review does not pass one (verification.py:51-56), and decide() sets verdict=VERIFIED (line 109) then audits and returns without ever calling remember(). So every manually approved identity is verified but NEVER recorded in identity_seen — even though the record already carries claim_ref. Manual/document review is described as the fallback 'every platform can run on day one' (review.py:5-7).
findings.failure_scenario: A platform using manual/document verification (the default with no provider contract) approves a business. identity_seen is never populated. The fraudster deletes the tenant, signs up again with the same commercial registration, is manually approved again, and onboarding-service's registry.seen() check returns False every time — the once-per-identity welcome grant is collected repeatedly. This is precisely the fraud stores.py/erasure.py claim identity_seen exists to stop.
findings.fix: Give ReviewService an IdentityRegistry and call remember(record.claim_ref, now) on every approval (and only on approval), mirroring VerificationService._announce; wire it in build_review().

findings.title: Manual/document claims cannot be created, so the review queue only surfaces async provider prompts a human can then approve without the provider answering
findings.detail: verify() looks up self._verifiers.get(claim_type) and raises UnsupportedClaim when absent (lines 60-64). _build_verifiers gives manual/document providers NO entry (container.py:257-258). Therefore a claim_type answered by manual/document is always rejected at submit — there is no code path that creates a manual-review record. The review queue (stores.pending_reviews, verdict==PENDING) can therefore only return records left PENDING by an ASYNC provider. ReviewService.decide() will happily settle those to VERIFIED.
findings.failure_scenario: A user submits an async (Nafath-style) claim; it sits PENDING awaiting the user's own phone approval. It appears in the human review-queue, and any holder of verification.review approves it via decide(), granting VERIFIED without the phone-holder ever confirming and without the provider's callback — a human silently overrides the 'a verdict is only ever what a provider said' invariant, and (per r2-03) without recording identity_seen. Separately, the manual/document review feature is effectively unreachable, so a platform relying on it has no working verification at all.
findings.fix: Decide the model explicitly: either add a submit path that creates manual/document claims as a distinct review-pending state (separate from async-callback PENDING), and make decide() refuse records that belong to an async provider awaiting its own callback; or remove the manual review surface. Do not let one PENDING state mean both 'awaiting the provider's phone answer' and 'awaiting a human'.

findings.title: identity_seen write failure is swallowed; the claimed fail-closed on the grant side is not enforced here
findings.detail: In _announce, registry.remember() is wrapped in try/except Exception: pass (lines 198-203). The comment asserts 'the grant side refuses rather than assuming', but nothing in this service enforces that — the verdict is still returned VERIFIED and the anti-abuse row is silently absent. Whether the once-per-identity grant fails open depends entirely on onboarding-service's behaviour when seen() returns False for an identity that was actually verified.
findings.failure_scenario: A transient datastore/CAS-exhaustion error during remember() (remember() itself falls back to a best-effort read after 8 contended retries, stores.py:117-119, but a raised exception is swallowed here) leaves an identity VERIFIED but not in identity_seen. onboarding-service calls /internal/verification/identity/{claim_ref}/seen, gets seen=false, and grants the once-per-identity gift; a repeat registration is also unseen and gifted again.
findings.fix: Do not silently swallow: on a remember() failure either fail the verification settlement (so it can be retried) or emit a loud WARN + metric and a durable outbox retry, so a missing anti-abuse key is observable rather than invisible. At minimum stop claiming a fail-closed the code does not implement.

findings.title: HttpVerifier POSTs to the profile URL without consulting EGRESS_ALLOWED_HOSTS, and VERIFY_PROVIDERS is runtime-overridable per tenant
findings.detail: HttpVerifier.verify() builds the request straight from self._p['url'] (lines 64-69) with the comment 'config only — never from a request, so no SSRF surface'. The URL is indeed not taken from the HTTP request body. But the service ships an SSRF allowlist EGRESS_ALLOWED_HOSTS (config.py:311-319) that this egress path never enforces, and provider selection (VERIFY_PROVIDERS) is overridable at RUNTIME per tenant through the operator surface (verifier_pool._providers_spec via RuntimeConfig; operator.py set_config with key VERIFY_PROVIDERS). The boot guard validates profile URLs are http(s) only in production (config.py:433) and does not re-validate runtime overrides against an allowlist.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator (or an attacker who has reached platform.config) repoints a claim type at a provider profile whose url targets an internal metadata endpoint or an internal service; every verification for that claim type then makes the pod issue an authenticated POST to that host. Because the egress allowlist is never checked on this path, there is no defense-in-depth catch. Note VERIFY_PROFILES itself is not shown to be runtime-settable, which limits the URL an override can reach; hence SPECULATIVE.
findings.fix: Enforce settings.egress_allowed_hosts against the resolved profile URL host inside HttpVerifier (or at pool build), returning ERROR for a host not on the allowlist; re-run the URL/host validation on any runtime VERIFY_PROVIDERS/VERIFY_PROFILES override, not only at boot.

findings.title: decide() never checks pending_until, so a human can approve an async prompt that has already lapsed
findings.detail: resolve() refuses a lapsed prompt (verification_service.py:134-140: now >= pending_until -> EXPIRED, not approval). decide() only refuses records already VERIFIED/REFUSED (review.py:78) and ignores pending_until entirely. A PENDING record whose pending_until has passed but which the sweep has not yet marked EXPIRED can still be approved to VERIFIED by a reviewer.
findings.failure_scenario: An async Nafath prompt lapses (nobody answered within VERIFY_PENDING_TTL_SECONDS). Before sweep_pending runs, a reviewer approves it via decide(); the claim becomes VERIFIED on a prompt that expired unanswered — the 'a late yes cannot be trusted to have come from the right person' rule (verification_service.py:135-136) is bypassed on the review path.
findings.fix: In decide(), treat a record with pending_until and now >= pending_until as EXPIRED and refuse the decision (or require it be explicitly re-opened as a new verification), consistent with resolve().

findings.title: Erasure writes with a version-blind put(), racing a concurrent resolve/decide and re-linking or losing state
findings.detail: VerificationErasure.erase() sets record.subject='' / provider_state={} and calls store.put(record) (erasure.py:59-66) with no CAS. A concurrent resolve() (also put(), per r2-01) or decide() (cas_put) can interleave: the erasure put and the settlement put race with last-writer-wins, so a settlement can resurrect a subject the erasure just cleared, or the erasure can overwrite a just-settled verdict with a stale copy read before settlement.
findings.failure_scenario: A DSAR erase runs while an in-flight provider callback resolves the same subject's record. The erasure reads the record, the resolve settles+writes, then the erasure put() writes back its stale copy (subject='' but old verdict/version), or vice-versa the resolve writes back subject-bearing data after erasure — the subject link the DSAR reported as severed is still present.
findings.fix: Perform erasure writes through cas_put with refetch-on-conflict, or serialize erasure against settlement; ensure the erasure's write is the terminal state under the optimistic lock.

findings.title: AI-connection URL is SSRF-validated only at write time; the delivery transport re-resolves DNS and never pins the validated IP
findings.detail: `_validate_conn_url` (app/api/internal.py:296-308) calls `ssrf.validate()` on create/update, which resolves the host and returns a `Target` carrying the ONE validated IP to connect to (ssrf.py:96). That `Target.ip` is thrown away. At invoke time `_conn_model` builds `HttpModel(conn.url, ...)` (internal.py:244) and the default transport `_httpx_transport` (http_provider.py:516-524) does `httpx.AsyncClient(...).post(url, ...)` against the raw hostname URL — a fresh DNS resolution, with NO re-validation and NO IP pin. The ssrf module's own docstring (ssrf.py:12-14) mandates both 'pin the connection to one validated IP (the transport never re-resolves)' and 'Re-run validate() on every delivery attempt' — neither is done for connection invocation. converse()/complete()/answer() all post to self._url the same way.
findings.failure_scenario: A tenant registers a connection with url=https://rebind.attacker.example whose A record is a public IP at create time (passes validate). The attacker then repoints the record to an internal host (e.g. an internal admin/metrics service reachable over HTTPS, or with ASSISTANT_CONN_ALLOW_PRIVATE_IPS/require_https relaxed, 169.254.169.254 / 127.0.0.1). On POST /internal/assistant/connections/{cid}/invoke, httpx re-resolves to the internal IP and issues the request; the response JSON is parsed and returned to the caller as the connection's `text` (or tool_call) result, exfiltrating internal responses, and the connection's credential (Bearer / minted GCP OAuth token) header is delivered to the rebind target. Classic DNS-rebinding SSRF the pinning was designed to close.
findings.fix: Pin at delivery: have `_validate_conn_url`/`ssrf.validate()` return the Target and pass the validated IP into the transport (connect to the IP with the original Host/SNI preserved), OR re-run ssrf.validate() inside `_conn_model`/the transport on every call and connect to the returned pinned IP. Do not let httpx re-resolve the hostname.

findings.title: Per-round-trip metering silently bills zero when a provider omits usage on tool-call responses
findings.detail: `_extract_converse` (http_provider.py:385-434) reads token counts only from body.usage/usageMetadata; if absent, tin=tout=0. `invoke_conversation` (connections.py:240-242) then computes cost via cost_micros(0,0,...) = 0 and records a call with zero tokens/zero cost. Several providers omit or zero the usage block on function-call (tool_call) turns, and a tool-calling conversation can run many such round trips before the final text turn.
findings.failure_scenario: A tenant configures a tool-declaring connection against a provider that returns tool_calls without a usage block. Every tool-call round trip is metered as calls+1 but tokens_in=tokens_out=cost_micros=0, so the platform performs (and pays the upstream provider for) real model work while the per-connection usage ledger under-counts and the tenant is under-billed — a money leak that scales with tool-call depth.
findings.fix: Detect a 200 response with a tool_call but no usage and either fail closed, estimate tokens from the serialized request/response, or flag the round trip as unmetered so billing can reconcile. Do not treat missing usage as zero cost.

findings.title: Any authenticated internal caller can invoke/list/read any tenant's AI connection because tenant comes from the request body and routes are default-open
findings.detail: The connection routes (create/list/get/update/delete/invoke/usage, internal.py:311-445) take `tenant` straight from the body/query and are guarded only by `require_internal_token`, whose per-route policy is default-open (internal.py:40-55: 'A route with no policy admits any authenticated caller'). There is no binding between the calling service identity and which tenants it may act for. `invoke_connection` spends the target tenant's stored credential and meters against it; `list_connections` returns every connection row (url + system_prompt) for an arbitrary tenant.
findings.failure_scenario: A lower-trust or compromised internal service that holds a valid X-Internal-Token (or is on the shared-token default) calls POST /internal/assistant/connections/{cid}/invoke with tenant=<victim> and any known/enumerated cid, burning the victim tenant's model credential and reading its system prompts and connection URLs — cross-tenant use with no allow-list stopping it. Severity depends entirely on INTERNAL_CALLER_POLICY being configured; default-open leaves it wide.
findings.fix: Add an explicit internal-policy allow-list for the /internal/assistant/connections/* routes and/or derive/authorize the tenant against the verified caller identity rather than trusting the body-supplied tenant.

findings.title: Model/embeddings HTTP transport reads the whole response body with no size cap
findings.detail: `_httpx_transport` (http_provider.py:519-524) and the embeddings transport (app/adapters/embeddings/http.py:72-75) call `resp.json()` on an httpx response with no max-size guard. httpx imposes no default response-size limit. For connections the response endpoint is tenant-controlled (the connection URL).
findings.failure_scenario: A tenant points a connection (or a DNS-rebind, see r2-01) at an endpoint that streams a multi-gigabyte body; `resp.json()` buffers it entirely into the worker's memory, OOM-killing the pod and taking down answering for every tenant on that replica. Only the request timeout bounds it, and a slow large body can stay under the timeout.
findings.fix: Set an httpx response/read byte limit (stream and enforce a max content length, reject over-size with a ModelError) on both transports.

findings.title: Neutral transcript is passed through with caller-supplied roles, allowing extra system turns to be injected past the connection's own system prompt
findings.detail: `_messages_payload` (http_provider.py:292-382) trusts each turn's `role`. In the chat shape (line 344-345) any turn whose role is not assistant/tool is appended verbatim, including role=='system'; in generate/anthropic shapes roles are coerced but content is still relayed unfiltered. `_normalize_messages` (connections.py:215-223) passes a caller list straight through with no role/shape validation. Only the connection's own system_prompt is guaranteed first.
findings.failure_scenario: An internal caller (or an end-user message it relays that reaches the transcript with an attacker-influenced role) inserts an additional {'role':'system', 'content': '...ignore prior instructions / call tool X with tenant Y...'} turn. Combined with tool-calling, this widens the model's instruction surface beyond the connection's fixed guardrail prompt. Marked speculative because roles are normally set by the trusted relaying service.
findings.fix: Validate/whitelist transcript roles at the seam (only user/assistant/tool allowed; reject or downgrade caller-supplied 'system' turns) in `_normalize_messages`.

findings.title: Conversation title is stored in plaintext while message bodies are encrypted
findings.detail: `ConversationStore.start` stores `title=title[:120]` in plaintext on the conversation row (conversations.py:126-129) and re-writes it plaintext on every add (line 146-148), whereas message content goes through `MessageCrypto.encrypt` (line 144). A conversation title is typically the first user utterance, which the module's own docstring flags as carrying identifiers ('why was invoice 8891 for +9665... not paid'). ASSISTANT_ENCRYPT_MESSAGES therefore does not protect the title. (Note: start()/add() are not currently wired to any route, so impact is latent until conversation writing is enabled.)
findings.failure_scenario: Once conversation creation is wired, a stolen database dump yields plaintext titles containing phone numbers / invoice ids / names for every conversation, defeating the at-rest encryption the service advertises for conversation content.
findings.fix: Encrypt the title with the same MessageCrypto, or derive a non-PII title, and never persist raw user text unencrypted when ASSISTANT_ENCRYPT_MESSAGES is on.

findings.title: invoke accepts unbounded max_tokens and an unbounded messages transcript
findings.detail: `ConnInvokeIn` (internal.py:396-407) bounds prompt to 100000 chars but sets no ceiling on `max_tokens` (ge=0 only) and no length/size cap on the `messages` list. `invoke_conversation` forwards both to the provider.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller sets max_tokens to a very large value or supplies an enormous messages transcript, inflating the upstream provider cost billed to the connection's credential and the outbound payload size, with no service-side guard.
findings.fix: Clamp max_tokens to a configured ceiling and cap the number/total size of transcript turns.

findings.title: No caps<=granter check: a tenant admin can grant capabilities it does not itself hold (default-open allowlist)
findings.detail: _guard_caps() (app/api/v1/authz.py:47-66) is the ONLY gate a tenant-scoped `authz.manage` caller passes when creating a role, updating a role, or setting a subject's direct capabilities. It calls forbidden_caps() (app/core/cap_policy.py:27-58), which rejects a cap ONLY if it (a) matches a denied prefix (`platform.` by default), (b) is a reserved cap (`authz.manage` by default), or (c) is outside a configured allowlist. The allowlist ships EMPTY (config.py:308 AUTHZ_TENANT_ASSIGNABLE_CAPS=""), and an empty allowlist is treated as 'no positive restriction' (cap_policy.py:52 `bool(allowlist) and c not in allowlist`). There is NO comparison against the caller's own capability set (grep confirms principal.caps is only consulted for the platform.authz/operator branch). So with the shipped default config, a caller holding only `authz.manage` can mint a role containing high-value caps it has never held (e.g. `wallet.payout`, `billing.refund`, `compliance.erase`) and assign it to itself via PUT /subjects/{subject}/roles, then obtain those caps in its next token from GET /internal/authz/effective (_subject_caps resolves assignment role IDs).
findings.failure_scenario: A tenant owner is provisioned with role caps=[authz.manage]. They POST /api/v1/roles {name:'x', capabilities:['wallet.payout','billing.refund']} (passes: neither is platform.* nor authz.manage, allowlist empty). They PUT /api/v1/subjects/<self>/roles {roles:['x']}. Identity's next /internal/authz/effective mints them a token carrying wallet.payout. They now drain wallet funds and issue refunds they were never granted — capabilities strictly above their own.
findings.fix: Enforce caps<=granter for a tenant-scoped caller: reject any assigned capability not present in principal.caps (with wildcard expansion consistent with the RBAC engine), independent of the allowlist. Keep the denylist/allowlist as an additional narrowing. Alternatively ship a non-empty curated AUTHZ_TENANT_ASSIGNABLE_CAPS default and add a boot guard that refuses self-service tenant role management while the allowlist is empty.

findings.title: ALLOW-policy vector inherits the same default-open gap: tenant admin can grant sensitive actions tenant-wide
findings.detail: _guard_policy() (app/api/v1/authz.py:69-88) correctly refuses wildcard action/resource for a tenant caller and runs the action through _guard_caps([action]). But because _guard_caps is default-open (see authz-r2-01) and does not compare against the caller's own caps, a tenant `authz.manage` holder can create {effect:'allow', action:'wallet.payout', resource:'wallet:*-but-not-literal-*'} style policies for any concrete, non-platform action. The CombinedEngine (app/adapters/policy/combined.py:16-25) treats a matching ABAC allow (AbacEngine, empty condition always holds) as equivalent to holding the capability, so the policy grants that action to any subject in the tenant whose request matches — a capability grant by another name, above the granter's own power.
findings.failure_scenario: Tenant admin (caps=[authz.manage]) POSTs /api/v1/policies {effect:'allow', action:'compliance.erase', resource:'subject:x'}. resource is not '*', action is not platform.*/authz.manage, allowlist empty -> accepted. Any request for compliance.erase on that resource now allows, granting an action the admin never held.
findings.fix: Same root fix as authz-r2-01: gate the policy's action (and ideally resource scope) against the caller's own effective capabilities, not merely the denylist. Consider also refusing broad non-'*' resource globs (e.g. containing '?' or prefix matches) for tenant callers.

findings.title: platform.* denial depends entirely on a mutable config prefix with no boot guard
findings.detail: The 'safe by default' claim in cap_policy.py rests on AUTHZ_TENANT_DENIED_CAP_PREFIXES containing 'platform.' (config.py:301) and AUTHZ_TENANT_DENIED_CAPS containing 'authz.manage' (config.py:304). Both are plain env strings with no validator/boot guard asserting the platform. prefix (or authz.manage) is present. An operator who sets AUTHZ_TENANT_DENIED_CAP_PREFIXES="" (e.g. to add a different prefix and fat-fingering it, or clearing it) silently removes the platform.* wall for every tenant-scoped caller, turning authz-r2-01 into a full platform-privilege escalation with zero startup warning.
findings.failure_scenario: Operator edits the denied-prefixes env to add a new prefix but leaves it empty/typo'd. Service boots healthy. A tenant admin now assigns platform.authz to itself via POST /api/v1/roles + PUT /subjects/self/roles, becoming a platform operator across all tenants.
findings.fix: Add an assert in Settings (like assert_pii_config_ok) that refuses to start in production unless authz_tenant_denied_cap_prefixes contains 'platform.' and authz_tenant_denied_caps contains 'authz.manage' (or an explicit override flag acknowledges the risk).

findings.title: set_roles records the audit event under principal.tenant, not the resolved write tenant
findings.detail: In set_roles (app/api/v1/authz.py:240-256) the write-ahead audit at line 248-253 uses tenant=principal.tenant, but the assignment is actually written to tenant=_op_tenant(principal) computed at line 254. For a platform operator whose token carries no tenant claim, principal.tenant is None while _op_tenant() resolves to 'global' (app/api/v1/authz.py:34-37), so the assignment.roles_assigned event is recorded under a tenant (None) different from where the grant landed ('global'). This is exactly the class of tenant-mislabeling the create_role handler was explicitly fixed for (see its comment at lines 128-130: 'Record under the tenant the role is ACTUALLY written to'), but the fix was not applied here.
findings.failure_scenario: A platform operator (no tenant claim) assigns roles; the grant lands in 'global' but the immutable audit row is stamped with an empty/None tenant, so a later 'who was granted what in global' query misses the event.
findings.fix: Compute tenant = _op_tenant(principal) BEFORE the audit call and pass that tenant to auditor.record(), matching create_role/update_role.

findings.title: bootstrap_tenant TOCTOU: concurrent retries can create duplicate same-name roles
findings.detail: bootstrap_tenant (app/api/internal.py:136-195) reads existing roles into a dict keyed by name (line 172), then for each requested role either updates the matched id or creates a new one (lines 175-184). There is no uniqueness constraint on (tenant, name) in the datastore and no lock, so two concurrent bootstrap calls for the same fresh tenant (a provisioning saga retried, or fired twice) can both observe name absent and both create() a role with the same name and distinct ids. RoleStore.by_name (app/core/stores.py:25-38) then returns whichever the store's (name asc, id/key) ordering yields first, so subsequent name-based resolution becomes nondeterministic, and the owner may be assigned one id while later name lookups resolve the other.
findings.failure_scenario: Provisioning saga retries bootstrap concurrently. Two 'owner-admin' roles are created with the same name. The owner is assigned role id A; a later name-keyed reconcile updates role id B's capabilities, leaving the owner on the stale role A.
findings.fix: Make bootstrap idempotency robust to concurrency: enforce a unique (collection,tenant,name) at the store level for roles, or perform create-if-absent through an atomic upsert keyed on (tenant,name), or serialize bootstrap per tenant. At minimum, de-duplicate by name after the read and before create.

findings.title: internal_effective `roles` query and CheckIn.extra_caps are unbounded, each driving per-item store/cache lookups
findings.detail: GET /internal/authz/effective (app/api/internal.py:83-108) accepts `roles` as an unbounded comma-separated query string; each token drives a _resolve_role() -> store find/get plus a cache round-trip in _role_caps (app/core/authz_service.py:194-219). Similarly CheckIn.extra_caps (app/api/internal.py:31) has no max_items. A caller (or a compromised internal peer) passing tens of thousands of role refs forces a proportional number of datastore reads on a single-worker event loop. Internal-token gated, so exposure is limited to authenticated service callers, but there is no per-request fan-out cap.
findings.failure_scenario: A buggy or hostile internal caller issues GET /internal/authz/effective?roles=<50000 comma-separated names>. Each unresolved name (REJECT mode still evaluates them until the first miss, IGNORE mode evaluates all) triggers store lookups, saturating the DB pool and stalling the PDP hot path for every tenant.
findings.fix: Bound the number of roles parsed per request (e.g. cap at a configured limit and 400 beyond it) and add max_items to CheckIn.extra_caps and the roles input.

findings.title: PAP admin gate ignores wildcard caps while the PDP honors them (fail-closed, but inconsistent)
findings.detail: require_any_capability (app/api/authz.py:32-41) uses exact membership (`c in held`), so a principal with caps=['*'] or ['platform.*'] is REFUSED at every PAP route, whereas the RbacEngine (app/adapters/policy/rbac.py:9-16) treats '*' and 'x.*' as granting. A genuine super-admin token expressed with a wildcard cannot administer authz. This is fail-closed (safe) but is a latent surprise: the service's own authorization does not follow the wildcard semantics it hands out to the rest of the platform, and an operator may 'grant' platform.* to an admin and find them locked out of authz management.
findings.failure_scenario: Operator mints an admin token with caps=['*'] expecting full access; every /api/v1/roles call returns 403, and the misconfiguration reads as a bug rather than a policy choice.
findings.fix: Either document that PAP gates require the exact platform.authz/authz.manage strings, or apply the same cap_matches() wildcard expansion used by the RBAC engine so wildcard admins behave consistently.

findings.title: refund() is a get-then-put TOCTOU → concurrent double refund at the gateway
findings.detail: refund() has no idempotency claim and no atomic counter (unlike settle()). The outstanding guard reads inv.refunded_minor, then calls gw.refund(), then does inv.refunded_minor = read + amt.
findings.failure_scenario: Two concurrent refund calls on a paid invoice both read refunded_minor=0, both pass the >outstanding check, both call gw.refund() — customer refunded twice; one write lost so refunded_minor understates.
findings.fix: Claim self._idempo.claim(f'refund:{payment_id}:{amt}') and/or accumulate refunded_minor via incr_if_below bounded by total_minor; call gateway only for the delta that atomically applied.

findings.title: wallet top-up gateway idempotency key omits fund; app claim key includes it
findings.detail: Gateway key f'topup:{tenant}:{payment_token}:{total}' (no fund) at :833 vs app claim key f'topup:{tenant}:{payment_token}:{total}:{fund}' at :848.
findings.failure_scenario: Same token+amount top-up to fund A then fund B in the gateway idempotency window: gateway dedupes (charges once, returns ok for B) but app claim differs (fund B) so it mints a second invoice and credits fund B — charged once, two funds credited (free stored value). Symmetric double-charge if a gateway ignores idempotency_key.
findings.fix: Include fund in the gateway idempotency key so both keys describe the same operation identity.

findings.title: consolidated active-mode groups wallet-pinned + card subs into one invoice charged to one method
findings.detail: _group_gateway_key returns '' for all subs in active mode; _charge_from_wallet opts in on sub.payment_gateway=='wallet' independent of mode, so a wallet sub and card subs land in one consolidated group charged via claimed[0][0].
findings.failure_scenario: renewal_invoice_mode=consolidated + renewal_gateway_mode=active + wallet_renewal_enabled: whole group debited from wallet (or wallet sub charged to a card) depending on claimed[0]; wallet-insufficient suspends the whole group.
findings.fix: Include the wallet opt-in in the grouping key regardless of mode (group wallet subs separately), or refuse to consolidate wallet-pinned subs.

findings.title: reverse_settlement re-introduces the lost-update on settled_minor/status settle() avoids
findings.detail: Reversal writes inv.settled_minor = settled_after and inv.status = 'open' from a read value — exactly what settle() refuses at :1561-1567.
findings.failure_scenario: Reversal racing a settlement (or two reversals): last writer wins with a stale value; persisted inv.status/settled_minor diverge from the atomic counter that invoice_state() uses; dunning/finance read the row.
findings.fix: In reversal don't write settled_minor from a read; derive status from the counter, or gate the row write behind the closed:{inv.id} claim.

findings.title: run_overage aggregates the wrong period window relative to run_cycle's period advance
findings.detail: run_overage reads sub.current_period_start/end (already advanced by run_cycle) and keys overage:{sub}:{period} off current_period_start.
findings.failure_scenario: If run_cycle advances the period before run_overage in the sweep, overage aggregates the next (empty) window and bills zero (revenue leak); across boundaries the same usage can fall into two overage keys.
findings.fix: Bill overage against an explicit closed period captured before the advance, keyed to that period.

findings.title: usage consume _IDEMPO retry-cache non-atomic: concurrent same-key double-fire over-meters
findings.detail: The incr_if_below counter is atomic but the _IDEMPO get/put straddle it (accepted-risk, documented). Round-1 documented exemption; re-affirmed here.
findings.failure_scenario: Two concurrent deliveries of the same at-least-once event with the same idempotency_key both miss prior, both pass incr_if_below, both count — for allow_and_bill this bills the duplicate as real overage.
findings.fix: Claim the idempotency key atomically (CAS put-if-absent) before the counter increment; refund the counter if the claim loses. Or re-affirm the accepted risk.

findings.title: partial refund sets pay.status='refunded', blocking a later full-refund webhook from voiding
findings.detail: Any partial refund() sets pay.status='refunded'; _apply_outcome's 'refund' branch is guarded by pay.status != 'refunded' at :2065-2081, so a later gateway refund webhook is skipped.
findings.failure_scenario: Partial 30% refund via API, then merchant refunds remaining 70% at the gateway; webhook skipped; invoice never flips to void, refunded_minor stuck at 30%, grant not fully clawed back.
findings.fix: Decide refund effect from amount-based inv.refunded_minor vs total, not a binary pay.status.

findings.title: Public operator Embedded-Signup route never binds phone_number_id -> tenant (diverges from the internal twin)
findings.detail: The internal onboarding route (app/api/internal.py:360-377) and the register route (internal.py:1002-1015) both call WhatsAppNumberIndex.bind(phone_number_id, tenant) after a successful exchange and audit a CONFLICT on first-wins collision. The human/operator route whatsapp_embedded_signup() calls onboarding.exchange() (operator.py:196-198) and returns the result WITHOUT ever binding the number in the routing index and without any conflict check. WhatsAppOnboarding.exchange() itself (app/core/whatsapp_onboarding.py:99-129) only writes the sealed credentials; it does not touch WhatsAppNumberIndex. Grep confirms operator.py contains no bind/number_index reference at all.
findings.failure_scenario: A shop onboarded through the operator UI has WHATSAPP_ACCESS_TOKEN/PHONE_NUMBER_ID/WABA_ID stored but wa_number_index has NO row for its phone_number_id. Every subsequent inbound webhook (app/api/webhooks.py:128-132 and _tenant_of) resolves tenant_of(phone_id) -> None -> tenant="", so inbound messages, message_echoes, history and contacts are recorded and fanned out with an empty tenant: the shop's customer replies are unattributable and a fast-path bus consumer cannot tell whose message it is. Separately, because this path skips the first-wins CONFLICT check, two tenants onboarding the same number via the operator route both silently 'succeed' with no whatsapp.number_bind_conflict audit trail -- the exact silent-collision gap round 1 closed on the internal path is still open on the human path.
findings.fix: After a successful exchange in whatsapp_embedded_signup(), call WhatsAppNumberIndex(datastore).bind(body.phone_number_id, body.tenant) and audit whatsapp.number_bind_conflict on CONFLICT, mirroring internal.py:360-377. Better: move the bind+conflict-audit inside WhatsAppOnboarding.exchange() (or a shared helper) so no onboarding entrypoint can forget it.

findings.title: WhatsApp marketing opt-out is stored and enforced GLOBALLY by phone, not per-tenant
findings.detail: apply_user_preferences() writes the opt-out via prefs.apply_event_opt_out(wa_id, event, ...) keyed only by the customer's wa_id (whatsapp_optout.py:44). The webhook value carries value.metadata.phone_number_id (resolvable to the owning tenant via WhatsAppNumberIndex) but it is discarded. The send path enforces it the same way: notifier._wa_recipient_allows() (app/core/notifier.py:395-401) does prefs.get(recipient) keyed on the bare phone with no tenant. PreferenceStore.get/set (stores.py:56-62) is keyed by `user` only. So the opt-out record is one global row per phone number across the whole platform.
findings.failure_scenario: A customer messages Shop A's WhatsApp number 'Stop promotions'. Meta posts user_preferences for Shop A's phone_number_id. The service records marketing opt-out for that phone GLOBALLY. Shop B (a different tenant the same person is a consented customer of) now has its legitimate, consented marketing template sends to that number silently suppressed at notifier.py:113-115. One tenant's inbound opt-out cross-suppresses every other tenant's marketing to that recipient -- a tenant-isolation break (and an availability/revenue hit for the other shops), the inverse of the per-tenant idempotency reasoning already applied elsewhere in this service.
findings.fix: Scope the marketing opt-out by (tenant, phone). Resolve the tenant from value.metadata.phone_number_id in apply_user_preferences (or pass it through the webhook fan-out) and key the Preference row per-tenant (e.g. the same len(tenant)+'|'+phone scheme used by CoexistenceStore.record_contact and the idempotency key). Pass the tenant into _wa_recipient_allows on the send path so the check reads the same per-tenant key.

findings.title: Inbound-message and receipt catch-up feeds return ALL tenants' data (incl. customer PII/message bodies) to any internal-token holder, with no tenant filter
findings.detail: GET /whatsapp/inbound (internal.py:415-...) and GET /notifications/receipts (internal.py:401-412) call InboundStore.changed_since / DeliveryStore.changed_since, which query on a constant kind with NO tenant filter (stores.py:272-276, 187-196) and return the full row including message body, sender phone, tenant, etc. The default internal-caller driver is `shared` (a single flat bearer token, require_internal_token internal.py:67-95) with default-open policy, so every product service that holds the shared token can poll these endpoints and read every OTHER tenant's inbound WhatsApp messages and delivery metadata. There is no `tenant` query parameter to constrain the read.
findings.failure_scenario: A product service legitimately provisioned with the shared X-Internal-Token for its own tenant's onboarding polls GET /whatsapp/inbound and receives the raw inbound messages (customer phone numbers + message content) of every shop on the platform. A compromised or over-privileged internal caller exfiltrates cross-tenant customer PII. Marked SPECULATIVE because this is presented as a deliberate platform reconciliation feed and may be gated by deployment-time NetworkPolicy/per-caller RS256 policy; still, out of the box it is an all-tenant PII feed behind one shared secret.
findings.fix: Offer a tenant-scoped variant (accept a `tenant` param and push it into the find where-clause) and/or restrict these feeds via a named internal-policy allow-list rather than default-open, so only the platform reconciliation caller -- not every internal peer -- can read the cross-tenant feed.

findings.title: apply_receipt uses non-atomic read-modify-write on the delivery row; concurrent receipts can regress receipt_status
findings.detail: apply_receipt() reads the delivery via by_provider_message_id(), compares ts >= d.receipt_ts in Python, then puts the mutated row (stores.py:172-177). This is a get-then-put with no CAS/version pin, unlike the number-index bind that round 1 correctly hardened. The monotonic guarantee ('a later read is not overwritten by an out-of-order delivered') holds only within a single webhook POST where statuses are applied sequentially.
findings.failure_scenario: Meta delivers a 'delivered' status in one webhook POST and a 'read' status in a near-simultaneous retry/second POST for the same wamid. Both handlers read the delivery with receipt_ts=0, both pass the ts>=receipt_ts guard, and whichever put() lands last wins by wall-clock rather than by receipt timestamp -- so a 'delivered' put arriving after the 'read' put silently regresses the delivery snapshot from read back to delivered. The append-only _RECEIPTS event log stays correct (each state is its own row), so only the delivery.receipt_status projection is affected, which bounds the impact.
findings.fix: Make the receipt-status update a CAS/version-pinned or conditional update (only advance if the stored receipt_ts is still < ts), or accept the event log as source of truth and derive the snapshot from it. At minimum document that the delivery.receipt_status field is best-effort under concurrent receipts.

findings.title: Webhook accepts any correctly-signed body with no timestamp/nonce freshness check (replayable)
findings.detail: receive() verifies X-Hub-Signature-256 over the raw body (webhooks.py:210-212) but performs no freshness/replay check -- no timestamp window, no nonce/event-id de-dup at the webhook layer. A captured, validly-signed POST body replays cleanly through _fan_out.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker who observes a signed webhook body (e.g. via a logging/proxy leak) can re-POST it repeatedly; each replay re-emits the bus events. Impact is bounded because the durable stores are idempotent (InboundStore keyed by wamid, receipts keyed by a deterministic eid, opt-outs are last-writer-wins toggles), so replays converge to the same state; the residual risk is duplicate at-most-once bus events and, for opt-out toggles, re-application of a resume that a later stop should have won. Marked SPECULATIVE/low given the strong downstream idempotency.
findings.fix: If Meta supplies a per-event id/timestamp usable here, add a short freshness window and/or a webhook-level seen-id cache to reject stale replays before fan-out; otherwise document that idempotency at the stores is the intended replay defense.

findings.title: Send returns literal 'wamid:unparsed' sentinel as the provider_message_id join key on unparseable-but-accepted responses
findings.detail: _post() returns the string 'wamid:unparsed' when Meta accepts a send (2xx) but the body cannot be parsed for messages[0].id (meta.py:104-108). That sentinel is stored as the delivery's provider_message_id and is the join key receipts match on via DeliveryStore.by_provider_message_id (stores.py:154-160, limit=1).
findings.failure_scenario: If two different sends both hit the unparseable-body branch, both deliveries carry provider_message_id='wamid:unparsed'. A later receipt (unlikely, since a real receipt carries a real wamid, but a mis-shaped/status webhook or a future code path calling apply_receipt with the sentinel) would resolve by_provider_message_id('wamid:unparsed') to whichever single row the store returns, attributing a receipt to an arbitrary one of the colliding deliveries. Low likelihood because real receipts carry real wamids; flagged as a latent non-unique join key.
findings.fix: Return an empty wamid (falsey) on unparseable bodies and mark the delivery 'sent-without-id', or generate a unique local sentinel per send (e.g. 'wamid:unparsed:'+uuid) so the join key is never shared across deliveries.
